ARRAY.doc:
Arrays: mutable sequences of a fixed length, of any element type.

An array is indexed from 0; `update` changes an element in place, and two
arrays are equal only when they are the same array, whatever they hold. An
array of length 0 is still an array of its own, so `array (0, x) = array (0, x)` is `false`.

`VECTOR` is the immutable counterpart, and `vector` and `copyVec` convert
between the two. `ARRAY_SLICE` describes a stretch of an array without
copying it, and `ARRAY2` is the two-dimensional version.

**See also** `VECTOR`, `ARRAY_SLICE`, `ARRAY2`, `MONO_ARRAY`, `LIST`

> **Erratum** `ARRAY/array-spec`. The specification writes `eqtype 'a array = 'a array`, which the Definition does not allow as a specification; it is
written here as an abbreviation of the top-level `array`, which admits
equality whatever its element type is.

members.name: array
members.doc:
The type of arrays, the one of the top-level environment.

Two arrays are equal when they are the same array: equality is identity,
not a comparison of the elements.

members.name: vector
members.doc: The type of the vectors that `vector` and `copyVec` work with.

members.name: maxLen
members.doc:
The greatest length an array may have.

> **Implementation** `Array.maxLen/value`. 100000000, the same as
`Vector.maxLen`.

**Example** `maxLen = 100000000`

members.name: array
members.doc:
`array (n, x)` is a new array of `n` elements, each of them `x`.

**Raises** `Size` if `n < 0` or `n > maxLen`.

**Law** `sub (array (n, x), i) = x` for `0 <= i andalso i < n andalso n <= maxLen`, and it is run for `n` from `Arb.intRange (0, 1048576)`, as the
tester cannot hold a longer one

**Example** `vector (array (3, #"x")) = Vector.fromList [#"x", #"x", #"x"]`

**Counterexample** `sub (array (maxLen + 1, 0), 0) = 0`, for there is no
array so long.

members.name: fromList
members.doc:
`fromList l` is a new array of the elements of `l`, in order.

**Raises** `Size` if `l` is longer than `maxLen`.

**Law** `sub (fromList l, i) = List.nth (l, i)` for `0 <= i andalso i < List.length l`

**Example** `sub (fromList [10, 20, 30], 1) = 20`

members.name: tabulate
members.doc:
`tabulate (n, f)` is a new array of `f 0`, `f 1`, ..., `f (n - 1)`.

`f` is applied in order of increasing index.

**Raises** `Size` if `n < 0` or `n > maxLen`.

> **Reading** `Array.tabulate/Size-before-f`. The specification does not say
whether the length is checked before `f` is applied. It is: a length out
of range raises `Size` without applying `f` at all, so no effect of `f`
happens for an array that is never made.

**Law** `sub (tabulate (n, f), i) = f i` for `0 <= i andalso i < n andalso n <= maxLen`, when `f` has no effects, and it is run for `n` from
`Arb.intRange (0, 1024)`, as a longer one takes too long for `make check`

**Example** `vector (tabulate (4, fn i => i * i)) = Vector.fromList [0, 1, 4, 9]`

**Counterexample** `sub (tabulate (maxLen + 1, fn i => i), 0) = 0`, for there
is no array so long.

members.name: length
members.doc:
`length arr` is the number of elements of `arr`.

**Law** `length (fromList l) = List.length l`

**Example** `length (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = 3`

members.name: sub
members.doc:
`sub (arr, i)` is the element of `arr` at position `i`, counting from 0.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i >= length arr`.

**Example** `sub (fromList [#"a", #"b"], 1) = #"b"`

members.name: update
members.doc:
`update (arr, i, x)` puts `x` at position `i` of `arr`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i >= length arr`.

**Law** `(update (arr, i, x); sub (arr, i)) = x` for `0 <= i andalso i < length arr`

**Example** `let val a = array (3, 0) in update (a, 1, 5); foldr (op ::) [] a end = [0, 5, 0]`

members.name: vector
members.doc:
`vector arr` is an immutable vector of the elements of `arr`.

It is a copy: a later `update` of `arr` does not touch it.

**Law** `vector arr = Vector.tabulate (length arr, fn i => sub (arr, i))`

**Example** `vector (fromList [1, 2]) = Vector.fromList [1, 2]`

members.name: copy
members.spec: val copy : {src : 'a array, dst : 'a array, di : int} -> unit
members.doc:
`copy {src, dst, di}` copies the elements of `src` into `dst`, starting at position `di`.

`src` and `dst` may be the same array, and then `di` must be 0: an array
cannot hold itself at any other position, so any other `di` raises
`Subscript`, and at 0 the copy changes nothing. Two stretches of one array
that overlap are what `ArraySlice.copy` is for.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `di < 0` or `di + length src > length dst`, and
then nothing has been copied.

**Law** `(copy {src = src, dst = dst, di = di}; sub (dst, di + i)) = sub (src, i)` for `0 <= di andalso di <= length dst - length src andalso 0 <= i andalso i < length src andalso src <> dst`

**Example** `let val a = fromList [1, 2, 3, 4] in copy {src = a, dst = a, di = 0}; vector a end = Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3, 4]`

**Counterexample** `let val b = array (1, 0) in copy {src = fromList [1, 2], dst = b, di = 0}; sub (b, 0) end = 1`, for the source does not fit.

members.name: copyVec
members.spec: val copyVec : {src : 'a vector, dst : 'a array, di : int} -> unit
members.doc:
`copyVec {src, dst, di}` copies the elements of the vector `src` into `dst`, starting at position `di`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `di < 0` or `di + Vector.length src > length dst`,
and then nothing has been copied.

**Law** `(copyVec {src = v, dst = dst, di = di}; sub (dst, di + i)) = Vector.sub (v, i)` for `0 <= di andalso di <= length dst - Vector.length v andalso 0 <= i andalso i < Vector.length v`

**Example** `let val a = array (4, 0) in copyVec {src = Vector.fromList [1, 2], dst = a, di = 1}; vector a end = Vector.fromList [0, 1, 2, 0]`

**Counterexample** `let val b = array (1, 0) in copyVec {src = Vector.fromList [1, 2], dst = b, di = 0}; sub (b, 0) end = 1`, for the
source does not fit.

members.name: appi
members.doc:
`appi f arr` applies `f` to the index and the element of each position, from 0 up, for its effect.

**Example** `let val r = ref [] in appi (fn (i, x) => r := (i, x) :: !r) (fromList ["a", "b"]); !r end = [(1, "b"), (0, "a")]`

members.name: app
members.doc:
`app f arr` applies `f` to every element, from 0 up, for its effect.

**Law** `app f arr = appi (fn (_, x) => f x) arr`

**Example** `let val s = ref 0 in app (fn x => s := !s + x) (fromList [1, 2, 3]); !s end = 6`

members.name: modifyi
members.doc:
`modifyi f arr` replaces the element at each position by `f` of the index and that element.

The array is changed in place, from 0 up.

**Example** `let val a = fromList [10, 20, 30] in modifyi (fn (i, x) => x + i) a; vector a end = Vector.fromList [10, 21, 32]`

members.name: modify
members.doc:
`modify f arr` replaces every element by `f` of it, in place, from 0 up.

**Law** `modify f arr = modifyi (fn (_, x) => f x) arr`

**Example** `let val a = fromList [1, 2, 3] in modify (fn x => x * 2) a; vector a end = Vector.fromList [2, 4, 6]`

members.name: foldli
members.doc:
`foldli f init arr` combines the elements from the left, giving `f` the index as well.

**Example** `foldli (fn (i, x, acc) => (i, x) :: acc) [] (fromList ["a", "b"]) = [(1, "b"), (0, "a")]`

members.name: foldri
members.doc:
`foldri f init arr` combines the elements from the right, giving `f` the index as well.

**Example** `foldri (fn (i, x, acc) => (i, x) :: acc) [] (fromList ["a", "b"]) = [(0, "a"), (1, "b")]`

members.name: foldl
members.doc:
`foldl f init arr` combines the elements from the left, as `List.foldl` does.

**Law** `foldl f init arr = foldli (fn (_, x, acc) => f (x, acc)) init arr`

**Example** `foldl (op ::) [] (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = [3, 2, 1]`

members.name: foldr
members.doc:
`foldr f init arr` combines the elements from the right, as `List.foldr` does.

**Law** `foldr f init arr = foldri (fn (_, x, acc) => f (x, acc)) init arr`

**Example** `foldr (op ::) [] (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = [1, 2, 3]`

members.name: findi
members.doc:
`findi p arr` is `SOME (i, x)` for the first position whose index and element satisfy `p`, or `NONE`.

`p` is applied from 0 up, and not after the first position that
satisfies it.

**Example** `findi (fn (i, x) => i > 0 andalso x = 0) (fromList [0, 5, 0]) = SOME (2, 0)`

members.name: find
members.doc:
`find p arr` is `SOME x` for the first element that satisfies `p`, or `NONE`.

**Law** `find p arr = Option.map #2 (findi (fn (_, x) => p x) arr)`

**Example** `find (fn x => x > 1) (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = SOME 2`

members.name: exists
members.doc:
`exists p arr` is `true` when some element satisfies `p`; it stops at the first that does.

**Law** `exists p arr = isSome (find p arr)`

**Example** `exists (fn x => x > 2) (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = true`

members.name: all
members.doc:
`all p arr` is `true` when every element satisfies `p`; it stops at the first that does not.

**Law** `all p arr = not (exists (not o p) arr)`

**Example** `all (fn x => x > 0) (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = true`

members.name: collate
members.spec: val collate : ('a * 'a -> order) -> 'a array * 'a array -> order
members.doc:
`collate cmp (a, b)` compares the elements of two arrays lexicographically with `cmp`.

This compares what the arrays hold, where `=` compares which array it
is.

**Law** `collate cmp (a, b) = List.collate cmp (foldr (op ::) [] a, foldr (op ::) [] b)`

**Example** `collate Int.compare (fromList [1, 2], fromList [1, 3]) = LESS`

ARRAY2.doc:
Two-dimensional arrays: mutable rectangles of elements, indexed by a row
and a column.

Rows and columns are counted from 0, and the first index is the row: `sub (arr, i, j)` is the element in row `i` and column `j`. An array of no rows
or no columns holds nothing but still has its dimensions.

The traversals take a region, a rectangle inside an array: its `base`,
the `row` and `col` it starts at, and how many rows and columns it covers,
where `NONE` means "to the edge". They also take a `traversal`, which says
whether they go along the rows or down the columns; that decides the order
the elements are visited in, and so what an effect sees.

**See also** `ARRAY`, `VECTOR`, `MONO_ARRAY2`

> **Erratum** `ARRAY2/sub-indices`. The specification's description of `sub`
says that "`i` gives the row index, and gives the column index"; the
second is `j`.

> **Erratum** `ARRAY2/sealed-and-equal-at-any-element`. The page asks for three
things that Standard ML cannot give together: it declares `structure Array2 :> ARRAY2`, it writes `eqtype 'a array`, and it says "Thus, the
type `ty array` admits equality even if `ty` does not". Any two hold; all
three cannot, because only the built-in type names of the language admit
equality whatever they hold -- `ref`, which the Definition names in
Section 4.4, and the `array` of the top level -- and no signature can
specify such a type name: through `eqtype 'a t`, a `ty t` admits equality
exactly when `ty` does, so an opaque seal makes a fresh type name and the
third clause fails at `real` and at a function type. The reading taken
here is that the seal and `eqtype 'a array` stand and the sentence does
not apply, as it is read in MLton and in SML/NJ: `Array2.array` is
abstract, and `real Array2.array` admits no equality. Poly/ML takes the
other reading and leaves the type a record, which lets a program reach
into it.

Why the sentence is taken to be a slip rather than a requirement: `ARRAY`
carries it too and has no defect there, because the top level pins `'a array` to `Array.array`, so that type \*is\* the built-in and the seal
settles nothing. `Array2` is optional and has no such anchor -- no system
has a top-level `'a array2` \-- so its seal bites. The paragraph it sits in
opens "As with 1-dimensional arrays", which is how adapted text reads;
`VECTOR` writes `eqtype 'a vector` and says nothing of the kind, so the
sentence is not boilerplate attached to every equality type; and
`MONO_ARRAY2` has no defect at all, because its `eqtype array` is
monomorphic and a record over a built-in array satisfies it. The
monomorphic two-dimensional arrays therefore do admit equality whatever
they hold, and are built on the implementation under the seal.

**See also** `MONO_ARRAY2`, `ARRAY`

members.name: array
members.doc:
The type of two-dimensional arrays.

Two are equal when they are the same array, as for `Array.array`.

members.name: region
members.spec:
type 'a region = {base : 'a array,
                  row : int,
                  col : int,
                  nrows : int option,
                  ncols : int option}
members.doc:
A rectangle inside an array: where it starts and how far it reaches.

`NONE` for `nrows` or `ncols` means "as far as the array goes". A region
is valid when it lies inside its base, and an empty one is valid too, so
a region that starts at the edge and covers nothing is allowed and
traverses nothing.

> **Reading** `Array2.region/Subscript-not-Overflow`. Whether a region lies
inside its array is decided without a sum that could overflow, so a region
whose `row + nrows` is no `int` raises `Subscript` and never `Overflow`.
`appi`, `foldi` and `modifyi` find that out before `f` is applied to
anything, so a bad region changes nothing.

how many columns, or NONE for all that are left

members.name: traversal
members.doc: Which way a traversal goes.

members.name: array
members.doc:
`array (r, c, x)` is a new array of `r` rows and `c` columns, every element `x`.

**Raises** `Size` if `r < 0`, `c < 0`, or the array would be too large.

> **Implementation** `Array2.array/Size`. How large is too large is not
fixed: an array is too large when the number of its elements is no
`int`, or when it exceeds what an array can hold.

**Law** `sub (array (r, c, x), i, j) = x` for `0 <= i andalso i < r andalso 0 <= j andalso j < c andalso r <= Array.maxLen div c`, and it is run for `r`
from `Arb.intRange (0, 1024)` and `c` from `Arb.intRange (0, 1024)`, as
the tester cannot hold a larger one

**Example** `dimensions (array (2, 3, 0)) = (2, 3)`

**Counterexample** `sub (array (Array.maxLen, 2, 0), 0, 0) = 0`, for there is
no array so large.

members.name: fromList
members.doc:
`fromList rows` is a new array of the lists of `rows`, one row each.

**Raises** `Size` if the lists are not all of one length, or if the array
would be too large.

**Law** `sub (fromList rows, i, j) = List.nth (List.nth (rows, i), j)` for `0 <= i andalso i < nRows (fromList rows) andalso 0 <= j andalso j < nCols (fromList rows)`

**Example** `let val a = fromList [[1, 2], [3, 4]] in (sub (a, 1, 0), dimensions a) end = (3, (2, 2))`

members.name: tabulate
members.spec: val tabulate : traversal -> int * int * (int * int -> 'a) -> 'a array
members.doc:
`tabulate trv (r, c, f)` is a new array of `r` rows and `c` columns whose element at `(i, j)` is `f (i, j)`.

`f` is applied in the order that `trv` gives.

**Raises** `Size` if `r < 0`, `c < 0` or the array would be too large.

> **Reading** `Array2.tabulate/Size-before-f`. The specification does not say
whether the dimensions are checked before `f` is applied. They are: an
array that is too large, or has a negative dimension, raises `Size`
without applying `f` at all.

> **Reading** `Array2.tabulate/traversal-order`. "Initialized in traversal
order" is read as: `f (0, 0)` is applied first whichever traversal is
asked for, and its result fills the array before the rest is
computed.

**Law** `sub (tabulate trv (r, c, f), i, j) = f (i, j)` for `0 <= i andalso i < r andalso 0 <= j andalso j < c andalso r <= Array.maxLen div c`, when
`f` has no effects, and it is run for `r` from `Arb.intRange (0, 32)` and
`c` from `Arb.intRange (0, 32)`, as a larger one takes too long for `make check`

**Example** `row (tabulate RowMajor (2, 3, fn (i, j) => 10 * i + j), 1) = Vector.fromList [10, 11, 12]`

**Counterexample** `sub (tabulate RowMajor (Array.maxLen, 2, fn _ => 0), 0, 0) = 0`, for there is no array so large.

members.name: sub
members.doc:
`sub (arr, i, j)` is the element of `arr` in row `i` and column `j`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i` or `j` is outside the array.

**Example** `sub (fromList [[1, 2], [3, 4]], 0, 1) = 2`

members.name: update
members.spec: val update : 'a array * int * int * 'a -> unit
members.doc:
`update (arr, i, j, x)` puts `x` in row `i` and column `j` of `arr`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i` or `j` is outside the array.

**Law** `(update (arr, i, j, x); sub (arr, i, j)) = x` for `0 <= i andalso i < nRows arr andalso 0 <= j andalso j < nCols arr`

**Example** `let val a = array (2, 2, 0) in update (a, 1, 0, 7); row (a, 1) end = Vector.fromList [7, 0]`

members.name: dimensions
members.doc:
`dimensions arr` is the pair of the number of rows and the number of columns.

**Example** `dimensions (fromList [[1, 2, 3]]) = (1, 3)`

members.name: nCols
members.doc:
`nCols arr` is the number of columns.

**Law** `nCols arr = #2 (dimensions arr)`

**Example** `nCols (fromList [[1, 2, 3]]) = 3`

members.name: nRows
members.doc:
`nRows arr` is the number of rows.

**Law** `nRows arr = #1 (dimensions arr)`

**Example** `nRows (fromList [[1, 2, 3]]) = 1`

members.name: row
members.doc:
`row (arr, i)` is a vector of the elements of row `i`, left to right.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i` is no row of `arr`.

**Law** `row (arr, i) = Vector.tabulate (nCols arr, fn j => sub (arr, i, j))`
for `0 <= i andalso i < nRows arr`

**Example** `row (fromList [[1, 2], [3, 4]], 1) = Vector.fromList [3, 4]`

members.name: column
members.doc:
`column (arr, j)` is a vector of the elements of column `j`, top to bottom.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `j` is no column of `arr`.

**Law** `column (arr, j) = Vector.tabulate (nRows arr, fn i => sub (arr, i, j))` for `0 <= j andalso j < nCols arr`

**Example** `column (fromList [[1, 2], [3, 4]], 1) = Vector.fromList [2, 4]`

members.name: copy
members.spec: val copy : {src : 'a region, dst : 'a array, dst_row : int, dst_col : int} -> unit
members.doc:
`copy {src, dst, dst_row, dst_col}` copies the region `src` into `dst`, with its top left corner at `(dst_row, dst_col)`.

The source and the destination may be one array and may overlap: every
element arrives as it was before the copy began.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `src` is not a valid region, or if it does not
fit into `dst` at that corner.

> **Reading** `Array2.copy/Subscript-dst-nothing-row-beyond`. The place the
region is copied to must be inside `dst` even when the region is empty,
so a corner outside `dst` raises although nothing would be copied.

**Example** `let val a = fromList [[1, 2], [3, 4]] in copy {src = {base = a, row = 0, col = 0, nrows = SOME 1, ncols = NONE}, dst = a, dst_row = 1, dst_col = 0}; row (a, 1) end = Vector.fromList [1, 2]`

members.name: appi
members.spec: val appi : traversal -> (int * int * 'a -> unit) -> 'a region -> unit
members.doc:
`appi trv f reg` applies `f` to the row, the column and the element of each position of the region, in the order `trv` gives.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `reg` is not a valid region.

> **Reading** `Array2.appi/nothing-rows-at-the-end`. "0 \<= \#row reg \<=
nRows" allows a region to begin at the edge of the array: such a region
and one of no rows or no columns are valid, and traverse nothing.

**Example** `let val r = ref [] in appi ColMajor (fn (i, j, _) => r := (i, j) :: !r) {base = array (2, 2, 0), row = 0, col = 0, nrows = NONE, ncols = NONE}; !r end = [(1, 1), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, 0)]`

members.name: app
members.spec: val app : traversal -> ('a -> unit) -> 'a array -> unit
members.doc:
`app trv f arr` applies `f` to every element of `arr`, in the order `trv` gives, for its effect.

**Law** `app trv f arr = appi trv (fn (_, _, x) => f x) {base = arr, row = 0, col = 0, nrows = NONE, ncols = NONE}`

**Example** `let val r = ref [] in app ColMajor (fn x => r := x :: !r) (fromList [[1, 2], [3, 4]]); !r end = [4, 2, 3, 1]`

members.name: foldi
members.doc:
`foldi trv f init reg` combines the elements of the region, giving `f` the row and the column as well.

The elements are combined in the order `trv` gives, the first with
`init`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `reg` is not a valid region.

**Example** `foldi RowMajor (fn (i, j, x, acc) => (i, j, x) :: acc) [] {base = fromList [[1, 2], [3, 4]], row = 1, col = 0, nrows = NONE, ncols = NONE} = [(1, 1, 4), (1, 0, 3)]`

members.name: fold
members.doc:
`fold trv f init arr` combines every element of `arr`, in the order `trv` gives.

**Law** `fold trv f init arr = foldi trv (fn (_, _, x, acc) => f (x, acc)) init {base = arr, row = 0, col = 0, nrows = NONE, ncols = NONE}`

**Example** `fold RowMajor (op ::) [] (fromList [[1, 2], [3, 4]]) = [4, 3, 2, 1]`

**Example** `fold ColMajor (op ::) [] (fromList [[1, 2], [3, 4]]) = [4, 2, 3, 1]`

members.name: modifyi
members.spec: val modifyi : traversal -> (int * int * 'a -> 'a) -> 'a region -> unit
members.doc:
`modifyi trv f reg` replaces each element of the region by `f` of its row, its column and that element.

The array is changed in place, in the order `trv` gives.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `reg` is not a valid region.

**Example** `let val a = fromList [[1, 2], [3, 4]] in modifyi RowMajor (fn (i, _, x) => x + 10 * i) {base = a, row = 0, col = 1, nrows = NONE, ncols = NONE}; column (a, 1) end = Vector.fromList [2, 14]`

members.name: modify
members.doc:
`modify trv f arr` replaces every element of `arr` by `f` of it, in the order `trv` gives.

**Law** `modify trv f arr = modifyi trv (fn (_, _, x) => f x) {base = arr, row = 0, col = 0, nrows = NONE, ncols = NONE}`

**Example** `let val a = fromList [[1, 2], [3, 4]] in modify RowMajor (fn x => x * x) a; row (a, 1) end = Vector.fromList [9, 16]`

ARRAY_SLICE.doc:
A stretch of an array, without a copy of it: a base array and a start and
a length inside it.

What `VECTOR_SLICE` is to a vector, this is to an array: a way to hand
part of a sequence to a function for nothing. A slice is a window on the
array, not a copy of it, so `update` through the slice changes the array,
and a change to the array is seen through the slice.

Positions inside a slice are counted from its own start.

**See also** `ARRAY`, `VECTOR_SLICE`, `MONO_ARRAY_SLICE`

members.name: slice
members.doc: The type of slices of an array.

members.name: length
members.doc:
`length sl` is the number of elements of `sl`.

**Example** `length (slice (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3, 4], 1, SOME 2)) = 2`

members.name: sub
members.doc:
`sub (sl, i)` is the element of `sl` at position `i`, counting from the start of the slice.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i >= length sl`.

**Law** `sub (slice (arr, i, NONE), k) = Array.sub (arr, i + k)` for `0 <= i andalso i < Array.length arr andalso 0 <= k andalso k < Array.length arr - i`

**Example** `sub (slice (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3, 4], 1, NONE), 0) = 2`

**Counterexample** `sub (slice (Array.fromList [1, 2], ~1, NONE), 1) = 1`,
for a slice cannot start before its array.

members.name: update
members.doc:
`update (sl, i, x)` puts `x` at position `i` of `sl`, and so of the array it is a slice of.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i >= length sl`.

**Law** `(update (sl, i, x); sub (sl, i)) = x` for `0 <= i andalso i < length sl`

**Example** `let val a = Array.fromList [1, 2, 3] in update (slice (a, 1, NONE), 0, 9); Array.vector a end = Vector.fromList [1, 9, 3]`

members.name: full
members.doc:
`full arr` is the whole of `arr` as a slice: `slice (arr, 0, NONE)`.

**Law** `base (full arr) = (arr, 0, Array.length arr)`

**Example** `length (full (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3])) = 3`

members.name: slice
members.spec: val slice : 'a Array.array * int * int option -> 'a slice
members.doc:
`slice (arr, i, NONE)` is the stretch of `arr` from position `i` to its end, and `slice (arr, i, SOME n)` the `n` elements from `i`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i > Array.length arr`, or, with `SOME n`, if `n < 0` or `i + n > Array.length arr`.

**Law** `base (slice (arr, i, SOME n)) = (arr, i, n)` for `0 <= i andalso i <= Array.length arr andalso 0 <= n andalso n <= Array.length arr - i`

**Example** `vector (slice (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3, 4], 1, SOME 2)) = Vector.fromList [2, 3]`

> **Reading** `ArraySlice.slice/Subscript-not-Overflow`. When `i + n` is no
`int` the slice does not exist, and `Subscript` says so, never `Overflow`;
`subslice`, `copy` and `copyVec` are the same with their sums, and so are
the slices of the monomorphic arrays.

members.name: subslice
members.spec: val subslice : 'a slice * int * int option -> 'a slice
members.doc:
`subslice (sl, i, NONE)` is the stretch of `sl` from position `i` on, and `subslice (sl, i, SOME n)` the `n` elements from `i`.

The bounds are those of `sl`, not of the array it is a slice of.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i > length sl`, or, with `SOME n`, if
`n < 0` or `i + n > length sl`.

**Law** `sub (subslice (sl, i, NONE), k) = sub (sl, i + k)` for `0 <= i andalso i < length sl andalso 0 <= k andalso k < length sl - i`

**Example** `vector (subslice (slice (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3, 4], 1, NONE), 1, SOME 1)) = Vector.fromList [3]`

**Counterexample** `sub (subslice (full (Array.fromList [1, 2]), ~1, NONE), 1) = 1`, for a subslice cannot start before its slice.

members.name: base
members.spec: val base : 'a slice -> 'a Array.array * int * int
members.doc:
`base sl` is the triple of the array that `sl` is a stretch of, where it starts in that array, and how long it is.

**Example** `let val (_, i, n) = base (slice (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3, 4], 1, SOME 2)) in (i, n) end = (1, 2)`

members.name: vector
members.doc:
`vector sl` is an immutable vector of the elements of `sl`, which is a copy.

**Law** `vector sl = Vector.tabulate (length sl, fn i => sub (sl, i))`

**Example** `vector (slice (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3], 1, NONE)) = Vector.fromList [2, 3]`

members.name: copy
members.spec: val copy : {src : 'a slice, dst : 'a Array.array, di : int} -> unit
members.doc:
`copy {src, dst, di}` copies the elements of the slice `src` into the array `dst`, starting at position `di`.

The slice may be a stretch of `dst` itself and the two may overlap:
every element arrives as it was before the copy began.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `di < 0` or `di + length src > Array.length dst`,
and then nothing has been copied.

**Example** `let val a = Array.fromList [1, 2, 3, 4] in copy {src = slice (a, 0, SOME 3), dst = a, di = 1}; Array.vector a end = Vector.fromList [1, 1, 2, 3]`

members.name: copyVec
members.spec: val copyVec : {src : 'a VectorSlice.slice, dst : 'a Array.array, di : int} -> unit
members.doc:
`copyVec {src, dst, di}` copies the elements of the vector slice `src` into `dst`, starting at position `di`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `di < 0` or `di + VectorSlice.length src > Array.length dst`, and then nothing has been copied.

**Example** `let val a = Array.array (3, 0) in copyVec {src = VectorSlice.slice (Vector.fromList [7, 8, 9], 1, NONE), dst = a, di = 0}; Array.vector a end = Vector.fromList [8, 9, 0]`

members.name: isEmpty
members.doc:
`isEmpty sl` is `true` when `sl` has no elements.

**Law** `isEmpty sl = (length sl = 0)`

**Example** `isEmpty (slice (Array.fromList [1], 1, NONE)) = true`

members.name: getItem
members.doc:
`getItem sl` is `NONE` for an empty slice and `SOME (x, rest)` for the first element and what follows it.

`rest` is a slice of the same array, so it is had for nothing.

**Example** `(case getItem (full (Array.fromList [1, 2])) of SOME (x, rest) => (x, length rest) | NONE => (0, 0)) = (1, 1)`

members.name: appi
members.doc:
`appi f sl` applies `f` to the index and the element of each position, from 0 up, for its effect.

The index is that of the element in the slice, counted from 0.

**Example** `let val r = ref [] in appi (fn (i, x) => r := (i, x) :: !r) (slice (Array.fromList ["a", "b", "c"], 1, NONE)); !r end = [(1, "c"), (0, "b")]`

members.name: app
members.doc:
`app f sl` applies `f` to every element, from 0 up, for its effect.

**Law** `app f sl = appi (f o #2) sl`

**Example** `let val s = ref 0 in app (fn x => s := !s + x) (slice (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3], 1, NONE)); !s end = 5`

members.name: modifyi
members.doc:
`modifyi f sl` replaces the element at each position by `f` of the index and that element, in place.

The index is that of the element in the slice, and the elements are
replaced from 0 up.

**Example** `let val a = Array.fromList [10, 20, 30] in modifyi (fn (i, x) => x + i) (slice (a, 1, NONE)); Array.vector a end = Vector.fromList [10, 20, 31]`

members.name: modify
members.doc:
`modify f sl` replaces every element by `f` of it, in place, from 0 up.

**Law** `modify f sl = modifyi (fn (_, x) => f x) sl`

**Example** `let val a = Array.fromList [1, 2, 3, 4] in modify (fn _ => 0) (slice (a, 1, SOME 2)); Array.vector a end = Vector.fromList [1, 0, 0, 4]`

members.name: foldli
members.doc:
`foldli f init sl` combines the elements from the left, giving `f` the index as well.

The index is that of the element in the slice, counted from 0.

**Example** `foldli (fn (i, x, acc) => (i, x) :: acc) [] (slice (Array.fromList ["a", "b", "c"], 1, NONE)) = [(1, "c"), (0, "b")]`

members.name: foldri
members.doc:
`foldri f init sl` combines the elements from the right, giving `f` the index as well.

The index is that of the element in the slice, counted from 0.

**Example** `foldri (fn (i, x, acc) => (i, x) :: acc) [] (slice (Array.fromList ["a", "b", "c"], 1, NONE)) = [(0, "b"), (1, "c")]`

members.name: foldl
members.doc:
`foldl f init sl` combines the elements from the left, as `List.foldl` does.

**Law** `foldl f init sl = foldli (fn (_, a, x) => f (a, x)) init sl`

**Example** `foldl (op ::) [] (full (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3])) = [3, 2, 1]`

members.name: foldr
members.doc:
`foldr f init sl` combines the elements from the right, as `List.foldr` does.

**Law** `foldr f init sl = foldri (fn (_, a, x) => f (a, x)) init sl`

**Example** `foldr (op ::) [] (full (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3])) = [1, 2, 3]`

members.name: findi
members.doc:
`findi p sl` is `SOME (i, x)` for the first position whose index and element satisfy `p`, or `NONE`.

The index is that of the element in the slice; `p` is applied from 0 up,
and not after the first position that satisfies it.

**Example** `findi (fn (_, x) => x = 3) (slice (Array.fromList [3, 1, 3], 1, NONE)) = SOME (1, 3)`

members.name: find
members.doc:
`find p sl` is `SOME x` for the first element that satisfies `p`, or `NONE`.

**Law** `find p sl = Option.map #2 (findi (fn (_, x) => p x) sl)`

**Example** `find (fn x => x > 1) (full (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3])) = SOME 2`

members.name: exists
members.doc:
`exists p sl` is `true` when some element satisfies `p`; it stops at the first that does.

Only the elements of the slice are looked at, not the rest of its array.

**Law** `exists p sl = isSome (find p sl)`

**Example** `exists (fn x => x = 1) (slice (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3], 1, NONE)) = false`

members.name: all
members.doc:
`all p sl` is `true` when every element satisfies `p`; it stops at the first that does not.

**Law** `all p sl = not (exists (not o p) sl)`

**Example** `all (fn x => x > 1) (slice (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3], 1, NONE)) = true`

members.name: collate
members.spec: val collate : ('a * 'a -> order) -> 'a slice * 'a slice -> order
members.doc:
`collate cmp (sl, tl)` compares the elements of two slices lexicographically with `cmp`.

**Law** `collate cmp (sl, sl') = List.collate cmp (foldr (op ::) [] sl, foldr (op ::) [] sl')`

**Example** `collate Int.compare (slice (Array.fromList [1, 2, 3], 1, NONE), full (Array.fromList [2])) = GREATER`

BIN_IO.doc:
Binary files: the imperative streams of bytes, with the ways of opening a
file.

It is `IMPERATIVE_IO` over `Word8.word`, with the same three `open`
functions as `TEXT_IO` and nothing else: there are no lines in a binary
file, no standard streams of bytes, and no `openString`.

**See also** `TEXT_IO`, `IMPERATIVE_IO`, `STREAM_IO`, `PRIM_IO`, `BYTE`

members.name: IMPERATIVE_IO
members.spec:
include IMPERATIVE_IO
  where type StreamIO.vector = Word8Vector.vector
  where type StreamIO.elem = Word8.word
  where type StreamIO.reader = BinPrimIO.reader
  where type StreamIO.writer = BinPrimIO.writer
  where type StreamIO.pos = BinPrimIO.pos

members.name: openIn
members.doc:
`openIn name` is a stream reading the bytes of the file `name` from its start.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the file cannot be opened, with the system's error as
the cause.

members.name: openOut
members.doc:
`openOut name` is a stream writing the file `name`, which it empties or creates.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the file cannot be opened.

> **Implementation** `BinIO.openOut/bytes-are-characters`. A byte written
here is the character of the same code read by `TEXT_IO`, and the other
way round: on POSIX nothing is translated between the two, for all 256
values.

**Example** `let val p = OS.FileSys.tmpName () val out = openOut p in output (out, Byte.stringToBytes "ab"); closeOut out; Word8Vector.length (inputAll (openIn p)) before OS.FileSys.remove p end = 2`

members.name: openAppend
members.doc:
`openAppend name` is a stream writing at the end of the file `name`, which it creates if it is not there.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the file cannot be opened.

**Example** `let val p = OS.FileSys.tmpName () val a = openAppend p in output (a, Byte.stringToBytes "ab"); closeOut a; let val b = openAppend p in output (b, Byte.stringToBytes "c"); closeOut b end; Byte.bytesToString (inputAll (openIn p)) before OS.FileSys.remove p end = "abc"`

BIT_FLAGS.doc:
A set of flags held as the bits of a word: what every collection of system
flags in `POSIX` has in common.

A `flags` value is a set. `flags` unites sets, `intersect` cuts them down,
`clear` takes one away from another, and `allSet` and `anySet` ask whether
a set contains another. The named flags of a structure are the one-element
sets, and `all` is every bit the system uses there -- which may be more
than the named flags, since a system knows bits that the specification
does not name.

`toWord` and `fromWord` reach the word underneath, for a program that has
to speak to something that is not SML.

**See also** `POSIX_FILE_SYS`, `POSIX_IO`, `POSIX_PROCESS`, `POSIX_TTY`,
`WORD`

members.name: flags
members.doc:
The type of a set of flags.

Two are equal when they hold the same flags.

members.name: toWord
members.doc:
`toWord fl` is the word whose bits are the flags of `fl`.

**Example** `Posix.FileSys.S.toWord Posix.FileSys.S.irwxu = 0wx1C0`

members.name: fromWord
members.doc:
`fromWord w` is the set of the flags that the bits of `w` name.

> **Reading** `BIT_FLAGS.fromWord/masks-the-rest`. The law `toWord o fromWord = (fn w => andb (w, toWord all))` is required for every word, those with
bits that no flag of this structure has included: such bits are dropped
rather than kept or refused.

**Example** `let open Posix.FileSys.S in fromWord 0wx100 = irusr end = true`

members.name: all
members.doc:
Every flag the system uses here.

> **Implementation** `BIT_FLAGS.all/every-bit-the-system-has`. It is every
bit of the underlying C value, so it may include flags the
specification does not name (`O_CLOEXEC`, `O_LARGEFILE`); that is what
lets those survive a trip through `fromWord` or a call that reads the
flags back from the system.

**Example** `let open Posix.FileSys.S in allSet (irwxu, all) end = true`

members.name: flags
members.doc:
`flags l` is the union of the sets of `l`: a flag is in it when it is in one of them.

**Example** `let open Posix.FileSys.S in toWord (flags [irusr, iwusr]) end = 0wx180`

members.name: intersect
members.doc:
`intersect l` is the intersection of the sets of `l`: a flag is in it when it is in all of them.

The intersection of no sets at all is `all`.

**Example** `let open Posix.FileSys.S in toWord (intersect [irwxu, flags [irusr, irgrp]]) end = 0wx100`

members.name: clear
members.doc:
`clear (fl, gl)` is `gl` without the flags of `fl`.

**Example** `let open Posix.FileSys.S in toWord (clear (irusr, irwxu)) end = 0wxC0`

members.name: allSet
members.doc:
`allSet (fl, gl)` is `true` when every flag of `fl` is in `gl`.

**Example** `let open Posix.FileSys.S in allSet (irusr, irwxu) end = true`

**Example** `let open Posix.FileSys.S in allSet (irwxu, irusr) end = false`

members.name: anySet
members.doc:
`anySet (fl, gl)` is `true` when some flag of `fl` is in `gl`.

**Example** `let open Posix.FileSys.S in anySet (irusr, flags [irusr, iwgrp]) end = true`

BOOL.doc:
Booleans: negation, and conversion to and from text.

The conditional `if`, and `andalso` and `orelse`, which evaluate their
second operand only when they must, are part of the language; `not` is
also in the top-level environment.

**See also** `STRING_CVT`

members.name: bool
members.doc:
The type of truth values, with the constructors `false` and `true`. It
is the top-level `bool`.

> **Erratum** `BOOL/bool-spec`. The specification writes `datatype bool = false | true`. The Definition (Section 2.9) does not allow `true` and
`false` to be specified, so the signature replicates the top-level
datatype instead; the meaning is the same.

members.name: not
members.doc:
`not b` is the negation of `b`.

**Law** `not (not b) = b`

**Example** `not true = false`

members.name: toString
members.doc:
`toString b` is `"true"` or `"false"`.

**Law** `fromString (toString b) = SOME b`

**Example** `toString false = "false"`

members.name: scan
members.doc:
`scan getc strm` reads a boolean from the character stream `strm`, which
`getc` reads.

It skips initial white space and then takes the word `true` or `false`,
in any mixture of upper and lower case. The answer is `SOME (b, rest)`,
with `rest` the stream after the word, or `NONE` when neither word is
there, in which case nothing has been consumed. What follows the word
stays in the stream, also when it is a letter: `"truer"` scans as `true`
and leaves `"r"`.

> **Reading** `Bool.scan/wsx-*`. "Initial whitespace" is what `Char.isSpace`
accepts, as for `StringCvt.skipWS`: the space, and the characters `\t`,
`\n`, `\v`, `\f` and `\r`.

**Example** `Option.map (fn (b, rest) => (b, Substring.string rest)) (scan Substring.getc (Substring.full " truer")) = SOME (true, "r")`

members.name: fromString
members.doc:
`fromString s` is the boolean that `s` begins with, read as `scan` reads
it, or `NONE`.

**Law** `fromString s = StringCvt.scanString scan s`

> **Reading** `Bool.fromString/none-not-whitespace-*`. The characters whose
codes are next to those of the white space characters (0, 8, 14, 31, 33,
95 and 127) are not white space: a string that begins with one of them
gives `NONE`.

The case of the letters does not matter, and blanks before the word are
skipped:

**Example** `fromString " TRUE" = SOME true`

BYTE.doc:
Between bytes and characters: the same eight bits read as a `Word8.word`
and as a `char`.

The conversions are of the codes, not of any encoding: the byte 200 is the
character whose code is 200, whatever a locale would make of it. Text that
comes in as bytes (from `BinIO`, a socket, `Word8Array`) becomes a string
here, and the other way round.

**See also** `CHAR`, `STRING`, `SUBSTRING`, `MONO_VECTOR`

> **Implementation** `Byte/free`. A `Word8Vector.vector` is a `string`
underneath in this library, although the type is abstract to a program,
so `bytesToString` and `stringToBytes` copy nothing.

members.name: byteToChar
members.doc:
`byteToChar b` is the character whose code is `b`.

> **Reading** `Byte.byteToChar/high-bytes-are-not-negative`. A byte is an
unsigned number: 200 is the character with code 200, and not the one
that a signed byte of \~56 would name.

**Law** `Char.ord (byteToChar b) = Word8.toInt b`

**Example** `byteToChar 0w65 = #"A"`

members.name: charToByte
members.doc:
`charToByte c` is the code of `c` as a byte.

**Law** `charToByte (byteToChar b) = b`

**Example** `charToByte #"a" = 0w97`

members.name: bytesToString
members.doc:
`bytesToString v` is the string of the characters whose codes are the bytes of `v`, in order.

**Law** `stringToBytes (bytesToString v) = v`

**Example** `bytesToString (stringToBytes "hi") = "hi"`

members.name: stringToBytes
members.doc:
`stringToBytes s` is the vector of the codes of the characters of `s`, in order.

**Law** `bytesToString (stringToBytes s) = s`

**Example** `Word8Vector.foldr (op ::) [] (stringToBytes "AB") = [0w65, 0w66]`

members.name: unpackStringVec
members.doc:
`unpackStringVec sl` is the string of the bytes of the vector slice `sl`.

**Law** `unpackStringVec sl = bytesToString (Word8VectorSlice.vector sl)`

**Example** `unpackStringVec (Word8VectorSlice.slice (stringToBytes "hello", 1, SOME 3)) = "ell"`

members.name: unpackString
members.doc:
`unpackString sl` is the string of the bytes of the array slice `sl`.

> **Reading** `Byte.unpackString/sees-the-current-contents`. An array can
change: the bytes are read when `unpackString` is called, so the string
holds what the slice had at that moment and is not touched by a later
update.

**Law** `unpackString sl = bytesToString (Word8ArraySlice.vector sl)`

**Example** `unpackString (Word8ArraySlice.slice (Word8Array.fromList [0w104, 0w105, 0w33], 0, SOME 2)) = "hi"`

members.name: packString
members.spec: val packString : Word8Array.array * int * substring -> unit
members.doc:
`packString (arr, i, ss)` writes the characters of the substring `ss` into `arr`, from position `i` on.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or if the characters would not fit, that
is if `i + Substring.size ss > Word8Array.length arr`.

**Law** `(packString (arr, i, ss); unpackString (Word8ArraySlice.slice (arr, i, SOME (Substring.size ss)))) = Substring.string ss` when `0 <= i andalso Substring.size ss <= Word8Array.length arr - i`

**Example** `let val a = Word8Array.array (4, 0w46) in packString (a, 1, Substring.full "ab"); unpackString (Word8ArraySlice.full a) end = ".ab."`

CHAR.doc:
Characters: their codes and order, the classes they belong to, and their
conversion to and from the text of SML and C character constants.

A character is a small non-negative integer, its code, and the characters
are ordered as their codes are. The signature is that of `Char`, whose
characters are the elements of `string`, and of the optional `WideChar`,
which is why it specifies a type `string` of its own.

The classes (`isAlpha`, `isSpace` and the rest) are those of the ASCII
character set and do not depend on a locale.

**See also** `STRING`, `SUBSTRING`, `STRING_CVT`

> **Erratum** `CHAR/string-types`. The specification writes the types of
`toString`, `scan`, `fromString`, `toCString` and `fromCString` with
`String.string` and `Char.char` rather than with the `string` and `char`
of the signature, because the text is always one of 8-bit characters, also
for `WideChar`. They are kept as written; that `Char.char` is `char` and
`Char.string` is `String.string` is a constraint on the structure `Char`.

> **Erratum** `CHAR/fromString-sample`. The third example of the page's table
for `fromString` is not the text of an SML string; the page of `STRING`
has the table as it was meant.

members.name: char
members.doc:
The type of characters.

> **Implementation** `Char.char/eight-bits`. `Char.char` is the top-level
`char`, a character of 8 bits: its codes run from 0 to 255.

members.name: string
members.doc: The type of strings of these characters: `String.string` for `Char`.

members.name: minChar
members.doc:
The character with the smallest code, 0.

**Example** `ord minChar = 0`

members.name: maxChar
members.doc:
The character with the largest code, `maxOrd`.

**Law** `ord maxChar = maxOrd`

**Example** `Char.ord Char.maxChar = 255`

members.name: maxOrd
members.doc:
The largest code of a character.

> **Implementation** `Char.maxOrd/value`. 255 for `Char`, and 1114111, the
last code point of Unicode, for `WideChar`.

**Example** `maxOrd = 255`

members.name: ord
members.doc:
`ord c` is the code of `c`, between 0 and `maxOrd`.

**Law** `chr (ord c) = c`

**Example** `ord #"A" = 65`

members.name: chr
members.doc:
`chr i` is the character whose code is `i`.

**Raises** `Chr` if `i < 0` or `i > maxOrd`.

**Law** `ord (chr i) = i` for `Int.<= (0, i) andalso Int.<= (i, maxOrd)`

**Example** `chr 97 = #"a"`

members.name: succ
members.doc:
`succ c` is the character after `c`, the one with the code `ord c + 1`.

**Raises** `Chr` if `c` is `maxChar`.

**Law** `pred (succ c) = c` for `c <> maxChar`

**Example** `succ #"a" = #"b"`

members.name: pred
members.doc:
`pred c` is the character before `c`, the one with the code `ord c - 1`.

**Raises** `Chr` if `c` is `minChar`.

**Example** `pred #"b" = #"a"`

members.name: compare
members.doc:
`compare (c, d)` orders two characters by their codes.

> **Reading** `Char.compare/127-128`. The codes are not negative, so 127 comes
before 128 and 255 after 0: a character is not a signed byte.

**Law** `compare (c, d) = Int.compare (ord c, ord d)`

**Example** `compare (#"a", #"b") = LESS`

`c < d`, `c <= d`, `c > d` and `c >= d` compare the codes of two
characters.

**Law** `(c < d) = Int.< (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c <= d) = Int.<= (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c > d) = Int.> (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c >= d) = Int.>= (ord c, ord d)`

**Example** `Char.< (#"Z", #"a") = true`

`c < d`, `c <= d`, `c > d` and `c >= d` compare the codes of two
characters.

**Law** `(c < d) = Int.< (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c <= d) = Int.<= (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c > d) = Int.> (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c >= d) = Int.>= (ord c, ord d)`

**Example** `Char.< (#"Z", #"a") = true`

`c < d`, `c <= d`, `c > d` and `c >= d` compare the codes of two
characters.

**Law** `(c < d) = Int.< (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c <= d) = Int.<= (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c > d) = Int.> (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c >= d) = Int.>= (ord c, ord d)`

**Example** `Char.< (#"Z", #"a") = true`

`c < d`, `c <= d`, `c > d` and `c >= d` compare the codes of two
characters.

**Law** `(c < d) = Int.< (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c <= d) = Int.<= (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c > d) = Int.> (ord c, ord d)`, and `(c >= d) = Int.>= (ord c, ord d)`

**Example** `Char.< (#"Z", #"a") = true`

members.name: contains
members.doc:
`contains s c` is `true` when `c` occurs in the string `s`.

Applied to `s` alone it gives a predicate, which suits the functions that
take one: `String.tokens (contains " ,;")`.

**Example** `contains "abc" #"b" = true`

members.name: notContains
members.doc:
`notContains s c` is `true` when `c` does not occur in `s`.

**Law** `notContains s c = not (contains s c)`

**Example** `notContains "abc" #"d" = true`

members.name: isAscii
members.doc:
`isAscii c` is `true` when the code of `c` is at most 127.

> **Reading** `Char.isAlpha/latin1`. The classes below are the sets that the
specification's discussion lists, whatever the locale: no character
above 127 is in any of them, and `toLower` and `toUpper` change the 52
letters of ASCII only.

**Example** `isAscii (chr 128) = false`

members.name: toLower
members.doc:
`toLower c` is the lower case letter for an upper case letter `c`, and `c`
otherwise.

**Law** `toLower (toUpper c) = toLower c`

**Example** `toLower #"Q" = #"q"`

members.name: toUpper
members.doc:
`toUpper c` is the upper case letter for a lower case letter `c`, and `c`
otherwise.

**Example** `toUpper #"a" = #"A"`

**Example** `toUpper #"1" = #"1"`

members.name: isAlpha
members.doc:
`isAlpha c` is `true` for a letter, `A` to `Z` and `a` to `z`.

**Law** `isAlpha c = (isUpper c orelse isLower c)`, as the specification
defines it

**Example** `isAlpha #"_" = false`

members.name: isAlphaNum
members.doc:
`isAlphaNum c` is `true` for a letter or a decimal digit.

**Law** `isAlphaNum c = (isAlpha c orelse isDigit c)`, as the specification
defines it

**Example** `isAlphaNum #"7" = true`

members.name: isCntrl
members.doc:
`isCntrl c` is `true` for a control character: a code below 32, or 127.

**Example** `isCntrl #"\n" = true`

members.name: isDigit
members.doc:
`isDigit c` is `true` for a decimal digit, `0` to `9`.

**Example** `isDigit #"a" = false`

members.name: isGraph
members.doc:
`isGraph c` is `true` for a character that leaves a mark when printed:
codes 33 to 126.

**Example** `isGraph #" " = false`

members.name: isHexDigit
members.doc:
`isHexDigit c` is `true` for a hexadecimal digit: `0` to `9`, `a` to `f`
and `A` to `F`.

**Example** `isHexDigit #"F" = true`

members.name: isLower
members.doc:
`isLower c` is `true` for a lower case letter, `a` to `z`.

**Example** `isLower #"a" = true`

members.name: isPrint
members.doc:
`isPrint c` is `true` for a printable character, the space included: codes
32 to 126.

**Law** `isPrint c = (isGraph c orelse c = #" ")`, as the specification
defines it

**Example** `isPrint #" " = true`

members.name: isSpace
members.doc:
`isSpace c` is `true` for white space: the space and the characters `\t`,
`\n`, `\v`, `\f` and `\r`.

**Law** `isSpace c = ((#"\t" <= c andalso c <= #"\r") orelse c = #" ")`, as
the specification defines it

**Example** `isSpace #"\t" = true`

members.name: isPunct
members.doc:
`isPunct c` is `true` for a graphical character that is neither a letter
nor a digit.

**Law** `isPunct c = (isGraph c andalso not (isAlphaNum c))`, as the
specification defines it

**Example** `isPunct #"_" = true`

members.name: isUpper
members.doc:
`isUpper c` is `true` for an upper case letter, `A` to `Z`.

**Example** `isUpper #"a" = false`

members.name: toString
members.doc:
`toString c` is the text that stands for `c` inside an SML string
constant.

A printable character is itself, except that the backslash and the double
quote get a backslash in front. The control characters with a name are
`\a`, `\b`, `\t`, `\n`, `\v`, `\f` and `\r`; the other codes below 32
are written `\^@` to `\^_`, and codes from 127 up as a backslash and three
decimal digits.

**Law** `fromString (toString c) = SOME c`

**Example** `toString #"\n" = "\\n"`

**Example** `toString #"\255" = "\\255"`

members.name: scan
members.doc:
`scan getc strm` reads one character from `strm` in the notation of SML
string constants.

A printable character other than the backslash stands for itself; a
backslash begins an escape sequence: the named ones, `\^c` for a control
character, `\ddd` with three decimal digits, `\uxxxx` with four
hexadecimal ones, `\\` and `\"`. The answer is `NONE` when the stream
begins with a character that is not printable or with an escape that
is malformed or names no character.

> **Reading** `Char.scan/formatting`. A formatting sequence, a backslash, white
space and another backslash, stands for nothing. Such sequences are
passed over before the character, and after it as well, so that what is
left of the stream never begins with one.

**Example** `Option.map (fn (c, rest) => (c, Substring.string rest)) (scan Substring.getc (Substring.full "\\tab")) = SOME (#"\t", "ab")`

members.name: fromString
members.doc:
`fromString s` is the character that the text `s` begins with, read as
`scan` reads it, or `NONE`.

**Law** `fromString s = StringCvt.scanString scan s`

> **Reading** `Char.fromString/printable-only-all-rejected`. A first character
outside the printable range, codes 32 to 126, gives `NONE`, and so does
a backslash by itself; every other printable character but the double
quote, of which below, is converted to itself.

> **Reading** `Char.fromString/unescaped-double-quote`. The specification
has the text read "as allowed in an SML program", where a double quote
that no backslash precedes ends a constant and is no character, and
names only characters that do not print and bad escapes as what gives
`NONE`. The first is followed: a double quote by itself gives `NONE`, as
in MLton and SML/NJ, where Poly/ML converts it. The page of `STRING` has
no such words and lists what stops a scan, so `String.scan` converts the
same double quote; the two pages differ, and each is followed.

**Example** `fromString "\\n" = SOME #"\n"`

**Example** `fromString "\"" = NONE`

**Example** `fromString "\\\"" = SOME #"\""`

members.name: toCString
members.doc:
`toCString c` is the text that stands for `c` inside a C string constant.

A printable character is itself, except that the backslash, the double
quote, the single quote and the question mark get a backslash in front.
The control characters with a name in C are `\a`, `\b`, `\t`, `\n`, `\v`,
`\f` and `\r`; every other character is a backslash and three octal
digits.

**Law** `fromCString (toCString c) = SOME c`

**Example** `toCString #"\000" = "\\000"`

members.name: fromCString
members.doc:
`fromCString s` is the character that the text `s` begins with in the
notation of C, or `NONE`.

The escapes are those of C: the named ones, `\ooo` with one to three
octal digits and `\x` with any number of hexadecimal ones. There are no
formatting sequences, and a double quote without a backslash is
rejected.

> **Reading** `Char.fromCString/hex-huge-does-not-fit`. A `\x` escape whose
value is no character gives `NONE` however many digits it has:
`Overflow` is not raised.

> **Reading** `Char.fromCString/printable-only-all-converted`. Every printable
character but the double quote and the backslash is converted to itself,
the single quote included; what does not print is rejected.

**Example** `fromCString "\\x41" = SOME #"A"`

COMMAND_LINE.doc:
The name of the program and the arguments it was given.

**See also** `OS`, `UNIX`

members.name: name
members.doc:
`name ()` is the name under which the program was called.

> **Implementation** `CommandLine.name/system`. What the operating system
passed to the program, which need not be a path that leads to it.

**Example** `size (name ()) > 0 = true`

members.name: arguments
members.doc:
`arguments ()` is the list of the arguments that follow the name, in order.

The name is not among them: a command of `n` words, the name included,
gives `n - 1` arguments.

> **Reading** `CommandLine.arguments/none-under-the-runner`. Which arguments
a program sees is "operating system and implementation-specific": what
the system passes after the name, with nothing taken away, and the empty
list when it passes none.

COMPILER.doc:
What a program can ask of the compiler it runs beside: in the REPL
(`rune-repl`, docs/repl.md) the compiler is in the same program as the
code it compiled, and a program compiles more of itself with `use`.

A program compiled by `rune` and run by `runevm` has no compiler beside
it: there `use` raises `Fail`, and the rest is there to be set and read
with nothing reading it.

This signature is Rune's own. Poly/ML keeps the same things in its
structure PolyML.Compiler, and SML/NJ in Compiler.Control.

> **Deviation** `COMPILER/not-in-the-specification`. The specification
regards a program as interactive (Chapter 8 of the Definition) and says
nothing of how one is fed to the compiler, so the REPL's controls are
every implementation's own.

**See also** `RUNTIME`

members.name: use
members.doc:
`use file` compiles the top-level declarations of `file` and runs
them, one after another, as if they had been typed at the REPL.

Each extends the declarations before it, and those after it see them.
A declaration that does not compile stops the file there: its error is
reported, and the declarations before it are kept. One whose running
raises an exception stops the file too, and the exception goes on to
the caller of `use`, its effects and the declarations before it kept.
`use` may be called by a declaration that `use` is running.

**Raises** `Fail` in a program that has no compiler beside it, or when a
declaration of the file does not compile; `IO.Io` if the file cannot
be read.

members.name: compile
members.spec: val compile : {read : unit -> char option, file : string, line : int} -> unit -> unit
members.doc:
`compile {read, file, line}` reads top-level declarations from `read`
and is the function that runs them, as if they had been typed at the
REPL.

It reads up to a `;` that ends a declaration at the top level, or to
the end of what `read` gives (`NONE`); a caller that wants all of a
reader compiles from it until it is at its end. `file` and `line` say
where the characters are from, for the positions of errors and
traces. The declarations are compiled and run one after another when
the function is called, each extending those before it, as with
`use`: a declaration that does not compile stops them, its error
reported, and one that raises stops them, the exception going on to
the caller. Poly/ML's PolyML.compiler is the same, a reader and its
parameters in, a function that runs what it read out.

**Raises** `Fail` in a program that has no compiler beside it; the
function raises `Fail` where a declaration does not compile.

members.name: printDepth
members.doc:
How deep the REPL prints a value, from the outside in.

The levels it counts are those of a list, a tuple, a record, a
constructor's argument and a `ref`'s content; past them it writes
`...` for the rest. At 0 or below the REPL says nothing of what a
declaration declared.

members.name: printLength
members.doc:
How many items of a list, an array or a vector the REPL prints (100);
the rest print as one `...`.

members.name: stringLength
members.doc:
How many characters of a string the REPL prints (1,000); the rest
print as `...` after the closing quote.

members.name: prompt1
members.doc: What the REPL writes before it reads a declaration.

members.name: prompt2
members.doc: What the REPL writes before each line that continues a declaration.

members.name: location
members.spec: type location = {file : string, startLine : int, startPosition : int, endLine : int, endPosition : int}
members.doc:
Where in a source what a printer shows came from: the file, and the
line and position it begins and ends at.

members.name: context
members.spec: datatype context = ContextLocation of location | ContextProperty of string * string
members.doc:
What a block of a printer's output says beside its text: where it came
from, or a property by name. Rune's REPL lays out the text alone.

members.name: pretty
members.spec:
datatype pretty =
    PrettyBlock of int * bool * context list * pretty list
  | PrettyBreak of int * int
  | PrettyLineBreak
  | PrettyString of string
  | PrettyStringWithWidth of string * int
members.doc:
A document for `prettyPrint` to lay out, in Poly/ML's shape: text,
places where a line may break, and blocks of them.

`PrettyBlock (indent, consistent, context, items)` lays its items
on one line where they fit; where they do not, a break of the block
starts a new line `indent` further in than the block began, every
break of the block where `consistent` and only those it needs where
not. `PrettyBreak (blanks, offset)` is `blanks` spaces where the line
does not break there, and where it does, the new line is `offset`
further in. `PrettyLineBreak` always breaks the line,
`PrettyString s` is `s`, and `PrettyStringWithWidth (s, w)` is `s`
laid out as if it were `w` characters wide.

members.name: prettyPrint
members.spec: val prettyPrint : (string -> unit) * int -> pretty -> unit
members.doc:
`prettyPrint (out, width) p` lays `p` out in lines of `width`
characters where it can, and gives `out` the text, piece by piece.

**Example** `let val b = ref "" in prettyPrint (fn s => b := !b ^ s, 3) (PrettyBlock (2, false, [], [PrettyString "ab", PrettyBreak (1, 0), PrettyString "cd"])); !b end = "ab\n  cd"`

members.name: lineLength
members.doc:
How wide the REPL lays out a value where its output is not a terminal.

It is the width of what the REPL's own printers make and what those of
`addPrettyPrinter` make; on a terminal, the terminal's width is.

members.name: addPrettyPrinter
members.doc:
`addPrettyPrinter f` makes `f` the REPL's printer of the values of a
type, as Poly/ML's PolyML.addPrettyPrinter does.

The type is the one `f`'s third argument has where `addPrettyPrinter`
is applied, which the compiler sees there: a datatype or an abstract
type, at any arguments. `f depth args v` is what `v` shows as,
`depth` the levels the REPL still shows, and `args` how to show the
type's arguments: `()` for a type of none, for one a function of a
value and a depth, and for more a tuple of them. A later printer of
the same type takes the place of an earlier one.

Where the type is not known where it is applied -- a type variable,
in a function that installs printers -- or is declared by the same
top-level declaration, nothing is installed; nor is anything in a
program that has no compiler beside it, where nothing prints.

DATE.doc:
A moment as a person writes it down: a year, a month, a day and a time of
day, in some time zone.

A `date` is what `TIME` is not: a calendar reading. `fromTimeUniv` and
`fromTimeLocal` turn a time into one, `toTime` turns one back, and the
pair are inverse only as far as the calendar is -- a date carries fields
that a time does not, and a time carries a fraction of a second that a
date does not.

The `offset` of a date is the time zone it is read in, as a duration west
of UTC: `NONE` means the local zone of the machine, `SOME zeroTime` means UTC. A date with an offset is arithmetic; a local date is
whatever the system's calendar says, daylight saving time and all.

The fields given to `date` need not be in range: what is over is carried
into the field above it, so the thirty-second of January is the first of
February.

**See also** `TIME`, `TIMER`, `OS_PROCESS`

> **Implementation** `DATE/the-C-calendar`. Local dates are converted by the C
library, so the local zone is the machine's and the calendar is the one it
keeps; dates at a fixed offset, and UTC, are computed with the proleptic
Gregorian calendar, which is how "leap years follow the Gregorian
calendar" is read for years before it was adopted.

members.name: weekday
members.spec: datatype weekday = Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat | Sun
members.doc: The days of the week.

members.name: month
members.spec:
datatype month
  = Jan
  | Feb
  | Mar
  | Apr
  | May
  | Jun
  | Jul
  | Aug
  | Sep
  | Oct
  | Nov
  | Dec
members.doc: The months of the year.

members.name: date
members.doc: The type of a calendar reading.

members.name: Date
members.doc: Raised when a date cannot be made, converted or printed: a field is out of range, or the time does not fit.

members.name: date
members.spec:
val date : {year : int,
            month : month,
            day : int,
            hour : int,
            minute : int,
            second : int,
            offset : Time.time option} -> date
members.doc:
`date {year, month, day, hour, minute, second, offset}` is that date, with the fields carried into range.

`offset` is the zone: `NONE` for the local one, `SOME t` for the zone
`t` west of UTC. The weekday and the day of the year are worked out.

**Raises** `Date` if the date cannot be represented.

> **Reading** `Date.date/fields-carry-upward`. Seconds, minutes, hours, days
and months outside their range are carried into the field above, up to
the year; an offset is reduced modulo twenty-four hours with the whole
days moved into the hours. A local date is normalised by the C library
instead.

**Example** `(fn d => (month d, day d, hour d)) (date {year = 2001, month = Jan, day = 32, hour = 25, minute = 0, second = 0, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = (Feb, 2, 1)`

> **Implementation** `Date.date/any-year`. The specification asks for the years
from about 1900 to 2200, where the laws of `year` hold on every
implementation; Rune's dates reach much further. The calendar of a date at
an offset is computed and not looked up, so a year has its dates as long
as the count of its days from 1970 is an `int`: the year \~5 and the year
100000 too, and with the 63-bit `int` every year up to about 12.6 \* 10^15
either way. Beyond, `date` raises `Date`. A local date is made by the C
library, whose fields are C `int`s: a field, or the year less 1900, that
one cannot hold raises `Date`. The suite takes a date or `Date` beyond the
range of a 32-bit `time_t`. `toTime` raises `Date` from about the year
148000 on, where the microseconds no longer fit an `int`, and `fmt` for a
year that C's `int` of 32 bits cannot hold.

members.name: year
members.doc:
`year d` is the year of `d`, as a number and not counted from 1900.

**Law** `year (date r) = #year r`, and `month (date r) = #month r`, and `day (date r) = #day r`, and `hour (date r) = #hour r`, and `minute (date r) = #minute r`, and `second (date r) = #second r`, when `let val {year = y, month = m, day = d, hour = h, minute = mi, second = s, offset = off} = r val leap = (y mod 4 = 0 andalso y mod 100 <> 0) orelse y mod 400 = 0 val days = case m of Feb => if leap then 29 else 28 | Apr => 30 | Jun => 30 | Sep => 30 | Nov => 30 | _ => 31 in 1900 <= y andalso y <= 2200 andalso 1 <= d andalso d <= days andalso 0 <= h andalso h <= 23 andalso 0 <= mi andalso mi <= 59 andalso 0 <= s andalso s <= 59 andalso (case off of NONE => true | SOME t => Time.< (Time.fromSeconds ~86400, t) andalso Time.< (t, Time.fromSeconds 86400)) end`, and it is run for `r` from
`DateArb.fieldsInRange (1900, 2200)`: in the years every implementation
supports, the specification's 1900 to 2200, a date of fields in range
keeps them

**Law** `(year (date r) = #year r) handle Date => true`, and `(month (date r) = #month r) handle Date => true`, and `(day (date r) = #day r) handle Date => true`, and `(hour (date r) = #hour r) handle Date => true`, and
`(minute (date r) = #minute r) handle Date => true`, and `(second (date r) = #second r) handle Date => true`, when `let val {year = y, month = m, day = d, hour = h, minute = mi, second = s, offset = off} = r val leap = (y mod 4 = 0 andalso y mod 100 <> 0) orelse y mod 400 = 0 val days = case m of Feb => if leap then 29 else 28 | Apr => 30 | Jun => 30 | Sep => 30 | Nov => 30 | _ => 31 in 1 <= d andalso d <= days andalso 0 <= h andalso h <= 23 andalso 0 <= mi andalso mi <= 59 andalso 0 <= s andalso s <= 59 andalso (case off of NONE => true | SOME t => Time.< (Time.fromSeconds ~86400, t) andalso Time.< (t, Time.fromSeconds 86400)) end`, and it is run
for `r` from `DateArb.fieldsInRange (valOf Int.minInt, valOf Int.maxInt)`:
in another year an implementation may raise `Date` instead, as the
specification lets it, but it does not give other fields. Rune's dates
reach much further than 1900 to 2200 (`Date.date/any-year`)

**Example** `year (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 19, minute = 6, second = 45, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = 1995`

**Counterexample** `year (date {year = valOf Int.maxInt, month = Jan, day = 1, hour = 0, minute = 0, second = 0, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = valOf Int.maxInt`, for the days to such a year are past the largest int.

members.name: month
members.doc:
`month d` is the month of `d`.

**Example** `month (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 19, minute = 6, second = 45, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = Mar`

members.name: day
members.doc:
`day d` is the day of the month of `d`, from 1.

**Example** `day (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 19, minute = 6, second = 45, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = 8`

members.name: hour
members.doc:
`hour d` is the hour of `d`, from 0 to 23.

**Example** `hour (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 19, minute = 6, second = 45, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = 19`

members.name: minute
members.doc:
`minute d` is the minute of `d`, from 0 to 59.

**Example** `minute (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 19, minute = 6, second = 45, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = 6`

members.name: second
members.doc:
`second d` is the second of `d`, from 0 to 59, or up to 61 for a leap second.

**Example** `second (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 19, minute = 6, second = 45, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = 45`

members.name: weekDay
members.doc:
`weekDay d` is the day of the week of `d`.

**Example** `weekDay (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 19, minute = 6, second = 45, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = Wed`

members.name: yearDay
members.doc:
`yearDay d` is the day of the year of `d`, from 0 for the first of January.

**Example** `yearDay (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 0, minute = 0, second = 0, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = 66`

members.name: offset
members.doc:
`offset d` is the zone of `d`: `NONE` for the local one, `SOME t` for `t` west of UTC.

**Example** `offset (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 19, minute = 6, second = 45, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = SOME Time.zeroTime`

members.name: isDst
members.doc:
`isDst d` is `SOME true` when `d` is in daylight saving time, `SOME false` when it is not, `NONE` when that is unknown.

> **Reading** `Date.isDst/UTC-has-none`. A date at a fixed offset is not in
daylight saving time: `SOME true` is wrong for it, and `NONE` and `SOME false` are both right.

The suite assumes that no zone has daylight saving time both in January
and in July.

**Example** `isDst (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 19, minute = 6, second = 45, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = SOME false`

members.name: localOffset
members.doc:
`localOffset ()` is how far the local zone is west of UTC, now.

> **Reading** `Date.localOffset/now-and-modulo-a-day`. The specification does
not say whether daylight saving time counts, and takes offsets modulo
twenty-four hours; the suite accepts the offset in force now, or an hour
more, reduced modulo a day, west of UTC.

**Example** `LargeInt.abs (Time.toSeconds (localOffset ())) <= 86400 = true`

members.name: fromTimeLocal
members.doc:
`fromTimeLocal t` is the moment `t` read in the local zone, with `offset` `NONE`.

> **Implementation** `Date.fromTimeLocal/the-machines-zone`. Which zone that
is depends on the machine, so the suite's checks of local dates are
written to hold in any of them: the offset is `NONE`, whole minutes, and
less than a day from UTC.

The suite's moments are noon UTC on 15 January and 15 July 2001, away from
the changes of every zone, and the time at which it runs.

**Example** `offset (fromTimeLocal Time.zeroTime) = NONE`

members.name: fromTimeUniv
members.doc:
`fromTimeUniv t` is the moment `t` read in UTC.

> **Reading** `Date.fromTimeUniv/second-it-falls-in`. The date is that of the
second the time falls in: a fraction of a second is dropped, also for
times before the epoch, where dropping is towards the earlier second.

The suite assumes that the clock of the machine shows a year from 2020 to
2199\.

**Law** `toTime (fromTimeUniv t) = Time.fromSeconds (Time.toSeconds t)` for
`Time.>= (t, Time.zeroTime)`

**Example** `toString (fromTimeUniv (Time.fromSeconds 86400)) = "Fri Jan 02 00:00:00 1970"`

members.name: toTime
members.doc:
`toTime d` is the moment that `d` names.

> **Reading** `Date.toTime/read-in-its-own-zone`. A date is "interpreted in
its own time zone": one at offset `t` west of UTC is the UTC reading of
its fields plus `t`. A local date is converted by the C library.

**Raises** `Date` if the moment does not fit in a `Time.time`.

**Example** `Time.toSeconds (toTime (date {year = 1970, month = Jan, day = 2, hour = 0, minute = 0, second = 0, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime})) = 86400`

members.name: compare
members.doc:
`compare (d, e)` orders two dates by year, month, day, hour, minute and second, in that order.

> **Reading** `Date.compare/ignores-the-offset`. The fields are compared as
they are written: two dates that name the same moment in different zones
do not compare equal, and one written later in its own zone is the
greater.

**Example** `compare (date {year = 2000, month = Dec, day = 31, hour = 0, minute = 0, second = 0, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}, date {year = 2001, month = Jan, day = 1, hour = 0, minute = 0, second = 0, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = LESS`

members.name: fmt
members.doc:
`fmt s d` is `d` written out by the directives of `s`, as C's `strftime` writes them.

**Raises** `Date` if `d` is not a valid date, which `scan` can produce.

> **Implementation** `Date.fmt/strftime-in-the-C-locale`. The work is done by
`strftime` in the "C" locale as it stood when the program started; only
the directives the specification lists are passed on, and any other
`%c` gives `c`. The specification names no text for `%Z` on a UTC date,
and the suite accepts `"UTC"`, `"GMT"`, `"Z"` or nothing.

**Example** `fmt "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M" (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 19, minute = 6, second = 45, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = "1995-03-08 19:06"`

> **Implementation** `Date.fmt/zone-names`. `%Z` is the C library's name of the
zone for a local date, `UTC` for a date at the offset zero and nothing for
one at any other offset. A `%` that ends the format is written as it is.

members.name: toString
members.doc:
`toString d` is `d` in the 24 characters of `"Wed Mar 08 19:06:45 1995"`, which is `fmt "%a %b %d %H:%M:%S %Y" d`.

**Raises** `Date` if `d` is not a valid date.

**Law** `toString d = fmt "%a %b %d %H:%M:%S %Y" d`

**Example** `toString (date {year = 1995, month = Mar, day = 8, hour = 19, minute = 6, second = 45, offset = SOME Time.zeroTime}) = "Wed Mar 08 19:06:45 1995"`

members.name: scan
members.doc:
`scan getc src` reads a date in the layout of `toString`, after leading whitespace.

> **Reading** `Date.scan/does-not-validate`. It reads exactly that layout and
checks nothing beyond it: the weekday is taken as written rather than
worked out, and the date it gives is a local one (`offset` and `isDst`
both `NONE`). So `scan` can give a date that `fmt` and `toString` then
refuse.

**Example** `Option.map (toString o #1) (scan Substring.getc (Substring.full " Wed Mar 08 19:06:45 1995")) = SOME "Wed Mar 08 19:06:45 1995"`

members.name: fromString
members.doc:
`fromString s` is `SOME` of the date that `s` begins with, after whitespace, or `NONE`.

**Law** `fromString s = StringCvt.scanString scan s`

**Example** `Option.map toString (fromString "  Wed Mar 08 19:06:45 1995 and more") = SOME "Wed Mar 08 19:06:45 1995"`

DISPLAY.doc:
What a program shows beside what it prints: an output in several forms
\-- text, HTML, an image -- of which the front shows the best it can
(docs/kernel.md).

In a Jupyter notebook an output is the cell's display output, which a
later `update` of the same id replaces; at the REPL's terminal, and in a
program compiled by `rune`, its `text/plain` form is printed, or else its
first.

> **Deviation** `DISPLAY/not-in-the-specification`. The specification knows
no front but a text stream; this signature is Rune's own.

**See also** `REPL`

members.name: bundle
members.doc: The forms of an output, by MIME type: `("text/html", "hi")`, `("text/plain", "hi")`.

members.name: display
members.doc: `display b` shows the output `b`.

members.name: displayAs
members.doc:
`displayAs (id, b)` shows `b` as the output named `id`, which `update`
replaces.

members.name: update
members.doc:
`update (id, b)` replaces the output named `id` with `b`, where the
front can; elsewhere it shows `b`.

members.name: clear
members.doc:
`clear wait` clears the outputs the cell has shown, at once or, with
`wait`, when the next comes; nothing where the front cannot.

DYNAMIC.doc:
Dynamic modules: units of code that a program loads while it runs
(docs/units.md, Dynamic modules).

A program declares `structure X = _dynamic "path" : SIG` and is compiled
against the signature alone; a module declares `_export structure Y : SIG = ...` and is compiled to a unit's file (`rune --units --emit-units`).
When the program reaches the declaration, the unit at `path` is loaded,
its top level runs, and `X` is what it exported, where the module was
compiled against the same signature: a constructor's tag is its place in
the signature's datatype, a type the signature leaves abstract stays
abstract, and an exception the module raises is the program's to
handle. A program that loads a module is built in units (`rune --units`), whose units the module links against.

`Dynamic.load` is the untyped form: a unit that registers what it offers
through a structure of the program (a plugin). A virtual module, `structure X = _virtual : SIG`, is the same boundary inside one program: its
implementation is the structure `X` that a unit before it exports, which
the program's build file chooses (docs/build.md, Virtual modules).

This signature is Rune's own.

> **Deviation** `DYNAMIC/not-in-the-specification`. The Definition has no
modules that come while a program runs.

**See also** `RUNTIME`

members.name: Mismatch
members.doc:
`Mismatch` is raised where a module does not fit what the program was compiled against.

That is a module loaded through `_dynamic` that was compiled against
another signature than the program, or exports no structure, and a
virtual module (`_virtual`) that has no implementation or one of
another signature. Its argument names the file or the module, and both
fingerprints.

members.name: load
members.doc:
`load file` loads the unit in `file` into the running program and runs
its top level, as `Runtime.load file ()` does.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the file cannot be read, and `Fail` if it is not a
unit's file or names what no unit loaded exports.

members.name: reload
members.doc:
`reload file` loads the unit in `file` again, for every `_dynamic` declaration that loaded it.

It runs the unit's top level, and each declaration's structure is then
the new module's, so a call through it reaches the new code, and a
function taken from it before is the old one. Where the new module
implements another signature, nothing changes.

A module whose signature has an abstract type is not loaded again: a
value of the type that the program holds could be of another
representation in the new module.

**Raises** `Mismatch` if no declaration loaded `file`, one did through a
signature with an abstract type, or the new module implements another
signature; `IO.Io` and `Fail` as `load`.

GENERAL.doc:
The types, exceptions and values of the top-level environment that belong
to no other structure.

Everything `General` specifies is also available without a structure in
front, and `General` is the one structure whose members the language itself
uses: `raise Bind` is what a `val` binding does when its pattern does not
match, `Div` is what division by zero raises. The exceptions here are those
the specification calls the standard ones; an implementation may raise them
from anywhere its description says it may.

**See also** `OPTION`, `LIST`, `STRING`

members.name: unit
members.doc:
The type with one value, the empty tuple `()`, which is what a function
that is called for its effect returns.

members.name: exn
members.doc:
The type of exception values, the top-level `exn`.

An exception declaration adds a constructor to it, so the type is open:
it grows as a program declares exceptions, and a value of it cannot be
taken apart except by a pattern that names a constructor. It does not
admit equality.

> **Erratum** `GENERAL/exn-spec`. The specification writes `type exn = exn`,
which is read as: the type of this structure is the top-level one.

members.name: Bind
members.doc: Raised when the pattern of a `val` binding does not match the value.

members.name: Match
members.doc: Raised when no rule of a `case`, a `fn` or a `handle` matches.

members.name: Chr
members.doc:
Raised by `Char.chr`, `Char.succ` and `Char.pred` for a code that is no
character.

members.name: Div
members.doc: Raised by `div`, `mod`, `quot` and `rem` when the divisor is zero.

members.name: Domain
members.doc:
Raised by a function that is given an argument outside its domain, such
as `Real.floor` of a NaN or `IntInf.log2` of a number that is not
positive.

> **Erratum** `GENERAL/domain-math`. The specification says that the functions
of `MATH` raise it. They do not: a mathematical function answers with a
NaN or an infinity instead, and it is `REAL` and `INT_INF` that raise
`Domain`.

members.name: Fail
members.doc:
Raised where a program has nothing better to raise; its argument says
what went wrong.

members.name: Overflow
members.doc:
Raised by an arithmetic operation whose result is not representable, such
