`update (arr, i, r)` writes the encoding of `r` at position `i` of `arr`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `arr` is shorter than `bytesPerElem * (i + 1)`.

**Law** `(update (arr, i, r); subArr (arr, i)) = r` for `0 <= i andalso i < Word8Array.length arr div bytesPerElem`, except that a NaN comes back as
some NaN

**Example** `let val a = Word8Array.array (8, 0w0) in PackReal64Little.update (a, 0, 1.0); Word8Array.sub (a, 7) end = 0wx3F`

**Counterexample** `(PackReal64Little.update (Word8Array.array (4, 0w0), 0, 1.0); true)`, for the eight bytes of the real are not all there.

PACK_WORD.doc:
Reading and writing a word in a vector or an array of bytes, in a fixed
byte order.

A structure of this signature packs words of `bytesPerElem` bytes: the
name says how many bits and which end comes first, so `PackWord32Big` puts
the most significant byte first and `PackWord32Little` the least. This is
what a program uses to read a binary file or a protocol whose layout is
given in bytes, whatever the byte order of the machine it runs on.

Positions are counted in words, not in bytes: element `i` of a vector is
the bytes from `bytesPerElem * i` on.

**See also** `WORD`, `PACK_REAL`, `BYTE`, `MONO_VECTOR`

> **Implementation** `PackWord/sizes`. The library has `PackWord16`,
`PackWord32` and `PackWord64`, each `Big` and `Little`.

members.name: bytesPerElem
members.doc:
The number of bytes of one word.

**Example** `PackWord32Big.bytesPerElem = 4`

members.name: isBigEndian
members.doc:
Whether the most significant byte comes first.

**Example** `PackWord32Little.isBigEndian = false`

members.name: subVec
members.doc:
`subVec (v, i)` is the word at position `i` of the byte vector `v`, with zeros in the bits above it.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or if the bytes of element `i` are not
all in `v`.

> **Reading** `PackWord.subVec/Subscript-not-Overflow`. The bound is tested
without the product `bytesPerElem * (i + 1)`, so a huge `i` raises
`Subscript` and not `Overflow`.

**Example** `PackWord16Big.subVec (Word8Vector.fromList [0w1, 0w2], 0) = 0wx102`

**Example** `PackWord16Little.subVec (Word8Vector.fromList [0w1, 0w2, 0w3, 0w4], 1) = 0wx403`, for the index counts elements of two bytes, not
bytes.

members.name: subVecX
members.doc:
`subVecX (v, i)` is the word at position `i` of `v`, with its top bit copied into the bits above it.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or if the bytes of element `i` are not
all in `v`.

**Example** `PackWord16Big.subVecX (Word8Vector.fromList [0wxFF, 0wxFE], 0) = 0wxFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFE`

members.name: subArr
members.doc:
`subArr (arr, i)` is the word at position `i` of the byte array `arr`, with zeros above it.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or if the bytes of element `i` are not
all in `arr`.

**Example** `PackWord32Big.subArr (Word8Array.fromList [0w0, 0w0, 0w1, 0w0], 0) = 0wx100`

members.name: subArrX
members.doc:
`subArrX (arr, i)` is the word at position `i` of `arr`, with its top bit copied into the bits above it.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or if the bytes of element `i` are not
all in `arr`.

**Example** `PackWord32Little.subArrX (Word8Array.fromList [0wxFF, 0wxFF, 0wxFF, 0wxFF], 0) = 0wxFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF`

members.name: update
members.spec: val update : Word8Array.array * int * LargeWord.word -> unit
members.doc:
`update (arr, i, w)` writes the low `bytesPerElem` bytes of `w` at position `i` of `arr`.

What does not fit in that many bytes is dropped.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or if the bytes of element `i` are not
all in `arr`.

**Law** `(update (arr, i, w); subArr (arr, i)) = LargeWord.andb (w, LargeWord.- (LargeWord.<< (0w1, Word.fromInt (8 * bytesPerElem)), 0w1))`
for `0 <= i andalso i < Word8Array.length arr div bytesPerElem`: `w` with
the bits above `8 * bytesPerElem` cleared

**Example** `let val a = Word8Array.array (2, 0w0) in PackWord16Big.update (a, 0, 0wx1234); Word8Array.vector a end = Word8Vector.fromList [0wx12, 0wx34]`

**Counterexample** `(PackWord16Big.update (Word8Array.array (1, 0w0), 0, 0wx1234); true)`, for the two bytes of the word are not both there.

POSIX.doc:
The POSIX interface: the system calls of a Unix-like system, gathered into
eight substructures.

Where `OS` offers what any system can do, this offers what POSIX
prescribes, and offers it plainly: `fork`, `exec`, `dup`, `stat`, the
signals, the password and group files, the terminal settings. Failure is
always `OS.SysErr`, carrying the `errno` the call set, which
`Posix.Error` names.

The `where type` clauses tie the substructures together: a `file_desc`
from `FileSys` is the one `IO` reads from, a `pid` from `Process` is the
one `ProcEnv` reports, and so on. Each part can therefore be used with the
others without conversion.

**See also** `OS`, `UNIX`, `BIT_FLAGS`, `PRIM_IO`

> **Erratum** `POSIX/opaque-in-the-page`. The page declares
`structure Posix :> POSIX`, so the types that no `where` clause fixes are
abstract; the suite matches `Posix` against this signature both
transparently and opaquely.

members.name: Error
members.doc: The conditions the system reports, and their names.

members.name: Signal
members.doc: The signals, by name and by number.

members.name: Process
members.spec:
structure Process : POSIX_PROCESS
  where type signal = Signal.signal
members.doc: Processes: making them, replacing them, waiting for them, ending them.

members.name: ProcEnv
members.spec:
structure ProcEnv : POSIX_PROC_ENV
  where type pid = Process.pid
members.doc: The process's own identity and its environment.

members.name: FileSys
members.spec:
structure FileSys : POSIX_FILE_SYS
  where type file_desc = ProcEnv.file_desc
  where type uid = ProcEnv.uid
  where type gid = ProcEnv.gid
members.doc: Files and directories as POSIX has them, with modes and file status.

members.name: IO
members.spec:
structure IO : POSIX_IO
  where type pid = Process.pid
  where type file_desc = ProcEnv.file_desc
  where type open_mode = FileSys.open_mode
members.doc: Reading, writing, duplicating and locking file descriptors.

members.name: SysDB
members.spec:
structure SysDB : POSIX_SYS_DB
  where type uid = ProcEnv.uid
  where type gid = ProcEnv.gid
members.doc: The password and group databases of the system.

members.name: TTY
members.spec:
structure TTY : POSIX_TTY
  where type pid = Process.pid
  where type file_desc = ProcEnv.file_desc
members.doc: Terminals: their modes, their speeds and their control characters.

POSIX_ERROR.doc:
The conditions the system reports when a call fails, and their names.

A failing POSIX call raises `OS.SysErr` with a `syserror`, which is the
`errno` the call left behind. The values below are the conditions POSIX
names; comparing with one of them is how a program asks why a call failed:

```f () handle OS.SysErr (_, SOME e) => if e = Posix.Error.noent then ... else ...```

Which condition a call reports is POSIX's business, not this library's,
and POSIX leaves some of it open: removing a directory that is not empty
may give `exist` or `notempty`, and a system may report something no name
here covers. `errorName` names those too.

**See also** `OS`, `POSIX`, `POSIX_FILE_SYS`, `POSIX_IO`

> **Erratum** `POSIX_ERROR.syserror/spec-writes-OS.Process`. The
page writes `eqtype syserror = OS.Process.syserror`; `OS.Process` has no
such type, the description says it "is identical to the type
`OS.syserror`", and `eqtype t = ty` is not a specification SML allows. It
is written `type syserror = OS.syserror`, which admits equality.

> **Reading** `Posix.Error/which-error-is-posix's`. Which condition a failing
call reports is prescribed by POSIX and not by this library; where POSIX
allows two, the suite accepts either.

members.name: syserror
members.doc: The type of a condition the system reports: the `syserror` of `OS`.

members.name: toWord
members.doc:
`toWord e` is the number the system gives `e`, its `errno` value.

The numbers are the system's: POSIX fixes the names, not the numbers.

**Example** `toWord noent = 0w2` on Linux and macOS

members.name: fromWord
members.doc:
`fromWord w` is the condition whose `errno` value is `w`.

**Law** `fromWord (toWord e) = e`

members.name: errorMsg
members.doc:
`errorMsg e` is the text the system gives for `e`, meant for a person to read.

It is `OS.errorMsg e`, the message of an `OS.SysErr` that carries `e`.

**Example** `errorMsg noent = "No such file or directory"`

members.name: errorName
members.doc:
`errorName e` is a short name for `e`, meant for a program.

> **Implementation** `Posix.Error.errorName/the-posix-names`. For the
conditions POSIX names it is the name below -- `"noent"` for `noent` \--
and for the others it is the name `OS.errorName` invents.

**Example** `errorName noent = "noent"`

members.name: syserror
members.doc:
`syserror s` is `SOME` of the condition that `errorName` calls `s`, or `NONE`.

**Law** `syserror (errorName e) = SOME e` for every condition, named here
or not.

**Example** `syserror "noent" = SOME noent`

members.name: acces
members.doc:
Permission is refused.

> **Implementation** `Posix.Error.acces/not-for-the-superuser`. Permission
bits do not stop a privileged process, so the suite's checks of this and
of `perm` hold for an ordinary user and pass trivially as root.

members.name: again
members.doc: Nothing is ready; try again.

members.name: badf
members.doc: The file descriptor is not open, or not open the right way.

members.name: badmsg
members.doc: The message is not of the right kind.

members.name: busy
members.doc: What was asked for is in use.

members.name: canceled
members.doc: The operation was cancelled.

members.name: child
members.doc: The process has no child to wait for.

members.name: deadlk
members.doc: Waiting would deadlock.

members.name: dom
members.doc: The argument is outside the domain of the function.

members.name: exist
members.doc: The file is there already.

members.name: fault
members.doc: An address given to the system is not one the process may use.

members.name: fbig
members.doc: The file would grow past what the system or the process allows.

members.name: inprogress
members.doc: The operation has started and is not finished.

members.name: intr
members.doc: A signal arrived before anything was done.

members.name: inval
members.doc:
An argument is not one the call accepts.

> **Implementation** `Posix.Error.inval/rename-into-itself`. Renaming a
directory into itself is taken to report this condition.

members.name: io
members.doc: The device reported a failure.

members.name: isdir
members.doc: The name is a directory where one is not allowed.

members.name: loop
members.doc: Too many symbolic links were followed; they may lead in a circle.

members.name: mfile
members.doc: The process has as many files open as it may.

members.name: mlink
members.doc: The file has as many links as it may.

members.name: msgsize
members.doc: The message is longer than may be sent at once.

members.name: nametoolong
members.doc: The name, or one of its arcs, is too long.

members.name: nfile
members.doc: The system has as many files open as it may.

members.name: nodev
members.doc: The device does not offer this operation.

members.name: noent
members.doc: The name names nothing.

members.name: noexec
members.doc: The file is not a program the system can run.

members.name: nolck
members.doc: No lock is free.

members.name: nomem
members.doc: There is not enough memory.

members.name: nospc
members.doc: There is no room left on the device.

members.name: nosys
members.doc: The system does not have this call.

members.name: notdir
members.doc: The name is not a directory where one is needed.

members.name: notempty
members.doc: The directory is not empty.

members.name: notsup
members.doc: The operation is not supported here.

members.name: notty
members.doc: The descriptor is not a terminal.

members.name: nxio
members.doc: The device or the address is not there.

members.name: perm
members.doc: The operation is not permitted, whatever the permission bits say.

members.name: pipe
members.doc:
A pipe or a socket is written that nobody reads.

> **Reading** `Posix.Error.pipe/or-the-signal`. Writing to such a pipe either
ends the writer with `Posix.Signal.pipe` or, when that signal is ignored
or caught, fails with this condition; the suite accepts both.

members.name: range
members.doc: The result is outside the range the type can hold.

members.name: rofs
members.doc: The file system may only be read.

members.name: spipe
members.doc: The descriptor cannot be positioned: it is a pipe, a socket or a terminal.

members.name: srch
members.doc: There is no such process.

members.name: toobig
members.doc: The argument list is longer than the system allows.

members.name: xdev
members.doc: The link would cross from one file system to another.

POSIX_FILE_SYS.doc:
Files and directories as POSIX has them: opening them, linking and
removing them, and reading and setting what the system records about them.

Where `OS_FILE_SYS` offers what any system can do, this offers the system
calls: `open`, `creat`, `link`, `mkfifo`, `stat`, `chmod`, `chown`,
`umask`. What it gives back for an open file is a `file_desc`, which
`POSIX_IO` reads and writes.

Permissions are a set of flags, the substructure `S`, and so are the
options of `openf`, the substructure `O`; both are `BIT_FLAGS`. What
`stat` reports is an `ST.stat`, which the functions of `ST` take apart.

Every failure raises `OS.SysErr` with the `errno` the call left; the
conditions are the ones `POSIX_ERROR` names.

**See also** `OS_FILE_SYS`, `POSIX_IO`, `POSIX`, `BIT_FLAGS`, `TIME`

> **Erratum** `POSIX_FILE_SYS/flexible-types`. The types are kept as the page
writes them. What the text says about them is checked in the suite rather
than written here: `uid`, `gid` and `file_desc` are those of
`Posix.ProcEnv`, `dirstream` is `OS.FileSys.dirstream`, and `access_mode`
is `OS.FileSys.access_mode`.

> **Reading** `Posix.FileSys/empty-path-raises`. An empty path raises
`OS.SysErr` with `noent`, as the system would, although inside the library
the empty string means "use the descriptor instead".

members.name: uid
members.doc: The type of the number that names a user, the one of `Posix.ProcEnv`.

members.name: gid
members.doc: The type of the number that names a group.

members.name: file_desc
members.doc: The type of an open file descriptor.

members.name: fdToWord
members.doc:
`fdToWord fd` is the number the system knows `fd` by.

**Example** `fdToWord stdout = 0w1`

members.name: wordToFD
members.doc:
`wordToFD w` is the descriptor numbered `w`, whether or not it is open.

A descriptor is "a per-process unique, non-negative integer" of the
system, an `int` of C, which POSIX makes at least 32 bits wide
(`{INT_MAX}` is at least 2147483647). Beyond that an implementation may
wrap the word, as one that keeps a descriptor in such an `int` does, or
keep it, as Rune does up to its own `int`, of 63 bits.

**Law** `fdToWord (wordToFD w) = w` for `SysWord.<= (w, 0wx7FFFFFFF)`

**Counterexample** `let val w = SysWord.+ (SysWord.fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt), 0w1) in fdToWord (wordToFD w) = w end`, for the number of a
descriptor is an int, on Rune of 63 bits.

members.name: fdToIOD
members.doc: `fdToIOD fd` is `fd` as the `OS.IO.iodesc` that `OS.IO.poll` takes.

members.name: iodToFD
members.doc:
`iodToFD iod` is `SOME` of the descriptor that `iod` is, or `NONE` when it is not one.

**Law** `iodToFD (fdToIOD fd) = SOME fd`

**Example** `iodToFD (fdToIOD stdin) = SOME stdin`

members.name: dirstream
members.doc: The type of an open directory being read, the `dirstream` of `OS.FileSys`.

members.name: opendir
members.doc:
`opendir p` opens the directory `p` for reading.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` is no directory, or may not be read.

members.name: readdir
members.doc:
`readdir d` is `SOME` of the next name in `d`, or `NONE` when there are no more.

The names are arcs, and `"."` and `".."` are not among them.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the directory cannot be read.

members.name: rewinddir
members.doc: `rewinddir d` puts `d` back at its first name.

members.name: closedir
members.doc: `closedir d` closes `d`.

members.name: chdir
members.doc:
`chdir p` makes `p` the current directory of the process.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` is no directory, or may not be entered.

members.name: getcwd
members.doc:
`getcwd ()` is the current directory, as an absolute path.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if it cannot be found.

**Example** `getcwd () = OS.FileSys.getDir ()`

members.name: stdin
members.doc:
The descriptor the program reads its input from.

> **Implementation** `Posix.FileSys.stdin/is-0`. The three standard
descriptors are the words 0, 1 and 2, which POSIX fixes and the page
does not state.

members.name: stdout
members.doc: The descriptor the program writes its output to.

members.name: stderr
members.doc: The descriptor the program writes its errors to.

members.name: S
members.doc: The permission bits of a file, as a set of flags.

members.name: S.mode
members.doc: The type of a set of permission bits.

members.name: S.BIT_FLAGS
members.spec:
include BIT_FLAGS
  where type flags = mode

members.name: S.irwxu
members.doc:
Read, write and run, for the owner: `irusr`, `iwusr` and `ixusr` together.

> **Implementation** `Posix.FileSys.S/values-of-the-C-binding`. The bits
are the ones of the system's `<sys/stat.h>`: `irwxu` is 0700 through
`isuid` 04000 and `isgid` 02000, and `all` is 07777, every bit that
`chmod` sets, the sticky bit included.

members.name: S.irusr
members.doc: The owner may read.

members.name: S.iwusr
members.doc: The owner may write.

members.name: S.ixusr
members.doc: The owner may run it, or enter it when it is a directory.

members.name: S.irwxg
members.doc: Read, write and run, for the group.

members.name: S.irgrp
members.doc: The group may read.

members.name: S.iwgrp
members.doc: The group may write.

members.name: S.ixgrp
members.doc: The group may run it.

members.name: S.irwxo
members.doc: Read, write and run, for everyone else.

members.name: S.iroth
members.doc: Everyone may read.

members.name: S.iwoth
members.doc: Everyone may write.

members.name: S.ixoth
members.doc: Everyone may run it.

members.name: S.isuid
members.doc: Run the program as its owner rather than as whoever started it.

members.name: S.isgid
members.doc:
Run the program with the file's group.

> **Implementation** `Posix.FileSys.S.isgid/may-not-stick`. The owner may
always set `isuid`; `isgid` is only bound to stay set when the file's
group is one of the process's own groups.

members.name: O
members.doc: The options of `openf` and `createf`.

members.name: O.append
members.doc: Every write goes to the end of the file.

members.name: O.excl
members.doc: Fail rather than open a file that is there already; for `createf`.

members.name: O.noctty
members.doc:
Do not let this file become the process's controlling terminal.

> **Reading** `Posix.FileSys.O.noctty/only-for-terminals`. A regular file
never becomes a controlling terminal, so on one this flag is only
checked to leave reading as it was.

members.name: O.nonblock
members.doc: A read or a write that would wait fails instead.

members.name: O.sync
members.doc: A write returns only once the data have reached the device.

members.name: O.trunc
members.doc: Empty the file when opening it.

members.name: open_mode
members.doc: What a file is opened for.

members.name: openf
members.spec: val openf : string * open_mode * O.flags -> file_desc
members.doc:
`openf (p, mode, flags)` opens the file `p`, which must exist, and is a descriptor on it.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` names nothing, or may not be opened that
way.

members.name: createf
members.spec:
val createf : string * open_mode * O.flags * S.mode
              -> file_desc
members.doc:
`createf (p, mode, flags, perms)` opens `p`, making it with the permissions `perms` when it is not there.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` cannot be opened or made.

> **Reading** `Posix.FileSys.createf/existing-file-is-opened`. The page
speaks of the permissions only for a file that has to be made, so a file
that is there already is opened as it stands: neither its contents nor
its permissions are touched, unless `O.trunc` is given.

members.name: creat
members.doc:
`creat (p, perms)` is `createf (p, O_WRONLY, O.flags [O.trunc], perms)`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` cannot be opened or made.

members.name: umask
members.doc:
`umask m` makes `m` the set of permission bits withheld from files this process creates, and is the old one.

> **Reading** `Posix.FileSys.umask/not-for-chmod`. The mask applies to files
that are created; `chmod` sets what it is given, mask or no mask.

**Example** `let val old = umask (S.flags [S.iwoth]) in umask old = S.flags [S.iwoth] end = true`, which puts the mask back as it was

members.name: link
members.spec: val link : {old : string, new : string} -> unit
members.doc:
`link {old, new}` makes `new` another name for the file `old`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `old` names nothing, `new` is there already, or
the two are on different file systems.

members.name: mkdir
members.doc:
`mkdir (p, perms)` makes a directory `p` with the permissions `perms`, less the mask.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` is there already, or cannot be made.

> **Implementation** `Posix.FileSys.mkdir/shares-OS.FileSys`. `rmdir`, `chdir`,
`getcwd`, `unlink`, `rename`, `readlink`, the directory streams and
`access` are the functions of `OS.FileSys` under the names of POSIX, and
`mkdir` differs from `OS.FileSys.mkDir` in the mode only.

members.name: mkfifo
members.doc:
`mkfifo (p, perms)` makes a named pipe `p` with the permissions `perms`, less the mask.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` is there already, or cannot be made.

members.name: unlink
members.doc:
`unlink p` removes the name `p`; the file goes when its last name does.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` names nothing, or may not be removed.

members.name: rmdir
members.doc:
`rmdir p` removes the directory `p`, which must be empty.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` is not an empty directory, or may not be
removed.

members.name: rename
members.spec: val rename : {old : string, new : string} -> unit
members.doc:
`rename {old, new}` renames `old` to `new`, replacing what `new` named.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `old` names nothing, or the rename is refused.

members.name: symlink
members.spec: val symlink : {old : string, new : string} -> unit
members.doc:
`symlink {old, new}` makes `new` a symbolic link holding the text `old`.

`old` need not name anything.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `new` is there already, or cannot be made.

members.name: readlink
members.doc:
`readlink p` is the text that the symbolic link `p` holds.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` is no symbolic link.

members.name: dev
members.doc: The type of the number that names a device.

members.name: wordToDev
members.doc: `wordToDev w` is the device numbered `w`.

members.name: devToWord
members.doc:
`devToWord d` is the number of the device `d`.

**Law** `devToWord (wordToDev w) = w` for `SysWord.<= (w, SysWord.fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt))`

**Counterexample** `let val w = SysWord.+ (SysWord.fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt), 0w1) in devToWord (wordToDev w) = w end`, for the number of a
device is an int.

members.name: ino
members.doc: The type of the number that names a file within its device.

members.name: wordToIno
members.doc: `wordToIno w` is the file numbered `w`.

members.name: inoToWord
members.doc:
`inoToWord i` is the number of the file `i`.

**Law** `inoToWord (wordToIno w) = w` for `SysWord.<= (w, SysWord.fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt))`

**Counterexample** `let val w = SysWord.+ (SysWord.fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt), 0w1) in inoToWord (wordToIno w) = w end`, for the number of a
file is an int.

members.name: ST
members.doc: What the system records about a file, and the functions that read it.

members.name: ST.stat
members.doc: The type of what `stat` reports about one file.

members.name: ST.isDir
members.doc: `isDir st` is `true` when the file is a directory.

members.name: ST.isChr
members.doc: `isChr st` is `true` when the file is a character device, as `/dev/null` is.

members.name: ST.isBlk
members.doc:
`isBlk st` is `true` when the file is a block device.

No machine is sure to have a block device that a test may look at, so
the suite checks only that this is `false` of what is something else.

members.name: ST.isReg
members.doc: `isReg st` is `true` when the file is an ordinary file.

members.name: ST.isFIFO
members.doc: `isFIFO st` is `true` when the file is a pipe, named or not.

members.name: ST.isLink
members.doc: `isLink st` is `true` when the file is a symbolic link; only `lstat` reports one.

members.name: ST.isSock
members.doc: `isSock st` is `true` when the file is a socket.

members.name: ST.mode
members.doc: `mode st` is the permission bits of the file.

members.name: ST.ino
members.doc: `ino st` is the number that names the file within its device.

members.name: ST.dev
members.doc: `dev st` is the number of the device the file is on.

members.name: ST.nlink
members.doc: `nlink st` is how many names the file has.

members.name: ST.uid
members.doc: `uid st` is the user that owns the file.

members.name: ST.gid
members.doc:
`gid st` is the group of the file.

A new file has the effective group of the process or the group of its
directory, as the system decides; the suite takes either.

members.name: ST.size
members.doc: `size st` is the size of the file in bytes.

members.name: ST.atime
members.doc:
`atime st` is when the file was last read.

> **Implementation** `Posix.FileSys.ST.atime/whole-seconds`. The three
times are kept in whole seconds, so they have no fraction.

members.name: ST.mtime
members.doc: `mtime st` is when the contents of the file were last changed.

members.name: ST.ctime
members.doc:
`ctime st` is when what the system records about the file last changed.

> **Reading** `Posix.FileSys.ST.ctime/utime-sets-it-to-now`. `utime`
changes this time to now, not to either of the times it is given: it
is the record that changed, not the contents.

members.name: stat
members.doc:
`stat p` is what the system records about the file `p`, following symbolic links.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` names nothing.

**Example** `ST.isDir (stat "/") = true`

**Example** `ST.isChr (stat "/dev/null") = true`

members.name: lstat
members.doc:
`lstat p` is what the system records about `p` itself, without following a symbolic link.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` names nothing.

members.name: fstat
members.doc:
`fstat fd` is what the system records about the file that `fd` is open on.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not open.

**Example** `let val fd = openf ("/dev/null", O_RDONLY, O.flags []) in ST.isChr (fstat fd) before Posix.IO.close fd end = true`

members.name: access_mode
members.doc: What one may want to do with a file, for `access` to ask about.

members.name: access
members.spec: val access : string * access_mode list -> bool
members.doc:
`access (p, modes)` is `true` when the process may do all of `modes` to `p`, by its real user and group.

An empty list asks only whether `p` names something.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the question cannot be answered.

**Example** `access ("/", []) = true`

members.name: chmod
members.doc:
`chmod (p, perms)` sets the permission bits of `p` to `perms`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` names nothing, or the process does not own
it.

members.name: fchmod
members.doc:
`fchmod (fd, perms)` sets the permission bits of the file that `fd` is open on.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not open, or the process does not own the
file.

members.name: chown
members.spec: val chown : string * uid * gid -> unit
members.doc:
`chown (p, u, g)` makes `u` the owner and `g` the group of `p`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the change is refused.

> **Implementation** `Posix.FileSys.chown/only-what-is-allowed`. An
unprivileged process may not give a file away, so the suite only checks
setting the owner and group a file already has.

members.name: fchown
members.spec: val fchown : file_desc * uid * gid -> unit
members.doc:
`fchown (fd, u, g)` is `chown` on the file that `fd` is open on.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the change is refused.

members.name: utime
members.spec:
val utime : string
            * {actime : Time.time, modtime : Time.time} option
            -> unit
members.doc:
`utime (p, times)` sets when `p` was read and changed, or both to now when `times` is `NONE`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` names nothing, or its times may not be
set.

members.name: ftruncate
members.doc:
`ftruncate (fd, n)` makes the file that `fd` is open on `n` bytes long, cutting or extending it.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not open for writing, or cannot be
resized.

members.name: pathconf
members.spec: val pathconf : string * string -> SysWord.word option
members.doc:
`pathconf (p, name)` is `SOME` of the limit `name` for `p`, or `NONE` when it is unbounded.

The names are written without a prefix: `"NAME_MAX"`, `"PATH_MAX"`,
`"LINK_MAX"`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `p` names nothing, or `name` is not a limit the
system knows.

> **Implementation** `Posix.FileSys.pathconf/what-a-check-can-assume`. The
suite asks that `NAME_MAX` be bounded and lie between 13 and 255, and
allows `PATH_MAX` and `LINK_MAX` to be unbounded, `PATH_MAX` being at
most 65535 when it is not.

members.name: fpathconf
members.spec: val fpathconf : file_desc * string -> SysWord.word option
members.doc:
`fpathconf (fd, name)` is `pathconf` for the file that `fd` is open on.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not open, or `name` is not a limit the
system knows.

POSIX_IO.doc:
File descriptors: reading and writing them, duplicating them, positioning
them, locking them, and turning them into readers and writers.

A `file_desc` is the small number the system knows an open file by.
`Posix.FileSys` opens files and gives descriptors; this signature is what
a program does with one afterwards.

`mkBinReader` and the three like it bridge to the rest of the library:
they wrap a descriptor as a `PRIM_IO` reader or writer, which
`STREAM_IO` and then `TEXT_IO` or `BIN_IO` build streams on.

**See also** `POSIX_FILE_SYS`, `PRIM_IO`, `POSIX`, `TEXT_IO`, `BIN_IO`

> **Erratum** `POSIX_IO/flexible-types`. The types are kept as the page writes
them; the identities that `POSIX` states in its `where type` clauses --
`pid` is `Posix.Process.pid`, `file_desc` is `Posix.ProcEnv.file_desc`, and
`open_mode` is
`Posix.FileSys.open_mode` \-- are checked in the suite rather than written
here.

> **Reading** `Posix.IO/what-comes-from-posix`. Two things the page does not
state come from POSIX itself: a descriptor that has just been made has
`FD.cloexec` clear, and a process's own lock never blocks it, so `getlk`
reports `F_UNLCK` for it.

members.name: file_desc
members.doc: The type of an open file descriptor.

members.name: pid
members.doc: The type of the number that names a process, the one of `Posix.Process`.

members.name: pipe
members.spec: val pipe : unit -> {infd : file_desc, outfd : file_desc}
members.doc:
`pipe ()` is a pair of descriptors: what is written to `outfd` can be read from `infd`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if no pipe can be made.

**Example** `let val {infd, outfd} = pipe () in ignore (writeVec (outfd, Word8VectorSlice.full (Byte.stringToBytes "hi"))); Byte.bytesToString (readVec (infd, 2)) end = "hi"`

members.name: dup
members.doc:
`dup fd` is a new descriptor on the same open file as `fd`.

The two share their position, so reading through one moves the other.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not open, or no descriptor is free.

> **Reading** `Posix.IO.dup/lowest-available`. "The lowest one available" is
read strictly: closing a descriptor that was just opened and then
calling `dup` gives that same number back.

members.name: dup2
members.spec: val dup2 : {old : file_desc, new : file_desc} -> unit
members.doc:
`dup2 {old, new}` makes `new` a descriptor on the same open file as `old`, closing what `new` was on.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `old` is not open.

members.name: close
members.doc:
`close fd` closes `fd`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` was not open.

**Example** `((close (Posix.FileSys.wordToFD 0w999); "closed") handle OS.SysErr _ => "SysErr") = "SysErr"`

members.name: readVec
members.doc:
`readVec (fd, n)` reads at most `n` bytes from `fd` and is what it read.

A shorter vector than `n` means only that less was there; the empty
vector means the end of the file.

**Raises** `Size` if `n < 0`; `OS.SysErr` if the read fails.

**Example** `((readVec (Posix.FileSys.stdin, ~1); "read") handle Size => "Size") = "Size"`

members.name: readArr
members.doc:
`readArr (fd, sl)` reads into the stretch `sl` and is the number of bytes read, 0 at the end of the file.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the read fails.

members.name: writeVec
members.doc:
`writeVec (fd, sl)` writes the bytes of `sl` and is the number it wrote, which may be fewer.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the write fails.

members.name: writeArr
members.doc:
`writeArr (fd, sl)` writes the bytes of the array stretch `sl` and is the number it wrote.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the write fails.

members.name: whence
members.doc: What a position given to `lseek` or a lock is counted from.

members.name: FD
members.doc: The flags of a descriptor itself, which `dup` does not carry over.

members.name: FD.cloexec
members.doc:
Close this descriptor when the process runs another program.

A descriptor that has just been made does not have it.

members.name: O
members.doc: The flags of the open file that a descriptor is on, which `dup` shares.

members.name: O.append
members.doc: Every write goes to the end of the file.

members.name: O.nonblock
members.doc: A read or a write that would wait fails instead.

members.name: O.sync
members.doc: A write returns only once the data have reached the device.

members.name: open_mode
members.doc: What a file was opened for.

members.name: dupfd
members.spec:
val dupfd : {old : file_desc, base : file_desc}
            -> file_desc
members.doc:
`dupfd {old, base}` is `dup old`, but the number it gives is at least `base`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `old` is not open, or no such descriptor is
free.

members.name: getfd
members.doc:
`getfd fd` is the flags of the descriptor `fd` itself.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not open.

members.name: setfd
members.doc:
`setfd (fd, fl)` sets the flags of the descriptor `fd` to `fl`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not open.

members.name: getfl
members.doc:
`getfl fd` is the flags of the open file that `fd` is on, and what it was opened for.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not open.

members.name: setfl
members.doc:
`setfl (fd, fl)` sets the flags of the open file that `fd` is on.

What a file was opened for cannot be changed this way.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not open.

members.name: lseek
members.spec:
val lseek : file_desc * Position.int * whence
            -> Position.int
members.doc:
`lseek (fd, n, whence)` moves `fd` to `n` bytes from the place `whence` names, and is where it now is.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` cannot be positioned -- a pipe, a socket or
a terminal.

**Example** `let val {infd, ...} = pipe () in (lseek (infd, 0, SEEK_SET); "moved") handle OS.SysErr _ => "SysErr" end = "SysErr"`

members.name: fsync
members.doc:
`fsync fd` waits until what was written to `fd` has reached the device.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not open, or the write fails.

members.name: lock_type
members.doc: What a lock is for, and what `F_UNLCK` says when a lock is asked about.

members.name: FLock
members.doc:
A description of a stretch of a file and what is to be done with it.

> **Implementation** `Posix.IO.FLock/is-a-flock`. The lock operations are
`fcntl` with a `struct flock`, and a `flock` here is that record.

members.name: FLock.flock
members.doc: The type of a lock description.

members.name: FLock.flock
members.spec:
val flock : {
              ltype : lock_type,
              whence : whence,
              start : Position.int,
              len : Position.int,
              pid : pid option
            } -> flock
members.doc:
`flock {ltype, whence, start, len, pid}` describes a lock of kind `ltype` on the stretch that the rest names.

`len` of zero reaches to the end of the file, however far it grows.
`pid` is meaningful only in what `getlk` gives back.

members.name: FLock.ltype
members.doc:
`ltype fl` is the kind of lock `fl` describes.

**Law** `ltype (flock {ltype = t, whence = w, start = s, len = n, pid = p}) = t`, and `whence (flock {ltype = t, whence = w, start = s, len = n, pid = p}) = w`, and `start (flock {ltype = t, whence = w, start = s, len = n, pid = p}) = s`, and `len (flock {ltype = t, whence = w, start = s, len = n, pid = p}) = n`, and `pid (flock {ltype = t, whence = w, start = s, len = n, pid = p}) = p`

members.name: FLock.whence
members.doc: `whence fl` is what `start fl` is counted from.

members.name: FLock.start
members.doc: `start fl` is where the locked stretch begins.

members.name: FLock.len
members.doc: `len fl` is how long the locked stretch is, 0 meaning to the end of the file.

members.name: FLock.pid
members.doc: `pid fl` is the process holding the lock, when `getlk` found one.

members.name: getlk
members.doc:
`getlk (fd, fl)` asks what would block the lock `fl`, without taking it.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the question is refused.

> **Reading** `Posix.IO.getlk/F_UNLCK-means-free`. When nothing blocks the
described lock, POSIX reports that as an answer of kind `F_UNLCK`; and
since a process's own locks never block it, its own lock is reported
that way too.

members.name: setlk
members.doc:
`setlk (fd, fl)` takes or releases the lock `fl` without waiting.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if another process holds a lock in the way.

members.name: setlkw
members.doc:
`setlkw (fd, fl)` takes or releases the lock `fl`, waiting until it can.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the wait is interrupted or the lock is
refused.

members.name: mkBinReader
members.doc:
`mkBinReader {fd, name, initBlkMode}` is a `PRIM_IO` reader of bytes over `fd`.

`name` is what an `IO.Io` from it will carry; `initBlkMode` says whether
the descriptor starts in blocking mode.

> **Implementation** `Posix.IO.mkBinReader/positions`. Only a regular file
has positions, so `getPos`, `setPos`, `endPos` and `verifyPos` are
`NONE` for a pipe, a socket or a terminal.

members.name: mkTextReader
members.doc: `mkTextReader {fd, name, initBlkMode}` is a `PRIM_IO` reader of characters over `fd`.

members.name: mkBinWriter
members.spec:
val mkBinWriter : {
                    fd : file_desc,
                    name : string,
                    appendMode : bool,
                    initBlkMode : bool,
                    chunkSize : int
                  } -> BinPrimIO.writer
members.doc:
`mkBinWriter {fd, name, appendMode, initBlkMode, chunkSize}` is a `PRIM_IO` writer of bytes over `fd`.

`appendMode` says whether every write goes to the end of the file, and
`chunkSize` how much the writer likes to be given at a time.

members.name: mkTextWriter
members.spec:
val mkTextWriter : {
                     fd : file_desc,
                     name : string,
                     appendMode : bool,
                     initBlkMode : bool,
                     chunkSize : int
                   } -> TextPrimIO.writer
members.doc: `mkTextWriter {fd, name, appendMode, initBlkMode, chunkSize}` is a `PRIM_IO` writer of characters over `fd`.

POSIX_PROCESS.doc:
Processes: making them, replacing them, waiting for them and ending them.

`fork` splits the process in two and is the only way a POSIX program makes
another; the `exec` family replaces the program that a process is running,
and never returns. The two together are how a program runs another: fork,
then exec in the child, then `waitpid` in the parent. `UNIX` wraps that up
for the common case.

A child that has ended is remembered until it is waited for, and `wait`
and `waitpid` report how it ended as an `exit_status`.

**See also** `POSIX`, `UNIX`, `POSIX_SIGNAL`, `OS_PROCESS`

> **Erratum** `POSIX_PROCESS/flexible-types`. The types `signal` and
`pid` are left flexible here, as on the page; `POSIX` fixes `signal` to
`Posix.Signal.signal`, and the identities stated only in the text are checked in
the suite rather than written into the signature.

members.name: signal
members.doc: The type of a signal, the one of `Posix.Signal`.

members.name: pid
members.doc: The type of the number that names a process.

members.name: wordToPid
members.doc: `wordToPid w` is the process whose number is `w`.

members.name: pidToWord
members.doc:
`pidToWord pid` is the number of `pid`.

**Law** `pidToWord (wordToPid w) = w` for `SysWord.<= (w, SysWord.fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt))`

**Counterexample** `let val w = SysWord.+ (SysWord.fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt), 0w1) in pidToWord (wordToPid w) = w end`, for the number of a
process is an int.

members.name: fork
members.doc:
`fork ()` splits the process in two, and is `NONE` in the child and `SOME` of the child's number in the parent.

The child has a copy of everything the parent had: its memory, its open
descriptors and its current directory.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if no process can be made.

> **Implementation** `Posix.Process.fork/a-second-vm-where-there-is-none`.
Windows has no `fork`. There the VM starts a second one of itself and
hands it this one's whole state -- the heap, the stacks, the program,
the open files, the sockets and the directory streams -- and the child
carries on from the `fork` as a copy of the process would. That costs
about 12 milliseconds, and 3 more for each megabyte of live data, where
a `fork` the kernel makes costs almost nothing.

> **Limitation** `Posix.Process.fork/read-ahead-of-a-pipe`. Where the `fork`
is that second VM, what the C library has read ahead from a pipe or a
terminal, and the program has not taken yet, stays with the parent
alone: an input that can seek is put back to where the program had
read, and a pipe cannot be. A `fork` the kernel makes gives the child a
copy of it.

members.name: exec
members.doc:
`exec (path, args)` replaces the running program by the one at `path`, and does not return.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the program cannot be run.

> **Reading** `Posix.Process.exec/args-and-path`. The first item of `args` is
the new program's argument zero and is passed as it stands, not replaced
by `path`. And `path` is a pathname: a name with no slash in it is not
looked for along `PATH`, which is what `execp` is for.

members.name: exece
members.spec: val exece : string * string list * string list -> 'a
members.doc:
`exece (path, args, env)` is `exec` with `env` as the new program's environment.

Each string of `env` is written `"name=value"`, and the new program has
those variables and no others: an empty `env` is an empty environment.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the program cannot be run.

members.name: execp
members.doc:
`execp (file, args)` is `exec` with `file` looked for along `PATH` when it holds no slash.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the program cannot be found or run.

members.name: waitpid_arg
members.spec:
datatype waitpid_arg
  = W_ANY_CHILD
  | W_CHILD of pid
  | W_SAME_GROUP
  | W_GROUP of pid
members.doc: Which child `waitpid` is to wait for.

members.name: exit_status
members.spec:
datatype exit_status
  = W_EXITED
  | W_EXITSTATUS of Word8.word
  | W_SIGNALED of signal
  | W_STOPPED of signal
members.doc: How a process ended, or why it stopped.

members.name: fromStatus
members.doc:
`fromStatus st` is what the status `st` says about how the process ended.

> **Implementation** `Posix.Process.fromStatus/status-encoding`. An
`OS.Process.status` is an `int`: the exit code of a process that ended of
itself, 256 and the number of the signal that ended it, or 512 and the
number of the signal that stopped it.

**Example** `fromStatus OS.Process.success = W_EXITED`

**Example** `fromStatus (OS.Process.system "exit 3") = W_EXITSTATUS 0w3`

members.name: W
members.doc: The flags that say what `waitpid` is to wait for.

members.name: W.untraced
members.doc:
Report a child that has stopped as well as one that has ended.

> **Reading** `Posix.Process.W.untraced/needed-for-stopped`. Without it a
child that is merely stopped does not end the wait: `waitpid_nh`
gives `NONE`.

> **Implementation** `Posix.Process.W/only-untraced`. It is the only flag
here; the `WNOHANG` of POSIX is what `waitpid_nh` is, and is added by
that function itself.

members.name: wait
members.doc:
`wait ()` waits for any child to end and is its number and how it ended.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the process has no child.

members.name: waitpid
members.spec: val waitpid : waitpid_arg * W.flags list -> pid * exit_status
members.doc:
`waitpid (arg, flags)` waits for the child that `arg` names and is its number and how it ended.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if there is no such child.

members.name: waitpid_nh
members.spec: val waitpid_nh : waitpid_arg * W.flags list -> (pid * exit_status) option
members.doc:
`waitpid_nh (arg, flags)` is `waitpid` that does not wait: `NONE` when no such child has ended yet.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if there is no such child at all.

members.name: exit
members.doc:
`exit st` ends the process at once with the status `st`.

Nothing is flushed and no `OS.Process.atExit` action runs; it is the
`_exit` of POSIX.

members.name: killpid_arg
members.spec:
datatype killpid_arg
  = K_PROC of pid
  | K_SAME_GROUP
  | K_GROUP of pid
members.doc: Which process `kill` is to signal.

members.name: kill
members.doc:
`kill (arg, s)` sends the signal `s` to the process or the group that `arg` names.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if there is no such process, or the signal may not
be sent to it.

members.name: alarm
members.doc:
`alarm t` asks for `Posix.Signal.alrm` in `t`, and is the time left of the alarm that was set before.

> **Reading** `Posix.Process.alarm/zero-cancels`. A time of zero asks for no
alarm, as POSIX has it, so it cancels the outstanding one and still
reports the time that was left of it.

**Example** `alarm Time.zeroTime = Time.zeroTime` when no alarm was set

members.name: pause
members.doc: `pause ()` waits until a signal arrives.

members.name: sleep
members.doc:
`sleep t` waits for the time `t` and is the time left of it.

> **Reading** `Posix.Process.sleep/time-left`. The page does not say what the
result is; it is POSIX's "time left", which is zero when the wait ran
out and the rest when a signal cut it short.

**Example** `sleep Time.zeroTime = Time.zeroTime`

POSIX_PROC_ENV.doc:
The process's own identity: who it is, who owns it, which group and
session it belongs to, and what its environment holds.

The user and group identities come in two kinds. The \*real\* one is who
started the process; the \*effective\* one is whose permissions it acts
with, and the two differ for a program whose set-user-id bit is set. A
process may set them back to what they already are, and only a privileged
process may set them to anything else.

`uname`, `time`, `times` and `sysconf` ask the system about itself rather
than about the process.

**See also** `POSIX`, `POSIX_SYS_DB`, `POSIX_PROCESS`, `OS_PROCESS`, `TIME`

> **Erratum** `POSIX_PROC_ENV/flexible-types`. The types `pid` and `file_desc`
are left flexible here, as on the page; `POSIX` fixes `pid` to
`Posix.Process.pid`, and `file_desc` is the one `FileSys` and `IO` use.

> **Implementation** `Posix.ProcEnv/what-a-check-can-expect`. What these report
is whatever `id`, `uname`, `date` and `getconf` report on the machine, so
that is what the suite compares them with. The test runner gives every
program `/dev/null` for its standard input, so no descriptor a check sees
is a terminal.

members.name: pid
members.doc: The type of the number that names a process, the one of `Posix.Process`.

members.name: uid
members.doc: The type of the number that names a user.

members.name: gid
members.doc: The type of the number that names a group.

members.name: file_desc
members.doc: The type of an open file descriptor, the one of `Posix.FileSys`.

members.name: uidToWord
members.doc: `uidToWord u` is the number of the user `u`.

members.name: wordToUid
members.doc:
`wordToUid w` is the user numbered `w`, whether or not there is such a user.

**Law** `uidToWord (wordToUid w) = w` for `SysWord.<= (w, SysWord.fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt))`

**Example** `uidToWord (wordToUid 0w0) = 0w0`

**Counterexample** `let val w = SysWord.+ (SysWord.fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt), 0w1) in uidToWord (wordToUid w) = w end`, for the number of a
user is an int.

members.name: gidToWord
members.doc: `gidToWord g` is the number of the group `g`.

members.name: wordToGid
members.doc:
`wordToGid w` is the group numbered `w`.

**Law** `gidToWord (wordToGid w) = w` for `SysWord.<= (w, SysWord.fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt))`

**Counterexample** `let val w = SysWord.+ (SysWord.fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt), 0w1) in gidToWord (wordToGid w) = w end`, for the number of a
group is an int.

members.name: getpid
members.doc: `getpid ()` is the number of this process.

members.name: getppid
members.doc:
`getppid ()` is the number of the process that made this one.

**Example** `getppid () <> getpid () = true`

members.name: getuid
members.doc: `getuid ()` is the user that started this process.

members.name: geteuid
members.doc: `geteuid ()` is the user whose permissions this process acts with.

members.name: getgid
members.doc: `getgid ()` is the group of the user that started this process.

members.name: getegid
members.doc: `getegid ()` is the group whose permissions this process acts with.

members.name: setuid
members.doc:
`setuid u` makes `u` the user of this process.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the process may not become `u`.

> **Reading** `Posix.ProcEnv.setuid/own-is-allowed`. Setting the user to the
one the process already has is allowed and changes nothing. Becoming
another user, the superuser above all, is refused unless the process is
privileged already.

members.name: setgid
members.doc:
`setgid g` makes `g` the group of this process.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the process may not take the group `g`.

> **Reading** `Posix.ProcEnv.setgid/own-is-allowed`. As for `setuid`: a process
may always take the group it has, and only a privileged one may take
another.

members.name: getgroups
members.doc:
`getgroups ()` is the supplementary groups of this process.

> **Implementation** `Posix.ProcEnv.getgroups/compared-with-id-G`. The suite
compares the list with what `id -G` prints, which also lists the
effective group, so that group is added before comparing.

members.name: getlogin
members.doc:
`getlogin ()` is the name the user logged in under.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the system does not know it.

> **Reading** `Posix.ProcEnv.getlogin/may-not-be-known`. Without a terminal
the system may have no login name to give; the suite accepts either
`OS.SysErr` or a name that is a user of the machine.

members.name: getpgrp
members.doc: `getpgrp ()` is the process group this process is in.

members.name: setsid
members.doc:
`setsid ()` starts a new session with this process alone in it, and is its new process group.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if this process already leads a process group.

> **Reading** `Posix.ProcEnv.setsid/group-is-the-pid`. The process group it
returns is the process's own number, since the process becomes the
leader of a group of its own.

members.name: setpgid
members.spec: val setpgid : {pid : pid option, pgid : pid option} -> unit
members.doc:
`setpgid {pid, pgid}` puts the process `pid` into the process group `pgid`.

A `pid` of `NONE` is this process, and a `pgid` of `NONE` makes the
process the leader of a group of its own, numbered as the process is.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the move is refused.

members.name: uname
members.doc:
`uname ()` is what the system says about itself, as pairs of a field and its value.

The fields are `"sysname"`, `"nodename"`, `"release"`, `"version"` and
`"machine"`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the system cannot be asked.

**Example** `List.map #1 (uname ()) = ["sysname", "nodename", "release", "version", "machine"]`

members.name: time
members.doc: `time ()` is the time now, as `Time.now` gives it.

members.name: times
members.spec:
val times : unit
            -> {elapsed : Time.time,
                utime : Time.time,
                stime : Time.time,
                cutime : Time.time,
                cstime : Time.time}
members.doc:
`times ()` is how much time this process and the children it has waited for have used.

`elapsed` is wall-clock time from a fixed point in the past, `utime` and
`stime` this process's own user and system time, and `cutime` and
`cstime` those of the children it has waited for.

members.name: getenv
members.doc:
`getenv name` is `SOME` of the value of the environment variable `name`, or `NONE`.

**Law** `getenv name = OS.Process.getEnv name`

**Example** `getenv "A_VARIABLE_THAT_NOBODY_SETS" = NONE`

members.name: environ
members.doc: `environ ()` is the whole environment, each entry written `"name=value"`.

members.name: ctermid
members.doc:
`ctermid ()` is a path that names the controlling terminal of this process.

It is C's `ctermid`, which on Linux and macOS is `"/dev/tty"` whether or
not the process has a terminal: that path names whichever one it has.

**Example** `ctermid () = "/dev/tty"` on Linux and macOS

members.name: ttyname
members.doc:
`ttyname fd` is the path of the terminal that `fd` is open on.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not a terminal.

members.name: isatty
members.doc:
`isatty fd` is `true` when `fd` is open on a terminal.

A descriptor that is not open is no terminal: nothing is raised.

**Example** `isatty (Posix.FileSys.wordToFD 0w999) = false`

members.name: sysconf
members.doc:
`sysconf name` is the value the system gives for the limit or option `name`, such as `"CLK_TCK"`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the system does not know `name`.

> **Reading** `Posix.ProcEnv.sysconf/no-limit-raises`. A variable the system
knows but leaves unbounded is reported the same way as an unknown one --
the call gives `~1` and sets no `errno` \-- so this raises for both.

POSIX_SIGNAL.doc:
The signals a process may be sent, by name.

A signal is a number that the system uses to interrupt a process:
`Posix.Process.kill` sends one, `Unix.kill` sends one to a child, and
`Posix.Process.fromStatus` reports the one that ended a process. The names
below are the signals POSIX prescribes; `fromWord` reaches the others.

Nothing here installs a handler: this signature names signals, it does not
catch them.

**See also** `POSIX_PROCESS`, `UNIX`, `POSIX`

> **Implementation** `Posix.Signal/numbers-are-the-systems`. A signal is the
number the system gives it, which differs from system to system; the suite
checks each name against what the shell's `kill -l` calls that number.
Signals that would dump core, stop the process or be ignored by the runner
are checked by number only and never sent.

members.name: signal
members.doc:
The type of a signal.

Two are equal when they are the same signal.

members.name: toWord
members.doc:
`toWord s` is the number the system gives `s`.

**Example** `toWord kill = 0w9`

members.name: fromWord
members.doc:
`fromWord w` is the signal numbered `w`, which need not be one named here.

**Law** `fromWord (toWord s) = s`

**Example** `fromWord 0w15 = term`

members.name: abrt
members.doc: Abort: the process ended itself, as `abort` does.

members.name: alrm
members.doc: The alarm set by `Posix.Process.alarm` has gone off.

members.name: bus
members.doc: A memory access the hardware refused.

members.name: fpe
members.doc: An arithmetic fault, such as a division by zero.

members.name: hup
members.doc: The terminal the process was attached to has gone.

members.name: ill
members.doc: The processor met an instruction it cannot run.

members.name: int
members.doc: The interrupt character was typed, usually control-C.

members.name: kill
members.doc: End the process; it cannot be caught, blocked or ignored.

members.name: pipe
members.doc:
A pipe or a socket was written that nobody reads.

**See also** `POSIX_ERROR`

members.name: quit
members.doc: The quit character was typed, usually control-backslash.

members.name: segv
members.doc: The process touched memory that is not its own.

members.name: term
members.doc: Ask the process to end; the polite one, which may be caught.

members.name: usr1
members.doc: A signal with no meaning of its own, for a program to use.

members.name: usr2
members.doc: A second signal with no meaning of its own.

members.name: chld
members.doc: A child has stopped or ended.

members.name: cont
members.doc: Carry on after having been stopped.

members.name: stop
members.doc: Stop the process; it cannot be caught, blocked or ignored.

members.name: tstp
members.doc: Stop the process, from the terminal; usually control-Z.

members.name: ttin
members.doc: A background process tried to read from the terminal.

members.name: ttou
members.doc: A background process tried to write to the terminal.

POSIX_SYS_DB.doc:
The password and group databases: turning a user or group name into a
number, and back.

These read what the system keeps about its users and groups -- on a
classic Unix the files `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/group`, and in general
whatever the system's name service offers. They do not change anything.

**See also** `POSIX_PROC_ENV`, `POSIX`, `POSIX_FILE_SYS`

> **Erratum** `POSIX_SYS_DB/flexible-types`. The types `uid` and `gid` are left
flexible here, as on the page, which says only that they are "identical to
`Posix.ProcEnv.uid`"; `POSIX` fixes them.

> **Implementation** `Posix.SysDB/what-a-check-can-assume`. The suite assumes
that the user and the group numbered 0 exist and are called `root`, which
holds on Linux and the BSDs, and compares the other fields with what
`getent` prints.

members.name: uid
members.doc: The type of the number that names a user, the one of `Posix.ProcEnv`.

members.name: gid
members.doc: The type of the number that names a group.

members.name: Passwd
members.doc: What the system knows about a user.

members.name: Passwd.passwd
members.doc: The type of an entry of the password database.

members.name: Passwd.name
members.doc: `name pw` is the login name of `pw`.

members.name: Passwd.uid
members.doc: `uid pw` is the number of the user `pw`.

members.name: Passwd.gid
members.doc: `gid pw` is the number of that user's own group.

members.name: Passwd.home
members.doc: `home pw` is the path of that user's home directory.

members.name: Passwd.shell
members.doc: `shell pw` is the path of the program that user gets at login.

members.name: Group
members.doc: What the system knows about a group.

members.name: Group.group
members.doc: The type of an entry of the group database.

members.name: Group.name
members.doc: `name gr` is the name of `gr`.

members.name: Group.gid
members.doc: `gid gr` is the number of the group `gr`.

members.name: Group.members
members.doc: `members gr` is the login names of the users that belong to `gr` besides those whose own group it is.

members.name: getgrgid
members.doc:
`getgrgid g` is what the system knows about the group numbered `g`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if there is no such group.

**Law** `Group.gid (getgrgid g) = g`

**Example** `let val g = Posix.ProcEnv.wordToGid 0w0 in Group.gid (getgrgid g) = g end = true`

members.name: getgrnam
members.doc:
`getgrnam name` is what the system knows about the group called `name`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if there is no such group, and at once for an empty
name.

members.name: getpwuid
members.doc:
`getpwuid u` is what the system knows about the user numbered `u`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if there is no such user.

> **Reading** `Posix.SysDB/missing-raises-SysErr`. The C library reports a
name it does not find without setting an `errno`; this raises
`OS.SysErr` for it all the same, since the alternative would be to
return something that names nobody.

**Law** `Passwd.uid (getpwuid u) = u`

**Example** `Passwd.name (getpwuid (Posix.ProcEnv.wordToUid 0w0)) = "root"`

members.name: getpwnam
members.doc:
`getpwnam name` is what the system knows about the user called `name`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if there is no such user, and at once for an empty
name, which the primitive would otherwise take for a lookup by
number.

**Example** `Passwd.uid (getpwnam "root") = Posix.ProcEnv.wordToUid 0w0`

POSIX_TTY.doc:
Terminals: their modes, their speeds and the characters that control them.

What a terminal does with what is typed at it and with what is written to
it is held in a `termios`: four sets of flags, an array of control
characters, and two speeds. `TC.getattr` reads the settings of a
descriptor, `TC.setattr` writes them back, and everything in between is
how a `termios` is taken apart and put together.

The four sets of flags are `I` for what is done to input, `O` for what is
done to output, `C` for the line itself, and `L` for how the terminal
treats the program -- whether it echoes, whether it waits for a whole line
(`L.icanon`), whether typing the interrupt character sends a signal
(`L.isig`). Turning `L.icanon` and `L.echo` off is what a program does to
read keys as they are typed.

`V` names the positions in the array of control characters: which
character means end of file, which interrupts, which erases.

**See also** `POSIX_IO`, `POSIX_PROC_ENV`, `POSIX`, `BIT_FLAGS`

> **Erratum** `POSIX_TTY/flexible-types`. The types `pid` and `file_desc` are
left flexible here, as on the page; `POSIX` fixes them.

> **Implementation** `Posix.TTY/what-the-values-are`. A set of flags is a
`tcflag_t` word of the system, a speed is its `speed_t`, and the control
characters are a string of `V.nccs` characters; all of them are read and
written in one call.

members.name: pid
members.doc: The type of the number that names a process, the one of `Posix.Process`.

members.name: file_desc
members.doc: The type of an open file descriptor.

members.name: V
members.doc: The positions in the array of control characters, and the array itself.

members.name: V.eof
members.doc:
Where the end-of-file character stands.

> **Reading** `Posix.TTY.V/distinct-within-a-set`. POSIX lets `min` share
its position with `eof`, and `time` with `eol`, because a terminal is
either in canonical mode or not; so the positions are distinct within
each of the two sets and not across them.

members.name: V.eol
members.doc: Where the end-of-line character stands.

members.name: V.erase
members.doc: Where the character that erases one character stands.

members.name: V.intr
members.doc: Where the character that sends the interrupt signal stands.

members.name: V.kill
members.doc: Where the character that erases the whole line stands.

members.name: V.min
members.doc: Where the smallest number of characters a raw read waits for stands.

members.name: V.quit
members.doc: Where the character that sends the quit signal stands.

members.name: V.susp
members.doc: Where the character that suspends the program stands.

members.name: V.time
members.doc: Where the time a raw read waits, in tenths of a second, stands.

members.name: V.start
members.doc: Where the character that resumes output stands.

members.name: V.stop
members.doc: Where the character that holds output back stands.

members.name: V.nccs
members.doc: How many positions the array has.

members.name: V.cc
members.doc: The type of the array of control characters.

members.name: V.cc
members.doc:
`cc l` is the array in which each position of `l` holds its character, and every other position `#"\000"`.

**Example** `V.sub (V.cc [(V.eof, #"\^D")], V.eof) = #"\^D"`

members.name: V.update
members.spec: val update : cc * (int * char) list -> cc
members.doc:
`update (c, l)` is a copy of `c` in which each position of `l` holds its character.

**Raises** `Subscript` if a position is outside `[0, nccs)`.

**Example** `V.sub (V.update (V.cc [], [(V.intr, #"\^C")]), V.intr) = #"\^C"`

members.name: V.sub
members.doc:
`sub (c, i)` is the character at position `i`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i` is outside `[0, nccs)`.

**Example** `(V.sub (V.cc [], V.nccs) handle Subscript => #"x") = #"x"`

members.name: I
members.doc: What the terminal does with what is typed at it.

members.name: I.brkint
members.doc:
A break sends the interrupt signal.

> **Reading** `Posix.TTY.I/bits-are-posix's`. The page says nothing about
what bits these flags have; the suite follows POSIX and asks that
every named flag of `I` and `L` have non-zero bits of its own inside
`all`, comparing through `SysWord` rather than through `allSet`.

members.name: I.icrnl

members.name: I.ignbrk

members.name: I.igncr

members.name: I.ignpar

members.name: I.inlcr

members.name: I.inpck

members.name: I.istrip
members.doc: Drop the eighth bit of every character.

members.name: I.ixoff

members.name: I.ixon

members.name: I.parmrk

members.name: O

members.name: O.opost

members.name: C

members.name: C.clocal

members.name: C.cread

`compareSpeed (s, t)` orders two speeds, the slower first.
