members.name: termios
members.spec:
val termios : {iflag : I.flags,
               oflag : O.flags,
               cflag : C.flags,
               lflag : L.flags,
               cc : V.cc,
               ispeed : speed,
               ospeed : speed}
              -> termios
members.doc: `termios {iflag, oflag, cflag, lflag, cc, ispeed, ospeed}` is the settings those fields make.

members.name: fieldsOf
members.spec:
val fieldsOf : termios
               -> {iflag : I.flags,
                   oflag : O.flags,
                   cflag : C.flags,
                   lflag : L.flags,
                   cc : V.cc,
                   ispeed : speed,
                   ospeed : speed}
members.doc:
`fieldsOf t` is the fields of `t`, the record that `termios` takes.

**Law** `fieldsOf (termios r) = r`

members.name: getiflag
members.doc:
`getiflag t` is the input flags of `t`.

**Law** `getiflag t = #iflag (fieldsOf t)`, and `getoflag t = #oflag (fieldsOf t)`, and `getcflag t = #cflag (fieldsOf t)`, and `getlflag t = #lflag (fieldsOf t)`, and `getcc t = #cc (fieldsOf t)`

members.name: getoflag
members.doc: `getoflag t` is the output flags of `t`.

members.name: getcflag
members.doc: `getcflag t` is the line flags of `t`.

members.name: getlflag
members.doc: `getlflag t` is the local flags of `t`.

members.name: getcc
members.doc: `getcc t` is the array of control characters of `t`.

members.name: CF
members.doc: The speeds of a settings record, read and set.

members.name: CF.getospeed
members.doc: `getospeed t` is the speed at which `t` sends.

members.name: CF.getispeed
members.doc: `getispeed t` is the speed at which `t` receives.

members.name: CF.setospeed
members.doc:
`setospeed (t, s)` is `t` with `s` as the speed it sends at.

**Law** `CF.getospeed (CF.setospeed (t, s)) = s`

**Example** `CF.getospeed (CF.setospeed (termios {iflag = I.flags [], oflag = O.flags [], cflag = C.flags [], lflag = L.flags [], cc = V.cc [], ispeed = b9600, ospeed = b9600}, b38400)) = b38400`

members.name: CF.setispeed
members.doc:
`setispeed (t, s)` is `t` with `s` as the speed it receives at.

**Law** `CF.getispeed (CF.setispeed (t, s)) = s`

members.name: TC
members.doc:
The operations on a terminal itself: reading and writing its settings, and controlling its queues.

> **Reading** `Posix.TTY.TC/not-a-terminal-raises`. The page does not say
what happens on a descriptor that is not a terminal; POSIX reports
`notty`, so every operation here raises `OS.SysErr` for one.

members.name: TC.set_action
members.doc: When `setattr` is to take effect.

members.name: TC.sanow
members.doc: At once.

members.name: TC.sadrain
members.doc: Once what has been written has gone out.

members.name: TC.saflush
members.doc: Once what has been written has gone out, discarding what has come in.

members.name: TC.flow_action
members.doc: What `flow` is to do.

members.name: TC.ooff
members.doc: Hold output back.

members.name: TC.oon
members.doc: Let output go on.

members.name: TC.ioff
members.doc: Send the stop character, asking the terminal to hold back.

members.name: TC.ion
members.doc: Send the start character, asking the terminal to go on.

members.name: TC.queue_sel
members.doc: Which queue `flush` is to empty.

members.name: TC.iflush
members.doc: What has come in and not been read.

members.name: TC.oflush
members.doc: What has been written and not gone out.

members.name: TC.ioflush
members.doc: Both.

members.name: TC.getattr
members.doc:
`getattr fd` is the settings of the terminal `fd` is open on.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not a terminal.

members.name: TC.setattr
members.spec: val setattr : file_desc * set_action * termios -> unit
members.doc:
`setattr (fd, when, t)` gives the terminal the settings `t`, at the moment `when` names.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not a terminal, or the settings are
refused.

members.name: TC.sendbreak
members.doc:
`sendbreak (fd, n)` sends a break of `n` units, or of the usual length when `n` is 0.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not a terminal.

members.name: TC.drain
members.doc:
`drain fd` waits until what was written to the terminal has gone out.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not a terminal.

members.name: TC.flush
members.doc:
`flush (fd, which)` throws away what is in the queue that `which` names.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not a terminal.

members.name: TC.flow
members.doc:
`flow (fd, what)` holds the flow back or lets it go on, as `what` says.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not a terminal.

members.name: TC.getpgrp
members.doc:
`getpgrp fd` is the process group that the terminal sends its signals to.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not a terminal.

members.name: TC.setpgrp
members.doc:
`setpgrp (fd, pgid)` makes `pgid` the process group in the foreground of the terminal.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `fd` is not a terminal, or the change is
refused.

PRIM_IO.doc:
The layer under the streams: a reader is a source of elements, a writer a
sink for them, and both are records of the operations they happen to have.

A reader or a writer is a plain value that a program can make itself, out
of a file descriptor, a vector, a network connection or nothing at all.
Every operation is an `option`, because a source need not offer all of
them: a pipe cannot be positioned, a file cannot promise not to wait. What
is `NONE` is what the source cannot do; `augmentReader` and
`augmentWriter` fill in what can be built from the rest.

`readVec`, `readArr`, `writeVec` and `writeArr` are the operations that
may wait; the ones whose names end in `NB` never wait and answer `NONE`
instead. `block` waits until a read or a write would not; `canInput` and
`canOutput` say whether it would. A read returns fewer elements than asked
for when fewer are there, and the empty vector, or 0, at the end of the
stream.

`STREAM_IO` is the layer above: it buffers, keeps what was read, and turns
what these raise into the `cause` of an `IO.Io`.

**See also** `IO`, `STREAM_IO`, `TEXT_IO`, `BIN_IO`, `POSIX_IO`

> **Erratum** `PRIM_IO/slices-of-the-instances`. The specification
leaves `vector_slice` and `array_slice` abstract; in `TextPrimIO` and
`BinPrimIO` they are the slice types of the corresponding structures,
which is what every implementation does and what the suite relies on.

members.name: elem
members.doc: The type of the elements read and written.

members.name: vector
members.doc: The type of vectors of them: what a read returns and a write takes.

members.name: vector_slice
members.doc: The type of stretches of such a vector, which `writeVec` writes.

members.name: array
members.doc: The type of arrays of them: what `readArr` reads into.

members.name: array_slice
members.doc: The type of stretches of such an array, which `readArr` and `writeArr` work on.

members.name: pos
members.doc:
The type of positions in the source or the sink.

> **Implementation** `PRIM_IO.pos/of-the-instances`. `BinPrimIO.pos` is the
integer type of `Position`, and a position is the offset of a byte from
the start of the file, so `compare` is the order of those numbers.
`TextPrimIO.pos` is abstract, as the specification leaves it: a program
can compare positions and give them back to `setPos`, and nothing more.
`WideTextPrimIO.pos` is abstract as well, and a type of its own: nothing
says that a position in a stream of wide characters is one of a stream
of characters.

members.name: compare
members.doc:
`compare (p, q)` orders two positions: earlier in the stream is less.

**Law** `(compare (p, q) = EQUAL) = (p = q)`

**Example** `compare (0, 1) = LESS`

members.name: reader
members.spec:
datatype reader =
  RD of {name : string,
         chunkSize : int,
         readVec : (int -> vector) option,
         readArr : (array_slice -> int) option,
         readVecNB : (int -> vector option) option,
         readArrNB : (array_slice -> int option) option,
         block : (unit -> unit) option,
         canInput : (unit -> bool) option,
         avail : unit -> int option,
         getPos : (unit -> pos) option,
         setPos : (pos -> unit) option,
         endPos : (unit -> pos) option,
         verifyPos : (unit -> pos) option,
         close : unit -> unit,
         ioDesc : RuneIODesc.iodesc option}
members.doc:
A source of elements: its name, how much it likes to be read at a time, and the operations it has.

`readVec n` reads at most `n` elements and waits for at least one;
`readArr sl` reads into a stretch of an array and gives the number of
elements read; the `NB` pair do the same without waiting, and answer
`NONE` when they would have to. `block` waits until a read would not.
`canInput` says whether one would wait. `avail` is how many elements are
there without waiting, or `NONE` when that cannot be told. `getPos`,
`setPos`, `endPos` and `verifyPos` are the positions; `close` releases
the source; `ioDesc` is the descriptor the operating system knows it by,
for `OS.IO.poll`.

> **Reading** `PrimIO.reader/Size-for-a-negative-count`. The specification
recommends that a read of a negative number of elements raise `Size`,
and does not require it. The readers of this library raise it; MLton's
do not, and a reader a program makes need not.

> **Reading** `PRIM_IO.reader/after-close`. Once `close` has been called,
every function of the reader but `close` and `getPos` raises `IO.Io`
with the cause `IO.ClosedStream`. The specification says both that and
"raise `IO.ClosedStream`", so the suite accepts either from a reader
that Rune did not make.

> **Implementation** `PRIM_IO.reader/what-a-file-has`. The readers Rune makes
for a file offer `readVec`, `avail`, `close` and `ioDesc`, and the
positions only when the file has them; `augmentReader` derives the rest
that can be derived. Their `chunkSize` is 4096, and so is a writer's. A
file is a handle of the VM, 0, 1 and 2 for the standard ones, and
`ioDesc` is the descriptor of the system under it.

members.name: writer
members.spec:
datatype writer =
  WR of {name : string,
         chunkSize : int,
         writeVec : (vector_slice -> int) option,
         writeArr : (array_slice -> int) option,
         writeVecNB : (vector_slice -> int option) option,
         writeArrNB : (array_slice -> int option) option,
         block : (unit -> unit) option,
         canOutput : (unit -> bool) option,
         getPos : (unit -> pos) option,
         setPos : (pos -> unit) option,
         endPos : (unit -> pos) option,
         verifyPos : (unit -> pos) option,
         close : unit -> unit,
         ioDesc : RuneIODesc.iodesc option}
members.doc:
A sink for elements, with the operations of a reader turned around.

`writeVec sl` and `writeArr sl` write a stretch and give the number of
elements written, which may be fewer than the stretch holds; the caller
writes the rest. The `NB` pair never wait. `canOutput` says whether a
write would wait. The positions and `close` are as for a reader, and
`ioDesc` is again the descriptor.

> **Reading** `PRIM_IO.writer/after-close`. Once `close` has been called,
every function of the writer but `close` raises `IO.Io` with the cause
`IO.ClosedStream`.

> **Reading** `PRIM_IO.writer/partial-writes`. A write may write only part of
what it was given; `STREAM_IO` retries until everything is written.

members.name: openVector
members.doc:
`openVector v` is a reader that delivers the elements of `v` and is then at the end of its stream.

The data are there already, so the reader has every read operation and
waits for nothing.

**Example** `(case openVector (Byte.stringToBytes "abc") of RD {readVec = SOME read, ...} => Byte.bytesToString (read 2) | _ => "") = "ab"`

**Example** `(case openVector (Byte.stringToBytes "") of RD {name, ...} => name) = "<vector>"`

> **Reading** `PrimIO.openVector/readVecNB-is-there`. Nothing has to be
waited for, so `readVecNB` is present and always `SOME`, with `SOME` of
the empty vector once the vector is spent.

members.name: nullRd
members.doc:
`nullRd ()` is a reader that is at the end of its stream from the start.

> **Reading** `PrimIO.nullRd/is-a-closed-source`. It "acts like a reader that
is always at end-of-stream": every read gives nothing and waits for
nothing, it has no positions, and once closed it behaves as any other
closed reader.

**Example** `(case nullRd () of RD {readVec = SOME read, ...} => Word8Vector.length (read 10) | _ => ~1) = 0`

members.name: nullWr
members.doc:
`nullWr ()` is a writer that accepts everything and keeps nothing.

> **Reading** `PrimIO.nullWr/is-a-sink`. It "serves as a sink": every write
reports that it wrote all it was given, and once closed it behaves as
any other closed writer.

**Example** `(case nullWr () of WR {writeVec = SOME write, ...} => write (Word8VectorSlice.full (Byte.stringToBytes "abc")) | _ => ~1) = 3`

members.name: augmentReader
members.doc:
`augmentReader rd` is `rd` with the read operations that can be built from the ones it has.

A vector read becomes an array read by copying and the other way round;
a blocking read is a non-blocking one done after `block`; a
non-blocking read is a blocking one that `canInput` says will not wait.
An operation the reader already has is kept as it is, and the fields
that are not reads are unchanged.

> **Reading** `PrimIO.augmentReader/what-cannot-be-built`. What the table
does not reach stays `NONE`: there is no non-blocking read without
`canInput` or an `NB` operation to build it from, and no blocking read
without `block` or a blocking operation.

**Example** `(case augmentReader (RD {name = "one", chunkSize = 1, readVec = SOME (fn _ => Byte.stringToBytes "x"), readArr = NONE, readVecNB = NONE, readArrNB = NONE, block = NONE, canInput = NONE, avail = fn () => NONE, getPos = NONE, setPos = NONE, endPos = NONE, verifyPos = NONE, close = fn () => (), ioDesc = NONE}) of RD {readArr, readVecNB, ...} => (isSome readArr, isSome readVecNB)) = (true, false)`

members.name: augmentWriter
members.doc:
`augmentWriter wr` is `wr` with the write operations that can be built from the ones it has.

> **Implementation** `PrimIO.augmentWriter/the-whole-table`. The same table
as for a reader, turned around: every row of it is built, an operation
the writer has is kept as it is, and what cannot be reached stays
`NONE`.

**Example** `(case augmentWriter (WR {name = "one", chunkSize = 1, writeVec = SOME Word8VectorSlice.length, writeArr = NONE, writeVecNB = NONE, writeArrNB = NONE, block = NONE, canOutput = NONE, getPos = NONE, setPos = NONE, endPos = NONE, verifyPos = NONE, close = fn () => (), ioDesc = NONE}) of WR {writeArr, writeVecNB, ...} => (isSome writeArr, isSome writeVecNB)) = (true, false)`

REAL.doc:
Floating-point numbers: IEEE 754 arithmetic, the numbers that are not
ordinary (the infinities, the NaNs and the negative zero), and the
conversions to and from integers and text.

`Real` is the default structure, `LargeReal` the widest, and the sized
ones are `Real32` and `Real64`. A NaN, "not a number", is what an
operation answers where there is no value to give: it is equal to nothing,
itself included, so `==` is `false` for it and `compare` raises
`IEEEReal.Unordered`. Because of that the equality of the language is not available
at `real`; use `==` where equality is meant and `Real.compare` where an
order is.

There are two zeros, which `==` says are equal and `signBit` tells apart;
a computation that underflows keeps the sign it came from.

The functions that round come in two kinds: `realFloor` and its like stay
in `real`, `floor` and its like give an `int` and raise where the result
would not fit.

**See also** `MATH`, `IEEE_REAL`, `INTEGER`, `STRING_CVT`, `PACK_REAL`

> **Implementation** `Real.real/binary64`. `Real.real` is the top-level `real`,
the 64-bit IEEE double (`radix` 2, `precision` 53\), and so are `LargeReal`
and `Real64`; the optional `Real32` is binary32. The conversions to and
from text are correctly rounded, through the C library.

members.name: real
members.doc:
The type of floating-point numbers of this structure.

It does not admit equality: `=` would say that a NaN is equal to itself
and that the two zeros are different, and neither is what IEEE 754
means.

members.name: Math
members.spec: structure Math : MATH where type real = real
members.doc: The elementary functions at this type: `sqrt`, `sin`, `ln` and the rest.

members.name: radix
members.doc: The base in which the significand is written: 2 for every binary format.

members.name: precision
members.doc:
The number of digits of the significand, in base `radix`.

> **Implementation** `Real.precision/double`. 53 for binary64, which is 52
stored bits and the leading one that is not stored. The arithmetic must
show that precision and no more: `1.0 + 2^~52` is greater than `1.0`,
and `1.0 + 2^~53` rounds back to `1.0`.

members.name: maxFinite
members.doc: The largest finite number of this type.

members.name: minPos
members.doc: The smallest positive number of this type, which is subnormal and has few digits of precision.

members.name: minNormalPos
members.doc: The smallest positive normal number: the smallest with the full `precision` digits.

members.name: posInf
members.doc: Positive infinity, what a computation that grows without bound gives.

members.name: negInf
members.doc: Negative infinity.
`x + y` is the sum, correctly rounded.
`x - y` is the difference, correctly rounded.
`x * y` is the product, correctly rounded.

`x / y` is the quotient, correctly rounded.

Division by zero is not an error here: it gives an infinity of the
right sign, and `0.0 / 0.0` gives a NaN.

members.name: rem
members.doc:
`rem (x, y)` is what is left of `x` after taking away a whole number of `y`: `x - n * y` with `n` the quotient rounded towards zero.

It is computed exactly, whatever the magnitudes, and is a NaN when `x`
is infinite or `y` is zero; for an infinite `y` it is `x`.

> **Reading** `Real.rem/exact-multiple-negative-x`. The sign of a zero
remainder is left open: the specification asks for the sign of `x`, and
the definition `x - n * y` gives a positive zero.

`*+ (x, y, z)` is `x * y + z`.

> **Implementation** `Real.*+/fused`. Whether the multiplication and the
addition are rounded once or twice is left to the implementation.
`~x` is `x` with its sign bit inverted, the zeros and the NaNs included.

members.name: abs
members.doc: `abs x` is `x` with its sign bit clear.

members.name: min
members.doc:
`min (x, y)` is the smaller of the two, or the one that is not a NaN when the other is.

When both are NaNs the result is a NaN.

members.name: max
members.doc:
`max (x, y)` is the larger of the two, or the one that is not a NaN when the other is.

When both are NaNs the result is a NaN.

members.name: sign
members.doc:
`sign x` is \~1, 0 or 1, as `x` is negative, zero or positive.

**Raises** `Domain` if `x` is a NaN.

**Example** `sign ~0.0 = 0`

members.name: signBit
members.doc:
`signBit x` is `true` when the sign bit of `x` is set.

> **Reading** `Real.signBit/zeros`. It looks at the bit and not at the value,
so it tells the two zeros apart and answers for a NaN as well.

**Example** `signBit ~0.0 = true`

members.name: sameSign
members.doc:
`sameSign (x, y)` is `true` when `x` and `y` have the same sign bit.

**Law** `sameSign (x, y) = (signBit x = signBit y)`

members.name: copySign
members.doc: `copySign (x, y)` is `x` with the sign bit of `y`.

members.name: compare
members.doc:
`compare (x, y)` orders two reals.

**Raises** `IEEEReal.Unordered` if either is a NaN.

members.name: compareReal
members.doc:
`compareReal (x, y)` orders two reals, and answers `UNORDERED` where a NaN makes the question meaningless.

**Example** `compareReal (0.0 / 0.0, 1.0) = IEEEReal.UNORDERED`

`x < y`, `x <= y`, `x > y` and `x >= y` compare two reals.

Every one of them is `false` when either side is a NaN, so `x <= y` is
not the negation of `x > y`.

`x < y`, `x <= y`, `x > y` and `x >= y` compare two reals.

Every one of them is `false` when either side is a NaN, so `x <= y` is
not the negation of `x > y`.

`x < y`, `x <= y`, `x > y` and `x >= y` compare two reals.

Every one of them is `false` when either side is a NaN, so `x <= y` is
not the negation of `x > y`.

`x < y`, `x <= y`, `x > y` and `x >= y` compare two reals.

Every one of them is `false` when either side is a NaN, so `x <= y` is
not the negation of `x > y`.

`== (x, y)` is `true` when `x` and `y` are the same number.

The two zeros are the same number; a NaN is not even equal to itself.
This is the equality of IEEE 754 and what a program should use at
`real`. The specification writes it infix, which a program must declare
(`infix 4 ==`) before it can do the same.

**Example** `== (0.0, ~0.0) = true`

**Example** `== (0.0 / 0.0, 0.0 / 0.0) = false`
`!= (x, y)` is the negation of `== (x, y)`, so it is `true` when either is a NaN.

`?= (x, y)` is `true` when `x` and `y` are equal or either is a NaN: "unordered or equal".

**Law** `?= (x, y) = (unordered (x, y) orelse == (x, y))`

members.name: unordered
members.doc: `unordered (x, y)` is `true` when either is a NaN, so that no order relates them.

members.name: isFinite
members.doc: `isFinite x` is `true` when `x` is neither an infinity nor a NaN.

members.name: isNan
members.doc:
`isNan x` is `true` when `x` is a NaN.

**Example** `isNan (0.0 / 0.0) = true`

members.name: isNormal
members.doc: `isNormal x` is `true` when `x` is an ordinary number: finite, not zero and not subnormal.

members.name: class
members.doc: `class x` is which of the five kinds of number `x` is.

members.name: toManExp
members.spec: val toManExp : real -> {man : real, exp : int}
members.doc:
`toManExp x` is the significand and the exponent of `x`: the `man` and `exp` for which `x` is `man * radix^exp`.

> **Reading** `Real.toManExp/one`. The specification writes the range of the
significand as "1.0 \<= man \* radix \< radix", which for radix 2 means
`0.5 <= |man| < 1.0`: the convention of C's `frexp`, and not the one
that puts the point after the first digit. For a zero, an infinity or a
NaN the significand is `x` itself; the exponent of a zero is 0, and that
of an infinity or a NaN is left open.

**Example** `(fn {man, exp} => (toString man, exp)) (toManExp 8.0) = ("0.5", 4)`

members.name: fromManExp
members.spec: val fromManExp : {man : real, exp : int} -> real
members.doc:
`fromManExp {man, exp}` is `man * radix^exp`.

The result can be a zero or an infinity even for a finite `man` that is
not zero, where the product underflows or overflows. A zero, an infinity
or a NaN as `man` is the result.

**Example** `toString (fromManExp {man = 0.75, exp = 4}) = "12"`

**Law** `== (fromManExp (toManExp x), x)` for `isFinite x`

members.name: split
members.spec: val split : real -> {whole : real, frac : real}
members.doc:
`split x` is the whole part and the fractional part of `x`, each with the sign of `x`.

The whole part is `x` rounded towards zero. For an infinity the
fractional part is a zero, and for a NaN both are NaNs.

**Law** `== (#whole (split x) + #frac (split x), x)` for `not (isNan x)`

**Example** `(fn {whole, frac} => (toString whole, toString frac)) (split ~1.5) = ("~1", "~0.5")`

**Counterexample** `== (#whole (split (0.0 / 0.0)) + #frac (split (0.0 / 0.0)), 0.0 / 0.0)`, for a NaN is equal to nothing.

members.name: realMod
members.doc:
`realMod x` is the fractional part of `x`, with its sign.

**Law** `realMod x = #frac (split x)`

members.name: nextAfter
members.doc:
`nextAfter (x, y)` is the number of this type next to `x` in the direction of `y`.

> **Reading** `Real.nextAfter/equal-zeros-returns-r`. "If `r = t` then it
returns `r`": the two zeros are equal, so `nextAfter (~0.0, 0.0)` is
`~0.0`. C's `nextafter` returns `t` there, and MLton and Poly/ML follow
C.

A NaN in either argument gives a NaN, and an infinity `x` is the
result, whatever `y` is.

**Example** `== (nextAfter (0.0, 1.0), minPos) = true`

members.name: checkFloat
members.doc:
`checkFloat x` is `x` when it is finite, and raises otherwise.

It is how a program turns the silent results of IEEE arithmetic into
exceptions at the point it chooses.

**Raises** `Overflow` if `x` is an infinity; `Div` if `x` is a NaN.

members.name: realFloor
members.doc:
`realFloor x` is the largest whole number that is not greater than `x`, as a `real`.

An infinity and a NaN are returned as they are, by `realCeil`,
`realTrunc` and `realRound` too.

**Example** `toString (realFloor ~1.5) = "~2"`

> **Reading** `Real.realFloor/negzero-sign`. The specification is silent
about the sign of a zero result; IEEE 754 keeps the sign of the operand,
so `realFloor ~0.5` is `~0.0`. The same holds for `realCeil`,
`realTrunc` and `realRound`.

members.name: realCeil
members.doc:
`realCeil x` is the smallest whole number that is not less than `x`, as a `real`.

**Example** `toString (realCeil ~1.5) = "~1"`

members.name: realTrunc
members.doc:
`realTrunc x` is `x` rounded towards zero, as a `real`.

**Example** `toString (realTrunc ~1.5) = "~1"`

members.name: realRound
members.doc:
`realRound x` is `x` rounded to the nearest whole number, as a `real`.

> **Reading** `Real.realRound/tie-half`. A value exactly between two whole
numbers goes to the even one, as it does for `round`: the specification
states the rule under `round` alone, and IEEE 754's rounding to an
integral value agrees.

members.name: floor
members.doc:
`floor x` is the largest whole number that is not greater than `x`, as an `int`.

**Raises** `Overflow` if that number is outside the range of `Int.int`;
`Domain` if `x` is a NaN.

**Example** `floor ~1.5 = ~2`

> **Implementation** `Real.floor/at-the-ends-of-int`. An `int` has 63 bits and
a real 53, so near the ends of `int` not every integer is a real. `fromInt maxInt` is 2^62, which is one more than `maxInt`, and `floor` of it raises
`Overflow`; the largest real that `floor`, `ceil`, `trunc` and `round`
take is 2^62 - 512. `minInt` is a real, and `minInt - 0.5` is `minInt`
itself, so all four give `minInt` for it.

**Example** `(floor (fromInt (valOf Int.maxInt)) handle Overflow => 0) = 0`

**Example** `floor (fromInt (valOf Int.minInt)) = valOf Int.minInt`

members.name: ceil
members.doc:
`ceil x` is the smallest whole number that is not less than `x`, as an `int`.

**Raises** `Overflow` if it does not fit; `Domain` if `x` is a NaN.

**Example** `ceil ~1.5 = ~1`

members.name: trunc
members.doc:
`trunc x` is `x` rounded towards zero, as an `int`.

**Raises** `Overflow` if it does not fit; `Domain` if `x` is a NaN.

**Example** `trunc ~1.5 = ~1`

members.name: round
members.doc:
`round x` is `x` rounded to the nearest whole number, ties to even, as an `int`.

**Raises** `Overflow` if it does not fit; `Domain` if `x` is a NaN.

**Example** `round 2.5 = 2`

**Example** `round 3.5 = 4`

members.name: toInt
members.doc:
`toInt mode x` is `x` rounded to an `int` in the given rounding mode.

**Raises** `Overflow` if it does not fit; `Domain` if `x` is a NaN.

**Example** `toInt IEEEReal.TO_NEAREST 2.5 = 2`

members.name: toLargeInt
members.doc:
`toLargeInt mode x` is `x` rounded to a `LargeInt.int` in the given rounding mode.

Where `LargeInt` has no bounds this loses nothing, however large `x` is.

**Raises** `Overflow` if `x` is an infinity, or if the result does not fit
a bounded `LargeInt.int`; `Domain` if `x` is a NaN.

members.name: fromInt
members.doc:
`fromInt i` is `i` as a real, rounded in the current rounding mode when the type cannot hold it exactly.

The top-level `real` is this function.

**Example** `toString (fromInt ~7) = "~7"`

members.name: fromLargeInt
members.doc:
`fromLargeInt i` is `i` as a real, rounded once in the current rounding mode when the type cannot hold it exactly.

A magnitude beyond `maxFinite` gives an infinity of the sign of `i`.

> **Reading** `Real.fromLargeInt/tie-rounds-to-even-down`. The current
rounding mode is used; under the default one a value exactly between two
reals goes to the one whose last digit is even, and the digits that are
dropped decide the rest.

members.name: toLarge
members.doc: `toLarge x` is `x` as a `LargeReal.real`, which loses nothing.

members.name: fromLarge
members.doc:
`fromLarge mode x` is the number of this type nearest to `x`, rounded in the given mode.

> **Reading** `LargeReal/at-least-Real`. `LargeReal` is at least as wide as
`Real`, so this rounds only where it is wider.

members.name: fmt
members.doc:
`fmt spec x` is the text of `x` in the given notation.

`StringCvt.SCI`, `FIX` and `GEN` take a number of digits, and `EXACT`
writes as many as are needed to read the same number back. An infinity
is `"inf"` or `"~inf"` and a NaN is `"nan"`.

`SCI` and `FIX` write 6 digits after the point where the number is
`NONE`, and no point at all for `SOME 0`; `GEN` writes at most 12
significant digits where it is `NONE`.

**Raises** `Size` if `SCI` or `FIX` is given a negative number of digits,
or `GEN` fewer than 1. The specification says this happens "when
`fmt spec` is evaluated", before a real is given, so a partial
application already raises.

> **Reading** `Real.fmt/SCI-negzero`. A negative zero is written with its
sign, because the formats are described as `[~]?` and `signBit` is set;
MLton leaves the sign out.

> **Reading** `Real.fmt/GEN-integral-one`. In `GEN`, a number with no
fractional part is written without a point, as C's `gcvt` does, and the
shorter of the scientific and the fixed form is taken, a tie going to
the fixed one: `fmt (GEN NONE) 1.0` is `"1"` and `fmt (GEN NONE) 1000.0`
is `"1E3"`.

**Example** `fmt (StringCvt.FIX (SOME 2)) 3.14159 = "3.14"`

**Example** `fmt (StringCvt.SCI (SOME 2)) 1234.5 = "1.23E3"`

**Example** `fmt (StringCvt.GEN (SOME 3)) 1234.5 = "1230"`

**Example** `fmt (StringCvt.GEN (SOME 4)) 123456.0 = "123500"`, for the
digits beyond the four become zeros where the fixed form is the shorter.

**Example** `fmt StringCvt.EXACT 0.1 = "0.1"`, which is `fmt StringCvt.EXACT 0.1 = IEEEReal.toString (toDecimal 0.1)`.

members.name: toString
members.doc:
`toString x` is the text of `x` in the general notation with the default number of digits.

**Law** `toString x = fmt (StringCvt.GEN NONE) x`

**Example** `toString 1.0 = "1"`

**Example** `toString ~1.5E~5 = "~1.5E~5"`

members.name: scan
members.doc:
`scan getc strm` reads a real from `strm`.

It skips initial white space and then takes an optional sign and either
a decimal numeral with an optional point and exponent, or one of the
words `inf`, `infinity` and `nan` in any case. The answer is
`SOME (x, rest)`, or `NONE` when no numeral is there.

A numeral whose value is too large becomes an infinity and one too small
a zero; nothing is raised. A numeral that no real holds exactly is
rounded as `fromString` rounds it.

> **Reading** `Real.scan/what-is-left-in-the-stream`. A point needs a digit
after it, and so does the `E` of an exponent with its sign: what does not
complete is left in the stream. `"1."` gives 1.0 and leaves the point,
`"1E~"` gives 1.0 and leaves `E~`, and `"."`, `"~."` and `".E1"` give
`NONE`. Of the words the longest is tried first, so that `"infinit"` gives
infinity and leaves `init`.

> **Erratum** `REAL/scan-grammar-grouping`. The grammars of `scan` and of the
formats of `StringCvt.realfmt` lost their grouping on the pages. They are
read as `[+~-]?([0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)? | \.[0-9]+)([eE][+~-]?[0-9]+)?`, so that
the sign belongs to every alternative and the exponent may follow either.

**Example** `Option.map (fn (r, rest) => (toString r, Substring.string rest)) (scan Substring.getc (Substring.full "1.")) = SOME ("1", ".")`

members.name: fromString
members.doc:
`fromString s` is the real that the text `s` begins with, or `NONE`.

**Law** `fromString s = StringCvt.scanString scan s`

> **Reading** `Real.fromString/TO_NEGINF-negative`. The numeral is rounded in
the rounding mode that is in force, as in MLton and in C's `strtod`;
SML/NJ and Poly/ML always round to nearest. `Real32.fromString` rounds
once, straight to binary32, and not first to binary64.

**Example** `Option.map toString (fromString ".5e1x") = SOME "5"`

members.name: toDecimal
members.doc:
`toDecimal x` is the shortest decimal number that reads back as `x`.

`IEEEReal.toString` turns the result into text, and `fromDecimal` turns
it into `x` again. The conversion rounds to nearest, whatever rounding
mode is in force. For a zero, an infinity or a NaN the digits are none
and the exponent 0; the sign and the class are those of `x` in every
case.

> **Reading** `Real.toDecimal/shortest-digits`. The digits are the fewest
that `fromDecimal` reads back as the same real, not the exact expansion,
which every real has and which is long: `toDecimal 0.1` has the one
digit 1, where the real nearest to a tenth has 55.

**Example** `#digits (toDecimal 0.1) = [1]`

**Law** `== (valOf (fromDecimal (toDecimal x)), x) andalso signBit (valOf (fromDecimal (toDecimal x))) = signBit x` for `isNormal x orelse class x = IEEEReal.SUBNORMAL`

members.name: fromDecimal
members.doc:
`fromDecimal d` is the real nearest to the decimal number `d`, or `NONE` when a digit of `d` is outside 0 to 9.

The conversion rounds to nearest, whatever rounding mode is in force.
The class `ZERO` or `INF` gives a zero or an infinity and `NAN` a NaN,
each with the sign of `d`. For `NORMAL` and `SUBNORMAL` the value is
that of the digits, the exponent and the sign, whatever class it turns
out to have: no digits, or only zeros, give a zero, and a value too
large gives an infinity and one too small a zero.

**Example** `Option.map toString (fromDecimal {class = IEEEReal.NORMAL, sign = true, digits = [1, 5], exp = 1}) = SOME "~1.5"`

**Example** `isSome (fromDecimal {class = IEEEReal.NORMAL, sign = false, digits = [10], exp = 0}) = false`

REPL.doc:
What a program can ask of the REPL it runs in: its commands, as
functions, for init files, scripts and HOL4 (docs/repl.md, Commands).

In `rune-repl` the REPL puts its commands into the hooks of this
structure when it starts, as it puts its `use` into `Compiler`'s; in a
program compiled by `rune`, which has no REPL around it, every function
raises `Fail`.

> **Deviation** `REPL/not-in-the-specification`. The specification says
nothing of a REPL's commands; this signature is Rune's own.

**See also** `COMPILER`

members.name: command
members.doc:
`command line` runs a command of the REPL as if it had been typed:
`command ":set depth 5"`, with or without the `:`.

What the command writes goes where it would have gone.

**Raises** `Fail` where there is no REPL, or the command failed.

members.name: typeOf
members.doc:
`typeOf exp` is the type of the expression `exp`, which is not
evaluated, as `:type` shows it.

**Raises** `Fail` where there is no REPL or `exp` does not elaborate.

members.name: info
members.doc:
`info name` is what `:info` says of a name: what it is, and where it
was defined.

**Raises** `Fail` where there is no REPL or nothing has the name.

members.name: doc
members.doc:
`doc name` is the documentation `:doc` shows of a name of the Basis
Library, with its Markdown laid out for a terminal.

**Raises** `Fail` where there is no REPL or the name has none.

members.name: search
members.doc:
`search text` is what `:search` finds: values whose name holds the
text, or, where the text is a type, whose type is like it.

members.name: set
members.doc:
`set (setting, value)` changes a setting of the REPL, as `:set` does:
depth, length, string, width, feedback, prompt, prompt2, time.

**Raises** `Fail` where there is no REPL, or no such setting or value.

members.name: settings
members.doc: `settings ()` is each setting and its value, as `:show` lists them.

RUNTIME.doc:
What a program can ask about the machine it is running on: how much work it
has done, and how much memory that took.

The VM keeps these counters whether or not a program asks for them --
`runevm --count` and `runevm --stats` print them when it ends -- so reading
one costs a call and nothing else. None of them allocates, which is what
makes the nine numbers of a `stats` one consistent set: nothing but an
allocation moves the numbers of the heap, so they cannot drift apart while
they are being read.

This signature is Rune's own. Nothing here is portable, and a program that
only wants the time a computation took should use `Timer`, which is.

> **Deviation** `RUNTIME/not-in-the-specification`. The specification says
nothing about the implementation a program is running on: it has no
structure for allocation, for collection, or for what a call costs, and
deliberately so, since those are where implementations differ most. This
signature is therefore Rune's alone and a program that uses it does not
port. What the specification does give is `Timer`, whose `checkGCTime` is
the one thing it says about a collector.

**See also** `TIMER`, `OS_PROCESS`

members.name: stats
members.doc:
The counters of the VM, all of them since the program started.

`instructions` is the bytecode instructions executed, `bytes` and
`objects` what has been allocated in the heap -- including everything
since collected -- and `collections` the number of collections made:
`minorCollections` of them minor ones, which copy what of the nursery
is reached into the old space, `promoted` the bytes they copied, and
`majorCollections` of the whole heap -- full collections, and the
cycles of incremental marking of `runevm --gc low-pause`.

`live` is the bytes of objects in the heap: what the last collection
kept -- a minor one keeps every old object, dead or not -- plus what has
been allocated since. It is an upper bound on the live data, and is
exactly the live data just after a full collection, which `collect`
makes.
`heapSize` is the heap's size, the bytes of objects it holds before it
is collected, which grows as the collector needs it to.

The first three depend on the program and its input alone -- not on the
machine, the pointer width, the heap's size or when the collector ran --
so two runs of one program report the same. The other six depend on
the heap's size too, and so on `runevm --heap-size`, `--heap-fill`,
`--nursery` and `--gc`: two runs with the same options make the same
collections. None is a time: the collector's time is `Timer`'s
(`checkGCTime`) and `runevm --stats`'. `bytes` and
`live` leave out the boxes the representation makes for a real that
has no immediate, as `--count` does.

A value is 8 bytes and an object costs an 8-byte header and a payload
of 8-byte fields, so the smallest object is 16 bytes and a list cell,
one object of two fields, is 24.

members.name: stats
members.doc:
`stats ()` is the counters as they stand.

Reading them is itself work, so two calls with nothing between them do
not report the same `instructions`. Nothing between them allocates,
though, so the other five agree.

**Example** `#live (stats ()) <= #heapSize (stats ()) = true`

members.name: profile
members.doc:
`profile f` is what `f ()` returned, and what it cost: the difference
between the counters after it and the counters before.

What measuring costs is part of the answer, so `profile (fn () => ())`
is not all zero -- it is that cost, the instructions that read the
counters and at most one record, and subtracting it from another answer
removes it. It is the same number on every run and on every VM, since
the counters depend on the program and its input alone.

If `f` raises, the exception passes through and there are no counters:
this measures a call that returns.

**Example** `#objects (#2 (profile (fn () => ()))) <= 1`

members.name: collect
members.doc:
`collect ()` collects the heap now: a full collection.

Every unreachable object is freed. Under the collectors `runevm --gc`
chooses, what lives is marked where it lies -- the throughput
collector, the default, moves the objects of its sparsest blocks, and
the low-pause collector moves nothing -- which costs time proportional
to the live data and a little for every block of the heap; the copier
of `runevm --nursery 0` moves every surviving object but a large one,
which costs time proportional to the live data and to nothing else.
After it, the `live` of a `stats` is exactly the live data, where
otherwise it is an upper bound.

Nothing an SML program can see changes. Equality on a `ref` or an
`array` is the identity the collector maintains, not an address of the
moment, so this says when the cost of collecting is paid and never what
the program means.

**Example** `(collect (); #collections (stats ()) >= 1) = true`

members.name: share
members.doc:
`share ()` makes the equal immutable values of the heap one object
each, and is the bytes it freed.

It is what Poly/ML's PolyML.shareCommonData does before a heap is
saved.

Equal is as `=` has it, at any type: tuples, records, vectors and
values of a datatype whose fields are equal, strings of the same
characters, reals of the same bits, exception values of the same
constructor and argument. A `ref`, an `array`, a function and an
exception constructor keep their identity. A program that builds the
same values again and again --
terms, types, environments -- keeps one of each, the more so in an
image `save` writes after it.

It collects first and after, and it needs memory of its own about the
number of objects times 24 bytes; where it cannot have it, it shares
nothing and is 0. Nothing an SML program can see changes but `same`,
which may now say of two equal values that they are one.

**Example** `share () >= 0 = true`

members.name: frame
members.spec: type frame = { function : string, file : string, line : int, column : int }
members.doc:
One function on the call stack, and where in the source it has got to.

`function` is the name the compiler recorded, qualified by the structures
it is in; a function the source gives no name is `fn`. The position is
the call the function is waiting on, or, for the innermost frame, the
expression being evaluated. Where the program carries no position for
that instruction, `file` is `""` and both numbers are 0.

members.name: trace
members.doc:
`trace ()` is the frames, innermost first, of the call stack as it
stands, beginning with the function that called `trace`.

A tail call does not appear. It replaces the frame it is made from --
that is what makes a tail-recursive loop run in constant space -- so the
function it was made from is not on the stack to be reported.

**Example** `null (trace ()) = false`

members.name: printTrace
members.doc:
`printTrace out` writes the frames of `trace ()` to `out`, one to a
line, as the VM writes them under an uncaught exception.

members.name: same
members.doc:
`same (x, y)` is true when `x` and `y` are one object rather than two
equal ones.

It is the identity that `=` uses for a `ref` and an `array`, and it is
available where `=` is not: at a function type, at `real`, and at any
type that admits no equality. A collection does not change an answer.

What it says of anything else is not specified, and a program should not
ask. A value that is not in the heap at all -- an `int`, a `word`, a
`char`, `unit`, a constructor with no argument -- has no identity, and
the comparison is of the values themselves, so `same (1, 1)` is true and
`same (0.0, ~0.0)` is false because the two are different reals. Of the
rest, whether two equal values are one object is whatever the compiler
shared: two equal string constants are one, and two lists written
separately are two, until `share` makes them one.

**Example** `let val r = ref 0 in same (r, r) end = true`

members.name: world
members.doc:
Which of the two worlds a `save` came back in: the one that wrote the
image, or the one that was started from it.

members.name: save
members.doc:
`save file` writes the whole running program to `file` and is `Saved`.

A VM started as `runevm --restore file` carries on from inside that same
call, where it is `Restored`: one call and two worlds, as
`Posix.Process.fork` gives a pid to one process and 0 to another. The
file is not used up by being restored.

What is written is everything the program is made of -- the heap,
collected first (`collect`) so that it is the live data and no more,
the stacks, the counters, and the files it has open, which are opened again
by name and put back where they were left. What belongs to the process
rather than to the program is not: a socket, a directory stream and a
pipe are the system's, and a restored world does not have them. Nor is
what the program read ahead of its standard input and has not taken:
`TextIO.stdIn` in the restored world reads that world's standard input
from where it begins.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the image cannot be written.

members.name: restore
members.doc:
`restore file` becomes the world that `save` wrote to `file`. It does
not come back.

Where `save` gives two worlds one call, this gives one world another
call: the program carries on from inside the `save` that wrote the
image, where it is `Restored`. `runevm --restore file` does the same to
a VM that has just started; this does it to one that is running.

The image carries its own bytecode, so the program that runs afterwards
may be another program entirely -- it is a whole world, not a heap
dropped into this one. Nothing of the world that called `restore`
survives it: not its code, not its stack, not the files it had open.
Nothing written after the call is reached.

> **Implementation** `RUNTIME.restore/reads-before-it-replaces`. The image is
read into a world of its own and moved over only once it is whole, so a
file that is not an image, or is cut short, leaves the calling world
running and able to handle the exception. That is what makes the type
honest: `restore` either does not return or raises. The world it leaves
behind is let go at that moment -- its files closed, its heap and its
program freed -- so a program may restore as often as it likes without
growing.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the image cannot be read.

members.name: link
members.doc:
`link bytes` appends to the running program the unit that `bytes` is
the file of, and is the function that runs the unit's top-level
declarations.

A unit is a file of a program compiled a file at a time
(`rune --units --emit-units DIR`, docs/units.md): its code, and what it
names of the units compiled before it. Those must have been linked
first; what the unit names is found among what they declared, and its
code is checked as the VM checks a program's file. Nothing runs until
the function is called, and calling it again runs the declarations
again. A unit linked twice is two units, each with globals of its own;
the units linked after it see the second.

> **Implementation** `RUNTIME.link/the-last-unit-returns`. The top level of
a unit compiled with others ends by calling the next one's; linked
here, it returns to the caller instead.

**Raises** `Fail` if `bytes` is not a unit's file, is of another
instruction set, or names what no unit linked before it declared;
the message says which.

members.name: load
members.doc:
`load file` is `link` of what `file` holds.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the file cannot be read, and `Fail` as `link`
does.

members.name: catchInterrupt
members.doc:
`catchInterrupt ()` makes Ctrl-C, the user's interrupt, raise
`SML90.Interrupt` in the program from now on rather than end it.

It is true; it is false where the system has no interrupt to catch,
and the program goes on as before. The exception is raised where the
program next jumps back, as a loop does, or calls a function, or in a
read from a terminal that the interrupt cuts short, as a `raise` there
would raise it: the handlers, the frames and `trace` are what they
would be. A primitive that is running finishes first. The interrupt is
caught even where the program was started with it ignored, as a shell
starts one in the background, and a world started from an image that
`save` wrote catches it as the program that saved it did.

> **Implementation** `RUNTIME.catchInterrupt/polled`. The VM looks at the
interrupt at a jump back and at a call, in the interpreters and in the
code the JIT makes; the code of `runeopt` does not, and an interrupt
never comes to it.

members.name: maskInterrupt
members.doc:
`maskInterrupt b` says whether an interrupt waits rather than being
raised, and is what it said before.

From `maskInterrupt true` on, one waits until `maskInterrupt false`,
which raises it, if one came, as it returns. A section that an
interrupt must not cut in two is

```sml
let val was = maskInterrupt true
in (f () before ignore (maskInterrupt was))
   handle e => (ignore (maskInterrupt was); raise e)
end
```

The mask is off when a program starts, and a world started from an
image has the mask its program had.

**Raises** `SML90.Interrupt`, from `maskInterrupt false`, where one
waited.

**Example** `maskInterrupt (maskInterrupt true) = true`

members.name: version
members.doc:
The version of Rune that this program is running on, as
`runevm --version` prints it.

It is the name of the git tag of the commit Rune was built from, or
else that commit's abbreviated hash, with `-dirty` after it when the
tree had changes that were not committed.

The compiler and the VM are built from one string, so `rune --version`
says the same. It is not the version of the bytecode, which the VM
checks when it loads a program and which changes only when the file
format does.

**Example** `size version > 0 = true`

members.name: clock
members.doc:
`clock ()` is the time on a clock that never goes back, from a start
the system chooses.

`Time.now` is the time of day, which the system may set back or
forward; the difference of two `clock`s is time that passed. Its
resolution is the microsecond of a `Time.time`. A runner of tests times
its children by it (docs/plans/unit-testing.md, G1).

**Example** `Time.<= (clock (), clock ()) = true`

members.name: processors
members.doc:
`processors ()` is the number of processors this program may run on,
at least 1.

On Linux it counts the processors of the program's affinity mask, as
`nproc` does, and elsewhere the system's.

**Example** `processors () >= 1 = true`

SML90.doc:
What the 1990 library looked like, kept so that old programs still run.

Before the Basis Library there was the library of the first Definition:
`std_in` and `open_in` instead of `TextIO`, `explode` giving a list of
one-character strings instead of a list of characters, and an exception
for every arithmetic fault instead of `Overflow` and `Div`. This signature
is that library, and nothing here is meant for a new program.

The exceptions are raised where the new library raises `Overflow`, `Div`
or `Domain`, and the arithmetic and text functions are the old spellings
of what `MATH`, `CHAR` and `STRING` now offer.

**See also** `MATH`, `STRING`, `TEXT_IO`, `GENERAL`

> **Limitation** `SML90/is-history`. The page that defined this signature is no
longer among the specification's pages; it is transcribed from MLton's
library, which follows it, in the order the page had.

members.name: instream
members.doc: The type of an input stream, as the old library had it.

members.name: outstream
members.doc: The type of an output stream, as the old library had it.

members.name: Abs
members.doc:
Raised where `abs` of the least integer would overflow.

> **Implementation** `SML90.Abs/is-Overflow`. As in MLton and Poly/ML, `Abs`,
`Quot`, `Prod`, `Neg`, `Sum`, `Diff`, `Floor` and `Exp` are `Overflow`,
and `Mod` is `Div`: the operations of the Library raise those, and a
handler for one of the old names catches them.

members.name: Quot
members.doc: Raised by division that overflows; division by zero raises `Mod`.

members.name: Prod
members.doc: Raised by multiplication that overflows.

members.name: Neg
members.doc: Raised by negation that overflows.

members.name: Sum
members.doc: Raised by addition that overflows.

members.name: Diff
members.doc: Raised by subtraction that overflows.

members.name: Floor
members.doc: Raised by `floor` of a number no integer can hold.

members.name: Exp
members.doc: Raised by `exp` when the result is too large.

members.name: Sqrt
members.doc:
Raised by `sqrt` of a negative number.

> **Reading** `SML90.Sqrt/is-its-own-exception`. `Sqrt`, `Ln` and `Ord` are
exceptions of their own, as MLton and SML/NJ have them. Poly/ML makes
all three `Overflow`, which loses what went wrong.

members.name: Ln
members.doc:
Raised by `ln` of a number that is not positive.

> **Reading** `SML90.Ln/is-its-own-exception`. As `Sqrt`: an exception of its
own, not `Overflow`.

members.name: Ord
members.doc:
Raised by `ord` of the empty string.

> **Reading** `SML90.Ord/is-its-own-exception`. As `Sqrt`: an exception of
its own, not `Overflow` and not `Subscript`.

members.name: Mod
members.doc: Raised by the remainder of a division by zero.

members.name: Io
members.doc: Raised when an I/O operation fails, carrying the message alone.

members.name: Interrupt
members.doc:
Raised by the user's interrupt, Ctrl-C, in a program that has asked
for it with `Runtime.catchInterrupt`.

> **Implementation** `SML90.Interrupt/when-caught`. Until a program asks,
the interrupt ends it, as the system ends any process.

members.name: sqrt
members.doc:
`sqrt x` is the square root of `x`.

**Raises** `Sqrt` if `x` is negative.

**Example** `((sqrt ~1.0; "root") handle Sqrt => "Sqrt") = "Sqrt"`

members.name: exp
members.doc:
`exp x` is `e` to the power `x`.

**Raises** `Exp` if the result is too large.

members.name: ln
members.doc:
`ln x` is the natural logarithm of `x`.

**Raises** `Ln` if `x` is not positive.

**Example** `((ln 0.0; "log") handle Ln => "Ln") = "Ln"`

members.name: sin
members.doc: `sin x` is the sine of `x` radians.

members.name: cos
members.doc: `cos x` is the cosine of `x` radians.

members.name: arctan
members.doc: `arctan x` is the angle in radians whose tangent is `x`, between `~pi/2` and `pi/2`.

members.name: ord
members.doc:
`ord s` is the code of the first character of `s`.

**Raises** `Ord` if `s` is empty.

**Example** `ord "a" = 97`

members.name: chr
members.doc:
`chr n` is the one-character string whose character has the code `n`.

**Raises** `Chr` if `n` is no character's code.

**Example** `chr 97 = "a"`

members.name: explode
members.doc:
`explode s` is the characters of `s`, each as a string of its own.

The `explode` of `STRING` gives a list of characters; this is the older
one.

**Example** `explode "ab" = ["a", "b"]`

members.name: implode
members.doc:
`implode l` is the strings of `l`, one after another.

**Example** `implode ["a", "bc"] = "abc"`

members.name: lookahead
members.doc:
`lookahead f` is the next character of `f` as a string, without removing it, or the empty string at the end.

**Raises** `Io` if the stream cannot be read.

> **Reading** `SML90.lookahead/closed-stream-is-empty`. A stream that has been
closed is at its end, so it gives the empty string as well, and not `Io`.

members.name: std_in
members.doc: The standard input of the program.

members.name: std_out
members.doc: The standard output of the program.

members.name: open_in
members.doc:
`open_in name` is a stream reading the file `name`.

**Raises** `Io` if the file cannot be opened.

members.name: open_out
members.doc:
`open_out name` is a stream writing the file `name`, which it empties or creates.

**Raises** `Io` if the file cannot be opened.

members.name: close_in
members.doc: `close_in f` closes the input stream `f`.

members.name: close_out
members.doc: `close_out f` closes the output stream `f`.

members.name: input
members.doc:
`input (f, n)` is at most `n` characters read from `f`, and fewer at the end of the stream.

**Law** `(input (f, n) = "") = end_of_stream f` for `n > 0`

**Raises** `Io` if the stream cannot be read.

members.name: output
members.doc:
`output (f, s)` writes `s` to `f`.

**Raises** `Io` if the stream cannot be written.

members.name: end_of_stream
members.doc: `end_of_stream f` is `true` when nothing is left to read in `f`.

SOCKET.doc:
Sockets: connections between processes, on one machine or across a
network.

A socket carries two type variables that hold nothing but say what may be
done with it. The first is its address family, so that an address of one
family cannot be given to a socket of another; the second is what kind of
socket it is -- `dgram` for one that sends messages, `passive stream` for
one that is waiting for connections, `active stream` for one that is
connected. `listen` needs a passive socket, `accept` turns one into an
active one, and the send and receive functions need an active one. A
program that gets the family or the mode wrong does not compile.

`INET_SOCK` and `UNIX_SOCK` make the sockets of the two families;
`GENERIC_SOCK` makes one of any family.

The operations come in families of their own. `sendVec` and `sendArr`
differ in where the bytes come from, the primed forms take flags, and the
ones whose names end in `NB` never wait and answer `NONE` or `false`
instead. `Ctl` reads and sets the options of a socket.

**See also** `INET_SOCK`, `UNIX_SOCK`, `GENERIC_SOCK`, `NET_HOST_DB`, `OS_IO`

> **Erratum** `SOCKET/recvVecFrom-type-variable`. The page gives
`recvVecFrom` and the three like it the result `Word8Vector.vector * 'sock_type sock_addr`, a type variable that occurs nowhere else in the
type. That is a slip for `'af`: the address a message came from is in the
family of the socket, as it is for `recvArrFrom`, and as the description
says. It is written `'af` here.

> **Implementation** `SOCKET/ipv6-is-a-family-of-the-system`. The page names
no address family: "AF.list returns a list of all the available address
families", so the set is the system's. `INET6` is among them here, and
`INET6_SOCK`, which is Rune's own, has the sockets and addresses of it;
`NetHostDB` stays the IPv4 database the specification defines

> **Implementation** `Socket.sock/is-a-descriptor`. A socket is the system's
descriptor and a `sock_addr` the bytes of a `sockaddr`; the type variables
are phantoms and hold nothing. The `NB` forms put the descriptor into
non-blocking mode for the call and back afterwards. Sending to a peer that
has gone fails with the condition `pipe` rather than raising the signal of
that name.

members.name: sock
members.doc: The type of a socket: its address family, then what kind of socket it is.

members.name: sock_addr
members.doc: The type of an address in the family `'af`.

members.name: dgram
members.doc: The kind of a socket that sends messages, each to an address of its own.

members.name: stream
members.doc: The kind of a socket that carries a stream of bytes; `'mode` says whether it is listening or connected.

members.name: passive
members.doc: The mode of a stream socket that is waiting for connections.

members.name: active
members.doc: The mode of a stream socket that is connected.

members.name: AF
members.doc: The address families the system knows.

members.name: AF.addr_family
members.doc: The type of an address family, the one of `NetHostDB`.

members.name: AF.list
members.doc: `list ()` is the families this system has, each with its name.

members.name: AF.toString
members.doc:
`toString af` is the name of `af`.

**Example** `AF.toString INetSock.inetAF = "INET"`

members.name: AF.fromString
members.doc:
`fromString s` is `SOME` of the family called `s`, or `NONE`.

> **Reading** `Socket.AF.fromString/without-the-prefix`. A name is the C
constant without its leading `"AF_"`: `"INET"` and `"UNIX"`, so
`"AF_INET"` gives `NONE`.

**Law** `AF.fromString (AF.toString af) = SOME af`

members.name: SOCK
members.doc: The kinds of socket the system knows.

members.name: SOCK.sock_type
members.doc: The type of a kind of socket, as the system names it.

members.name: SOCK.stream
members.doc: A stream of bytes that arrives in order and whole.

members.name: SOCK.dgram
members.doc: Separate messages, which may be lost or arrive out of order.

members.name: SOCK.list
members.doc: `list ()` is the kinds this system has, each with its name.

members.name: SOCK.toString
members.doc:
`toString st` is the name of `st`.

**Example** `SOCK.toString SOCK.stream = "STREAM"`

members.name: SOCK.fromString
members.doc:
`fromString s` is `SOME` of the kind called `s`, or `NONE`.

**Law** `SOCK.fromString (SOCK.toString st) = SOME st`

members.name: Ctl
members.doc:
The options of a socket, read and set.

> **Implementation** `Socket.Ctl/defaults-are-the-systems`. The values a new
socket starts with are those of the C socket interface, which has every
flag here off. The suite sets `DEBUG` to `false` only, since turning it
on needs privileges.

members.name: Ctl.getDEBUG
members.doc: `getDEBUG sock` is `true` when the system is recording what the socket does.

members.name: Ctl.setDEBUG
members.doc: `setDEBUG (sock, b)` asks the system to record what the socket does, or to stop.

members.name: Ctl.getREUSEADDR
members.doc: `getREUSEADDR sock` is `true` when the socket may bind an address that was lately in use.

members.name: Ctl.setREUSEADDR
members.doc: `setREUSEADDR (sock, b)` allows or forbids binding an address that was lately in use.

members.name: Ctl.getKEEPALIVE
members.doc: `getKEEPALIVE sock` is `true` when the connection is checked while it is idle.

members.name: Ctl.setKEEPALIVE
members.doc: `setKEEPALIVE (sock, b)` asks for the connection to be checked while it is idle, or not.

members.name: Ctl.getDONTROUTE
members.doc: `getDONTROUTE sock` is `true` when messages go to the local network only.

members.name: Ctl.setDONTROUTE
members.doc: `setDONTROUTE (sock, b)` keeps messages on the local network, or lets them be routed.

members.name: Ctl.getLINGER
members.doc:
`getLINGER sock` is `SOME t` when closing waits up to `t` for what was sent, or `NONE` when it does not wait.

> **Implementation** `Socket.Ctl.getLINGER/whole-seconds`. The system keeps
the time in a `struct linger`, in whole seconds.

members.name: Ctl.setLINGER
members.spec: val setLINGER : ('af, 'sock_type) sock * Time.time option -> unit
members.doc:
`setLINGER (sock, SOME t)` makes closing wait up to `t`; `NONE` makes it not wait.

**Raises** `Time` if `t` is negative or is 2^31 seconds or more, which
the system's `int` cannot hold.

members.name: Ctl.getBROADCAST
members.doc: `getBROADCAST sock` is `true` when the socket may send to a broadcast address.

members.name: Ctl.setBROADCAST
members.doc: `setBROADCAST (sock, b)` allows or forbids sending to a broadcast address.

members.name: Ctl.getOOBINLINE
members.doc: `getOOBINLINE sock` is `true` when urgent data arrive in the ordinary stream.

members.name: Ctl.setOOBINLINE
members.doc: `setOOBINLINE (sock, b)` puts urgent data into the ordinary stream, or keeps them apart.

members.name: Ctl.getSNDBUF
members.doc: `getSNDBUF sock` is the size in bytes of the room the system keeps for what is sent.

members.name: Ctl.setSNDBUF
members.doc:
`setSNDBUF (sock, n)` asks for `n` bytes of room for what is sent.

> **Implementation** `Socket.Ctl.setSNDBUF/at-least`. The system may give
more room than was asked for -- Linux doubles it -- so the size read
back is only bound to be at least `n`.

members.name: Ctl.getRCVBUF
members.doc: `getRCVBUF sock` is the size in bytes of the room the system keeps for what arrives.

members.name: Ctl.setRCVBUF
members.doc: `setRCVBUF (sock, n)` asks for `n` bytes of room for what arrives.

members.name: Ctl.getTYPE
members.doc:
`getTYPE sock` is the kind of socket that `sock` is.

**Example** `let val s = INetSock.TCP.socket () in Ctl.getTYPE s = SOCK.stream before close s end = true`

members.name: Ctl.getERROR
members.doc: `getERROR sock` is `true` when the socket has an error waiting, which reading it clears.

members.name: Ctl.getPeerName
members.doc:
`getPeerName sock` is the address of the other end.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the socket is not connected.

members.name: Ctl.getSockName
members.doc:
`getSockName sock` is the address the socket is bound to.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if it is not bound.

members.name: Ctl.getNREAD
members.doc: `getNREAD sock` is how many bytes can be read from the socket without waiting.

members.name: Ctl.getATMARK
members.spec: val getATMARK : ('af, active stream) sock -> bool
members.doc:
`getATMARK sock` is `true` when the next byte to be read is the urgent one.

> **Implementation** `Socket.Ctl.getATMARK/the-last-byte-is-urgent`. The
mark falls where the host's TCP puts it: sending `"abc"` out of band
puts it after `"ab"`, the last byte being the urgent one.

members.name: sameAddr
members.doc: `sameAddr (a, b)` is `true` when the two addresses are the same one.

members.name: familyOfAddr
members.doc:
`familyOfAddr a` is the address family that `a` belongs to.

**Example** `familyOfAddr (INetSock.any 0) = INetSock.inetAF`

members.name: bind
members.doc:
`bind (sock, a)` gives the socket the address `a`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the address is in use or may not be taken.

members.name: listen
members.spec: val listen : ('af, passive stream) sock * int -> unit
members.doc:
`listen (sock, n)` makes the socket wait for connections, keeping up to `n` of them unanswered.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the socket is not bound.

members.name: accept
members.spec: val accept : ('af, passive stream) sock -> ('af, active stream) sock * 'af sock_addr
members.doc:
`accept sock` waits for a connection and is a socket on it and the address it came from.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the socket is not listening, or the wait
fails.

members.name: acceptNB
members.spec: val acceptNB : ('af, passive stream) sock -> (('af, active stream) sock * 'af sock_addr) option
members.doc:
`acceptNB sock` is `accept` that does not wait: `NONE` when no connection is there.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the socket is not listening.

members.name: connect
members.doc:
`connect (sock, a)` connects the socket to the address `a`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the connection is refused or cannot be made.

members.name: connectNB
members.doc:
`connectNB (sock, a)` is `connect` that does not wait, and is `true` when the connection is already made.

When it is `false` the connection is being made; `select` says when it
is done.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the connection is refused.

members.name: close
members.doc:
`close sock` closes the socket.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if it was not open.

members.name: shutdown_mode
members.doc: Which half of a connection `shutdown` is to end.

members.name: shutdown
members.spec: val shutdown : ('af, 'mode stream) sock * shutdown_mode -> unit
members.doc:
`shutdown (sock, mode)` ends the half of the connection that `mode` names, without closing the socket.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the socket is not connected.

> **Reading** `Socket.shutdown/peer-sees-the-end`. The page says only that
"further sends will be disallowed"; the other end of a socket shut down
for sending sees the end of its stream, after everything sent before it
has arrived.

**Example** `let val (a, b) = UnixSock.Strm.socketPair () in shutdown (a, NO_SENDS); Word8Vector.length (recvVec (b, 10)) end = 0`

members.name: sock_desc
members.doc: The type that names a socket to `select`, whatever its family and mode.

members.name: sockDesc
members.doc: `sockDesc sock` is the descriptor of `sock`, for `select`.

members.name: sameDesc
members.doc: `sameDesc (a, b)` is `true` when the two descriptors are of the same socket.

members.name: select
members.spec:
val select : {rds : sock_desc list, wrs : sock_desc list, exs : sock_desc list, timeout : Time.time option}
             -> {rds : sock_desc list, wrs : sock_desc list, exs : sock_desc list}
members.doc:
`select {rds, wrs, exs, timeout}` waits until one of the sockets is ready, and is those that are.

A `timeout` of `NONE` waits as long as it must.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if a descriptor is not one of an open socket, or
`timeout` is negative.

> **Implementation** `Socket.select/is-poll`. It is `OS.IO.poll`, so a
negative timeout is refused rather than taken to mean "no timeout".

**Example** `null (#rds (select {rds = [], wrs = [], exs = [], timeout = SOME Time.zeroTime})) = true`

members.name: ioDesc
members.doc: `ioDesc sock` is the socket as an `OS.IO.iodesc`, which `OS.IO.poll` takes.

members.name: out_flags
members.doc: How something is to be sent: without routing, or as urgent data.

members.name: in_flags
members.doc: How something is to be received: looking without taking, or taking urgent data.

members.name: sendVec
members.spec: val sendVec : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8VectorSlice.slice -> int
members.doc:
`sendVec (sock, sl)` sends the bytes of `sl` and is the number it sent, which may be fewer.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the socket is not connected, or the other end has
gone.

**Example** `let val (a, b) = UnixSock.Strm.socketPair () in ignore (sendVec (a, Word8VectorSlice.full (Byte.stringToBytes "hi"))); Byte.bytesToString (recvVec (b, 2)) end = "hi"`

members.name: sendArr
members.spec: val sendArr : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8ArraySlice.slice -> int
members.doc: `sendArr (sock, sl)` sends the bytes of the array stretch `sl` and is the number it sent.

members.name: sendVec'
members.spec: val sendVec' : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8VectorSlice.slice * out_flags -> int
members.doc: `sendVec' (sock, sl, flags)` is `sendVec` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: sendArr'
members.spec: val sendArr' : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8ArraySlice.slice * out_flags -> int
members.doc: `sendArr' (sock, sl, flags)` is `sendArr` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: sendVecNB
members.spec: val sendVecNB : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8VectorSlice.slice -> int option
members.doc: `sendVecNB (sock, sl)` is `sendVec` that does not wait: `NONE` when it would have to.

members.name: sendVecNB'
members.spec: val sendVecNB' : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8VectorSlice.slice * out_flags -> int option
members.doc: `sendVecNB' (sock, sl, flags)` is `sendVecNB` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: sendArrNB
members.spec: val sendArrNB : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8ArraySlice.slice -> int option
members.doc: `sendArrNB (sock, sl)` is `sendArr` that does not wait.

members.name: sendArrNB'
members.spec: val sendArrNB' : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8ArraySlice.slice * out_flags -> int option
members.doc: `sendArrNB' (sock, sl, flags)` is `sendArrNB` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: recvVec
members.spec: val recvVec : ('af, active stream) sock * int -> Word8Vector.vector
members.doc:
`recvVec (sock, n)` receives at most `n` bytes, waiting for at least one, and is what came.

The empty vector means that the other end has finished sending.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the socket is not connected; `Size` if `n` is
negative or more than `Word8Vector.maxLen`.

> **Reading** `Socket.recvVec/zero-returns-at-once`. "If `n` is 0 the empty
vector is returned": it is returned at once, without waiting for
anything, where the system's own call would wait.

**Example** `let val (a, _) = UnixSock.Strm.socketPair () in Word8Vector.length (recvVec (a, 0)) end = 0`

members.name: recvVec'
members.spec: val recvVec' : ('af, active stream) sock * int * in_flags -> Word8Vector.vector
members.doc: `recvVec' (sock, n, flags)` is `recvVec` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: recvArr
members.spec: val recvArr : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8ArraySlice.slice -> int
members.doc: `recvArr (sock, sl)` receives into the stretch `sl` and is the number of bytes that came, 0 at the end.

members.name: recvArr'
members.spec: val recvArr' : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8ArraySlice.slice * in_flags -> int
members.doc: `recvArr' (sock, sl, flags)` is `recvArr` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: recvVecNB
members.spec: val recvVecNB : ('af, active stream) sock * int -> Word8Vector.vector option
members.doc:
`recvVecNB (sock, n)` is `recvVec` that does not wait: `NONE` when nothing is there.

> **Reading** `Socket.recvVecNB/zero-is-SOME`. Since `recvVec (sock, 0)`
gives the empty vector without waiting, `recvVecNB (sock, 0)` is `SOME`
of the empty vector and not `NONE`, however little has arrived.

members.name: recvVecNB'
members.spec: val recvVecNB' : ('af, active stream) sock * int * in_flags -> Word8Vector.vector option
members.doc: `recvVecNB' (sock, n, flags)` is `recvVecNB` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: recvArrNB
members.spec: val recvArrNB : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8ArraySlice.slice -> int option
members.doc: `recvArrNB (sock, sl)` is `recvArr` that does not wait.

members.name: recvArrNB'
members.spec: val recvArrNB' : ('af, active stream) sock * Word8ArraySlice.slice * in_flags -> int option
members.doc: `recvArrNB' (sock, sl, flags)` is `recvArrNB` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: sendVecTo
members.spec: val sendVecTo : ('af, dgram) sock * 'af sock_addr * Word8VectorSlice.slice -> unit
members.doc:
`sendVecTo (sock, a, sl)` sends the bytes of `sl` as one message to the address `a`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the message cannot be sent.

members.name: sendArrTo
members.spec: val sendArrTo : ('af, dgram) sock * 'af sock_addr * Word8ArraySlice.slice -> unit
members.doc: `sendArrTo (sock, a, sl)` sends the bytes of the array stretch `sl` as one message to `a`.

members.name: sendVecTo'
members.spec: val sendVecTo' : ('af, dgram) sock * 'af sock_addr * Word8VectorSlice.slice * out_flags -> unit
members.doc: `sendVecTo' (sock, a, sl, flags)` is `sendVecTo` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: sendArrTo'
members.spec: val sendArrTo' : ('af, dgram) sock * 'af sock_addr * Word8ArraySlice.slice * out_flags -> unit
members.doc: `sendArrTo' (sock, a, sl, flags)` is `sendArrTo` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: sendVecToNB
members.spec: val sendVecToNB : ('af, dgram) sock * 'af sock_addr * Word8VectorSlice.slice -> bool
members.doc: `sendVecToNB (sock, a, sl)` is `sendVecTo` that does not wait, and is `true` when it sent.

members.name: sendVecToNB'
members.spec: val sendVecToNB' : ('af, dgram) sock * 'af sock_addr * Word8VectorSlice.slice * out_flags -> bool
members.doc: `sendVecToNB' (sock, a, sl, flags)` is `sendVecToNB` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: sendArrToNB
members.spec: val sendArrToNB : ('af, dgram) sock * 'af sock_addr * Word8ArraySlice.slice -> bool
members.doc: `sendArrToNB (sock, a, sl)` is `sendArrTo` that does not wait, and is `true` when it sent.

members.name: sendArrToNB'
members.spec: val sendArrToNB' : ('af, dgram) sock * 'af sock_addr * Word8ArraySlice.slice * out_flags -> bool
members.doc: `sendArrToNB' (sock, a, sl, flags)` is `sendArrToNB` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: recvVecFrom
members.spec: val recvVecFrom : ('af, dgram) sock * int -> Word8Vector.vector * 'af sock_addr
members.doc: `recvVecFrom (sock, n)` receives one message of at most `n` bytes, and is it and where it came from.

members.name: recvVecFrom'
members.spec: val recvVecFrom' : ('af, dgram) sock * int * in_flags -> Word8Vector.vector * 'af sock_addr
members.doc: `recvVecFrom' (sock, n, flags)` is `recvVecFrom` with the flags `flags`.

members.name: recvArrFrom
members.spec: val recvArrFrom : ('af, dgram) sock * Word8ArraySlice.slice -> int * 'af sock_addr
members.doc: `recvArrFrom (sock, sl)` receives one message into the stretch `sl`, and is its length and where it came from.

STREAM_IO.doc:
Streams as values: reading gives the elements and the stream that is left,
so a stream can be kept, read twice, and read from again where it was.

An instream is a position in a chain of segments that the reader fills in
as they are wanted, and reading never changes what a stream in hand holds:
`input f` twice gives the same elements twice, because the second call
works on the same `f`. That is what makes lookahead and backtracking
possible without a buffer of one's own, and what `TEXT_IO.scanStream`
uses.

The chain goes on after an end of stream, because a file may grow: a
stream past an end of stream reads what was appended since. So an end of
stream is a place in the chain, not a state of the stream, and a stream
may pass several of them. `input`, `input1` and `inputN` move past the one
they meet; `endOfStream` only looks.

An outstream, in contrast, is imperative: `output` writes, and holds what
the buffer mode says to hold. `getReader` and `getWriter` take the reader
or the writer back out and leave the stream truncated or terminated; after
that the stream is done with.

Whatever a reader or a writer raises is caught and raised again as the
`cause` of an `IO.Io`, with the name of that reader or writer.

**See also** `IO`, `PRIM_IO`, `TEXT_STREAM_IO`, `IMPERATIVE_IO`, `TEXT_IO`

members.name: elem
members.doc: The type of the elements.

members.name: vector
members.doc: The type of vectors of them, which a read returns and `output` takes.

members.name: instream
members.doc:
The type of the functional input streams.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.instream/segments-are-shared`. Two streams that share
a segment read the same elements from it: the reader is asked for a
chunk once, and the chunk stays in the chain. The chain continues past
an end of stream, so a stream that was kept from before an end of stream
still reads what was there.

members.name: outstream
members.doc: The type of the output streams, which are not functional: `output` changes what they hold.

members.name: out_pos
members.doc: A position in an outstream, together with the stream it is in.

members.name: reader
members.doc: The type of the readers the streams are built on, a `PRIM_IO.reader`.

members.name: writer
members.doc: The type of the writers the streams are built on, a `PRIM_IO.writer`.

members.name: pos
members.doc: The type of the positions of that reader and writer, a `PRIM_IO.pos`.

members.name: input
members.doc:
`input f` is the elements that are left in the current chunk and the stream after them.

At an end of stream it is the empty vector and the stream immediately
past that end of stream, so a following `input` reads what the source
has gained since.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the reader fails, or if it offers no way to read that
waits.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.input/Io-carries-the-reader`. The page of `IO` says
what the fields hold: the exception the reader raised is the `cause` and
the reader's own name is the `name`.

**Law** `let val (a, _) = input f val (b, _) = input f in a = b end`: a
stream in hand does not change

**Example** `Byte.bytesToString (#1 (input (mkInstream (BinPrimIO.openVector (Byte.stringToBytes "ab"), Byte.stringToBytes "")))) = "ab"`

members.name: input1
members.doc:
`input1 f` is `SOME` of the first element and the stream after it, or `NONE` at an end of stream.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the reader fails.

**Law** `isSome (input1 f) = not (endOfStream f)` when the reader does not
fail

A stream is a value, and reading from it gives another, so reading the
same stream twice gives the same element:

**Example** `let val s = TextIO.getInstream (TextIO.openString "abc") in (Option.map #1 (TextIO.StreamIO.input1 s), Option.map #1 (TextIO.StreamIO.input1 s)) end = (SOME #"a", SOME #"a")`

members.name: inputN
members.spec: val inputN : instream * int -> vector * instream
members.doc:
`inputN (f, n)` is `n` elements and the stream after them, or all there are before the next end of stream.

**Raises** `Size` if `n < 0`, or if the vector to be returned would be
longer than the greatest length of a vector.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.inputN/fewer-is-past-the-end-of-stream`. When fewer
than `n` elements come before an end of stream, the stream returned is
the one `inputAll` would give: immediately past that end of stream.
Exactly `n` elements that end at one leave the stream before it.

**Example** `let val (v, f) = inputN (mkInstream (BinPrimIO.openVector (Byte.stringToBytes "abc"), Byte.stringToBytes ""), 2) in (Byte.bytesToString v, Byte.bytesToString (#1 (inputAll f))) end = ("ab", "c")`

members.name: inputAll
members.doc:
`inputAll f` is everything up to the next end of stream, and the stream past it.
