**Example** `Byte.bytesToString (#1 (inputAll (mkInstream (BinPrimIO.openVector (Byte.stringToBytes "abc"), Byte.stringToBytes "")))) = "abc"`

members.name: canInput
members.spec: val canInput : instream * int -> int option
members.doc:
`canInput (f, n)` is how many of `n` elements, at most, can be read without waiting, or `NONE`.

`NONE` means that not even one element can be had without waiting.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.canInput/what-is-counted`. Counted are the elements
already in the chain, then what the reader's `readVecNB` yields, which
the stream keeps: such a lookahead commits the stream to those elements.
A reader without `readVecNB` is asked for `avail` instead.

**Raises** `Size` if `n < 0`.

**Example** `canInput (mkInstream (BinPrimIO.openVector (Byte.stringToBytes "abc"), Byte.stringToBytes ""), 2) = SOME 2`

members.name: closeIn
members.doc:
`closeIn f` marks the stream closed and closes its reader.

Closing a truncated or an already closed stream is allowed and does
nothing more. A closed stream reads as if it ended where what had
already been read ends.

**Example** `let val f = mkInstream (BinPrimIO.openVector (Byte.stringToBytes "ab"), Byte.stringToBytes "") in closeIn f; Byte.bytesToString (#1 (inputAll f)) end = ""`

members.name: endOfStream
members.doc:
`endOfStream f` is `true` when nothing is left before the next end of stream.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.endOfStream/does-not-consume`. It does not move past
the end of stream it finds, so it stays `true` until a read consumes it;
that read returns the empty vector, and only afterwards are elements
that the source gained seen.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the reader fails while it is asked for more.

**Example** `let val f = mkInstream (BinPrimIO.openVector (Byte.stringToBytes "a"), Byte.stringToBytes "") in (endOfStream f, endOfStream (#2 (inputAll f))) end = (false, true)`

members.name: output
members.doc:
`output (f, v)` writes the elements of `v`, holding back what the buffer mode allows.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the writer fails, or if the stream is closed or
terminated.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.output/Io-closed-writes-nothing`. The cause on a
closed or terminated stream is `ClosedStream`, from the list of `IO`,
and nothing is written.

**Example** `let val p = OS.FileSys.tmpName () val out = BinIO.getOutstream (BinIO.openOut p) in output (out, Byte.stringToBytes "hi"); closeOut out; Byte.bytesToString (BinIO.inputAll (BinIO.openIn p)) before OS.FileSys.remove p end = "hi"`

members.name: output1
members.doc:
`output1 (f, x)` writes the single element `x`.

**Raises** `IO.Io` as `output` does.

members.name: flushOut
members.doc:
`flushOut f` hands what the stream holds to its writer.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the writer fails.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.flushOut/empties-first`. The buffer is emptied before
it is passed on, so a writer that fails cannot cause the same elements
to be written twice. Flushing a terminated or a closed stream does
nothing.

members.name: closeOut
members.doc:
`closeOut f` flushes the stream, marks it closed and closes its writer.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the flush or the writer fails.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.closeOut/a-failed-flush-leaves-it-open`. Closing an
already closed stream does nothing; a terminated one is not flushed; and
when the flush fails the stream stays open, so that it can be closed
again. What it held is gone all the same: the buffer is emptied before
the writer is asked, as `flushOut` does it.

**Example** `(let val f = mkOutstream (BinPrimIO.nullWr (), IO.NO_BUF) in closeOut f; output1 (f, 0w0); "written" end handle IO.Io {cause = IO.ClosedStream, ...} => "closed") = "closed"`

members.name: mkInstream
members.doc:
`mkInstream (rd, v)` is a stream that reads `v` first and then what `rd` gives.

`v` is what was taken from the reader already and is being handed back;
the reader is augmented, so the stream uses whatever reads can be built
from it.

**Example** `Byte.bytesToString (#1 (inputAll (mkInstream (BinPrimIO.openVector (Byte.stringToBytes "bc"), Byte.stringToBytes "a")))) = "abc"`

members.name: getReader
members.doc:
`getReader f` is the reader of `f` and what was read ahead but not consumed, and truncates `f`.

The reader is the one that was given to `mkInstream`, not the augmented
one. The vector is, as the specification defines it, what `(closeIn f; #1 (inputAll f))` would give in its place: what was read ahead and not
consumed.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if `f` is closed or already truncated.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.getReader/Io-cause-is-ClosedStream`. A truncated
stream is one that has given its reader away; the cause is
`ClosedStream` for it as for a closed one.

**Example** `(case input1 (mkInstream (BinPrimIO.openVector (Byte.stringToBytes "abc"), Byte.stringToBytes "")) of SOME (_, g) => Byte.bytesToString (#2 (getReader g)) | NONE => "") = "bc"`

members.name: filePosIn
members.doc:
`filePosIn f` is the position of the element that would be read next.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the stream has no positions, or if it has been
truncated or closed.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.filePosIn/Io-closed`. The specification raises `Io`
for a truncated stream and says nothing of a closed one. A closed one
raises too, with the cause `ClosedStream`: closing closed the reader that
may have to be asked where it is, and the stream is done with, as a
truncated one is. MLton and SML/NJ give a position instead; Poly/ML
raises.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.filePosIn/what-is-unsupported`. "Does not support the
operation" means that the reader has no `getPos`, and the cause of the
`IO.Io` is then `RandomAccessNotSupported`, from the list of `IO`. A reader
that has `getPos` may still fail to tell where it is (a pipe), and the
chunks read then carry no position, which raises as well.

**Example** `(case input1 (mkInstream (BinPrimIO.openVector (Byte.stringToBytes "ab"), Byte.stringToBytes "")) of SOME (_, g) => filePosIn g | NONE => ~1) = 1`

members.name: setBufferMode
members.doc:
`setBufferMode (f, mode)` makes `f` hold back what `mode` says.

Changing to `NO_BUF` flushes what is held.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if that flush fails.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.setBufferMode/no-flush-between-buffers`. The
specification says that `NO_BUF` flushes and nothing of the other
changes. Changing between `LINE_BUF` and `BLOCK_BUF` does not flush:
what is held stays until the new mode lets it go.

**Law** `(setBufferMode (f, mode); getBufferMode f) = mode`

**Example** `let val f = mkOutstream (BinPrimIO.nullWr (), IO.NO_BUF) in setBufferMode (f, IO.BLOCK_BUF); getBufferMode f end = IO.BLOCK_BUF`

members.name: getBufferMode
members.doc:
`getBufferMode f` is the mode `f` holds back by.

**Law** `getBufferMode (mkOutstream (wr, mode)) = mode`

**Example** `let val p = OS.FileSys.tmpName () val out = BinIO.getOutstream (BinIO.openOut p) in getBufferMode out before (closeOut out; OS.FileSys.remove p) end = IO.BLOCK_BUF`

members.name: mkOutstream
members.doc:
`mkOutstream (wr, mode)` is a stream that writes through `wr`, holding back what `mode` says.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.mkOutstream/the-writer-is-augmented`. The
specification does not say whether the writer is augmented here; this
one augments it, and `getWriter` still gives back the writer that was
passed in.

**Example** `getBufferMode (mkOutstream (BinPrimIO.nullWr (), IO.LINE_BUF)) = IO.LINE_BUF`

members.name: getWriter
members.doc:
`getWriter f` flushes `f`, terminates it, and is its writer and its buffer mode.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if `f` is closed, or if the flush fails.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.getWriter/terminated-is-not-closed`. A stream that is
already terminated gives its writer and its mode again without flushing;
only a closed one raises.

**Law** `#2 (getWriter (mkOutstream (wr, mode))) = mode`

**Example** `#2 (getWriter (mkOutstream (BinPrimIO.nullWr (), IO.NO_BUF))) = IO.NO_BUF`

members.name: getPosOut
members.doc:
`getPosOut f` flushes `f` and is the position it is now at, together with `f` itself.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the writer has no positions, if the flush fails, or if
`f` is terminated or closed.

> **Implementation** `StreamIO.getPosOut/is-a-file-offset`. For a stream over
a file the position is the offset of a byte from the start of it, which
is what `BinPrimIO.pos` holds.

members.name: setPosOut
members.doc:
`setPosOut opos` flushes the stream of `opos`, moves it to that position, and is that stream.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the writer has no positions, if the flush fails, or if
the stream is terminated or closed.

> **Reading** `StreamIO.setPosOut/writes-over`. What is written after it
replaces what stood at that position; the stream is not truncated
there.

members.name: filePosOut
members.doc: `filePosOut opos` is the position that `opos` records, without its stream.

STRING.doc:
Strings: immutable sequences of characters, with the operations that take
them apart, put them together, compare them and write them as the text of
a string constant.

A string is indexed from 0 and is of a fixed length, `size s`; there is no
terminating character, so a string may hold any character, the one with
code 0 included. Taking a string apart never copies more than it must, but
every operation that makes one does copy, so building a long string by
repeated `^` costs time quadratic in the result: collect the pieces in a
list and `concat` them once.

The signature is that of `String`, whose characters are of type `char`, and
of the optional `WideString`, which is why it specifies a type `char` of
its own. The strings of the library are compared by their characters'
codes, and that order is what `<`, `compare` and `Substring.compare` use.

**See also** `CHAR`, `SUBSTRING`, `STRING_CVT`, `TEXT`, `MONO_VECTOR`

> **Erratum** `STRING/string-types`. The specification writes the types of
`toString`, `scan`, `fromString`, `toCString` and `fromCString` with
`String.string`, because the text of an escape is always of 8-bit
characters, also for `WideString`. They are kept as written.

members.name: string
members.doc:
The type of strings of these characters.

> **Implementation** `String.string/bytes`. `String.string` is the top-level
`string`, a sequence of 8-bit characters; `WideString.string` is one of
`WideChar.char`.

> **Implementation** `String.string/u-escape-above-255-rejected`. An escape
`\uXXXX` above 255 in a constant of type `string` or `char` is an error
when the program is compiled, for the characters have eight bits; at
`WideString.string` it is a character.

members.name: char
members.doc: The type of the characters of such a string: `Char.char` for `String`.

members.name: maxSize
members.doc:
The greatest length a string may have.

> **Implementation** `String.maxSize/value`. 1073741823, which is 2^30 - 1.

> **Implementation** `String.maxSize/Size-is-not-pinned`. With a bound of 2^30
\- 1 no check of the suite makes a string that is too long: `Size` from
`^`, `concat`, `implode` and `translate` is raised by the VM when the
bound is passed, and the suite checks it only on a system whose `maxSize`
is at most 2^26. The same holds for `StringCvt.padLeft` and `padRight`,
for `Substring.concat` and `concatWith`, and with `Vector.maxLen` for
`Vector.concat` and `VectorSlice.concat`.

members.name: size
members.doc:
`size s` is the number of characters of `s`.

**Example** `size "abc" = 3`

members.name: sub
members.doc:
`sub (s, i)` is the character of `s` at position `i`, counting from 0.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i >= size s`.

**Example** `sub ("abc", 1) = #"b"`

**Example** `(sub ("abc", 3) handle Subscript => #"!") = #"!"`

members.name: extract
members.spec: val extract : string * int * int option -> string
members.doc:
`extract (s, i, NONE)` is the characters of `s` from position `i` on, and `extract (s, i, SOME n)` the `n` characters from `i`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0`, if `i > size s`, or if `n` is given and
`i + n > size s`.

> **Reading** `String.extract/SOME-Subscript-not-Overflow-size`. The bound is
tested so that it cannot overflow: an `i` and an `n` whose sum is no
`int` raise `Subscript`, not `Overflow`.

**Example** `extract ("hello", 2, NONE) = "llo"`

members.name: substring
members.spec: val substring : string * int * int -> string
members.doc:
`substring (s, i, n)` is the `n` characters of `s` from position `i`.

**Law** `substring (s, i, n) = extract (s, i, SOME n)`

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0`, `n < 0` or `i + n > size s`.

**Example** `substring ("hello", 1, 3) = "ell"`

`s ^ t` is the characters of `s` followed by those of `t`.

It is infix with precedence 6.

**Raises** `Size` if the result would be longer than `maxSize`.

**Complexity** linear in `size s + size t`; both are copied.

**Example** `"ab" ^ "c" = "abc"`

members.name: concat
members.doc:
`concat l` is the strings of `l` one after another.

**Raises** `Size` if the result would be longer than `maxSize`.

**Law** `concat [s, t] = s ^ t`, and `concat [] = ""`

**Example** `concat ["a", "", "bc"] = "abc"`

members.name: concatWith
members.spec: val concatWith : string -> string list -> string
members.doc:
`concatWith sep l` is the strings of `l` one after another with `sep` between them.

There is no separator before the first or after the last, so
`concatWith sep []` is `""` and `concatWith sep [s]` is `s`.

**Raises** `Size` if the result would be longer than `maxSize`.

**Example** `concatWith ", " ["a", "b", "c"] = "a, b, c"`

members.name: str
members.doc:
`str c` is the string of the one character `c`.

**Example** `str #"a" = "a"`

members.name: implode
members.doc:
`implode l` is the string of the characters of `l`, in order.

**Raises** `Size` if the result would be longer than `maxSize`.

**Example** `implode [#"a", #"b"] = "ab"`

members.name: explode
members.doc:
`explode s` is the list of the characters of `s`, in order.

**Law** `implode (explode s) = s`

**Example** `explode "ab" = [#"a", #"b"]`

members.name: map
members.doc:
`map f s` is the string of the results of `f` on each character of `s`, from left to right.

**Example** `map Char.toUpper "abc" = "ABC"`

members.name: translate
members.doc:
`translate f s` applies `f` to each character of `s`, from left to right, and appends the strings it gives.

It is `map` for a function that may give any number of characters for
one, which is how a string is escaped or expanded.

**Raises** `Size` if the result would be longer than `maxSize`.

**Law** `translate f s = concat (List.map f (explode s))`

**Example** `translate (fn #"a" => "4" | c => str c) "banana" = "b4n4n4"`

members.name: tokens
members.spec: val tokens : (char -> bool) -> string -> string list
members.doc:
`tokens p s` is the non-empty pieces of `s` between the characters that satisfy `p`.

A run of delimiters counts as one, and a delimiter at either end leaves
nothing behind, so this is how a line is split into words.

**Example** `tokens Char.isSpace "  a  b " = ["a", "b"]`

**Law** `tokens p s = List.filter (fn t => Int.> (size t, 0)) (fields p s)`
when `p` has no effects

> **Reading** `String.tokens/order`. The specification says the tokens are
"derived from s from left to right", and not how often `p` is asked:
`p` is applied once to each character, from left to right.

members.name: fields
members.spec: val fields : (char -> bool) -> string -> string list
members.doc:
`fields p s` is the pieces of `s` that the characters satisfying `p` separate.

Every delimiter ends a field, so `n` delimiters give `n + 1` fields,
empty ones included; this is how a line of a table is read.

**Example** `fields (fn c => c = #",") "a,,b," = ["a", "", "b", ""]`

members.name: isPrefix
members.doc:
`isPrefix p s` is `true` when `s` begins with `p`.

**Example** `isPrefix "ab" "abc" = true`

members.name: isSubstring
members.doc:
`isSubstring p s` is `true` when `p` occurs anywhere in `s`.

The empty string occurs in every string.

**Complexity** the product of the two sizes in the worst case; the search
is the straightforward one.

**Example** `isSubstring "" "abc" = true`

members.name: isSuffix
members.doc:
`isSuffix p s` is `true` when `s` ends with `p`.

**Example** `isSuffix "bc" "abc" = true`

members.name: compare
members.doc:
`compare (s, t)` orders two strings by their characters' codes, lexicographically.

A string that is a prefix of another comes before it.

**Law** `compare (s, t) = collate Char.compare (s, t)`

**Example** `compare ("abc", "abd") = LESS`

**Example** `compare ("Z", "a") = LESS` for the capitals come first in ASCII.

members.name: collate
members.spec: val collate : (char * char -> order) -> string * string -> order
members.doc:
`collate cmp (s, t)` compares two strings lexicographically with `cmp` for the characters.

The answer is that of `cmp` on the first pair of characters at the same
position that are not `EQUAL`; if there is none, the shorter string is
`LESS`.

**Example** `collate Char.compare ("ab", "abc") = LESS`

`s < t`, `s <= t`, `s > t` and `s >= t` compare two strings as `compare` does.

**Example** `"abc" < "abd" = true`

`s < t`, `s <= t`, `s > t` and `s >= t` compare two strings as `compare` does.

**Example** `"abc" < "abd" = true`

`s < t`, `s <= t`, `s > t` and `s >= t` compare two strings as `compare` does.

**Example** `"abc" < "abd" = true`

`s < t`, `s <= t`, `s > t` and `s >= t` compare two strings as `compare` does.

**Example** `"abc" < "abd" = true`

members.name: toString
members.doc:
`toString s` is the text that stands for `s` inside an SML string constant.

Every character is written as `Char.toString` writes it: the printable
ones as themselves, with a backslash before a backslash or a double
quote, and the others as a named escape, `\^c`, or three decimal digits.

**Law** `toString s = translate Char.toString s`

**Example** `toString "a\tb\"" = "a\\tb\\\""`

members.name: scan
members.doc:
`scan getc strm` reads the characters that `strm` begins with in the notation of SML string constants.

It reads as many as it can and stops before the first that it cannot,
which makes it total: the answer is `SOME (s, rest)` with the characters
read, and `NONE` only when nothing at all could be read. A formatting
sequence, a backslash, white space and another backslash, stands for
nothing and is passed over, so a stream of one such sequence gives
`SOME ""`.

> **Reading** `String.scan/as-much-as-possible`. "The longest prefix" is
taken to mean that a character that cannot be read ends the scan rather
than failing it, and that an escape that is not one (`"a\\q"`) leaves
what came before it.

> **Reading** `String.fromString/unescaped-double-quote`. A double quote
without a backslash converts to itself, as in SML/NJ and Poly/ML; MLton
stops at it. `Char.scan` gives `NONE` for it, for the page of `CHAR` has
the text read "as allowed in an SML program" and this one does not.

> **Reading** `String.scan/empty-input-is-SOME-empty`. Nothing to read is no
failure: `fromString ""` is `SOME ""`. `NONE` is for a first character
that cannot be read, as in `fromString "\\q"`.

**Example** `fromString "" = SOME ""`

members.name: fromString
members.doc:
`fromString s` is the characters that the text `s` begins with, read as `scan` reads them, or `NONE`.

**Law** `fromString s = StringCvt.scanString scan s`

> **Reading** `String.fromString/format-first`. A formatting sequence counts
as read although it stands for no character, so a text of nothing but
such a sequence gives `SOME ""`, and so does one that a bad escape
follows.

**Example** `fromString "a\\nb" = SOME "a\nb"`, where the first text has a
backslash and an n in it: `size "a\\nb" = 4`.

members.name: toCString
members.doc:
`toCString s` is the text that stands for `s` inside a C string constant.

Every character is written as `Char.toCString` writes it, so the single
quote and the question mark are escaped as well, and what does not print
becomes a backslash and three octal digits.

**Example** `toCString "a\n?" = "a\\n\\?"`

members.name: fromCString
members.doc:
`fromCString s` is the characters that the text `s` begins with in the notation of C, or `NONE`.

There are no formatting sequences in C, and a double quote without a
backslash is not a character of a constant, so it ends the scan.

> **Reading** `String.fromCString/stops-at-hex-longest-sequence`. A `\x`
escape takes "the longest sequence" of hexadecimal digits: `"\x42C"` is
one escape of the value 1068, which is no character, and not `\x42`
followed by `C`.

**Example** `fromCString "\\x41" = SOME "A"`

STRING_CVT.doc:
The types and helpers of the conversions between values and text: the
formats of `fmt`, the readers of `scan`.

Every `scan` function of the library reads from a functional character
stream: a value of any type `'b` together with a reader, a function that
gives the next character and the rest of the stream, or `NONE` at the end.
A scanner takes a reader of characters and gives a reader of values, so it
works alike on strings, lists of characters, substrings and input streams,
and a program can build scanners of its own out of those of the library and
the helpers below. Nothing is consumed by a scan that fails: the caller
still has the stream it passed.

**See also** `CHAR`, `STRING`, `SUBSTRING`, `TEXT_IO`

members.name: radix
members.spec:
datatype radix
  = BIN
  | OCT
  | DEC
  | HEX
members.doc:
The base in which `Int.fmt`, `Word.fmt` and their `scan` functions write
and read a number.

members.name: realfmt
members.spec:
datatype realfmt
  = SCI of int option
  | FIX of int option
  | GEN of int option
  | EXACT
members.doc:
The notation in which `Real.fmt` writes a real number.

The argument is a number of digits; `NONE` asks for the default.

> **Reading** `StringCvt.SCI/carries-negative`. A constructor carries any
`int option`, also one that no format accepts, such as `SCI (SOME ~1)`:
`Size` is raised by `fmt`, not by the constructor.

members.name: reader
members.doc:
A reader of values of type `'a` from a stream of type `'b`: `NONE` at the
end of the stream, otherwise the next value and the rest of the stream.

members.name: padLeft
members.spec: val padLeft : char -> int -> string -> string
members.doc:
`padLeft c i s` is `s` with enough copies of `c` on its left to make it
`i` characters long.

A string that has `i` characters or more is returned as it is, also for a
negative `i`.

**Raises** `Size` if `i` is larger than `String.maxSize` and `s` is shorter
than `i`.

**Example** `padLeft #"0" 5 "42" = "00042"`

> **Reading** `StringCvt.padLeft/width-minInt`. For the smallest `int` the
difference `i - size s` does not exist as an `int`; `s` is returned all
the same, and `Overflow` is not raised.

members.name: padRight
members.spec: val padRight : char -> int -> string -> string
members.doc:
`padRight c i s` is `s` with enough copies of `c` on its right to make it
`i` characters long.

A string that has `i` characters or more is returned as it is.

**Raises** `Size` if `i` is larger than `String.maxSize` and `s` is shorter
than `i`.

**Example** `padRight #"." 5 "ab" = "ab..."`

members.name: splitl
members.doc:
`splitl p getc strm` is the string of the characters at the front of
`strm` that satisfy `p`, and the rest of the stream.

The rest begins with the first character that does not satisfy `p`.

> **Reading** `StringCvt.splitl/reads-no-further-than-first-failing`. "Will
often use lookahead characters" is taken to mean exactly one: the
character that stops the scan is read from the source, and nothing after
it.

**Example** `splitl Char.isDigit List.getItem (explode "12ab") = ("12", [#"a", #"b"])`

members.name: takel
members.doc:
`takel p getc strm` is the string of the characters at the front of `strm`
that satisfy `p`.

**Law** `takel p getc strm = #1 (splitl p getc strm)`

**Example** `takel Char.isDigit Substring.getc (Substring.full "12ab") = "12"`

members.name: dropl
members.doc:
`dropl p getc strm` is `strm` without the characters at its front that
satisfy `p`.

**Law** `dropl p getc strm = #2 (splitl p getc strm)`

**Example** `implode (dropl Char.isSpace List.getItem (explode "  x")) = "x"`

members.name: skipWS
members.doc:
`skipWS getc strm` is `strm` without the white space at its front.

White space is what `Char.isSpace` accepts.

**Law** `skipWS getc strm = dropl Char.isSpace getc strm`

**Example** `Substring.string (skipWS Substring.getc (Substring.full "  a")) = "a"`

members.name: cs
members.doc:
The stream that `scanString` makes of a string: a scanner can do nothing
with it but read it.

members.name: scanString
members.spec: val scanString : ((char, cs) reader -> ('a, cs) reader) -> string -> 'a option
members.doc:
`scanString scan s` applies the scanner `scan` to the characters of `s`,
from the first.

The answer is `SOME v` when `scan` reads a value `v`, whatever follows it
in `s`, and `NONE` when it reads none. This is how every `fromString` of
the library is made from its `scan`.

**Example** `scanString (Int.scan DEC) "12abc" = SOME 12`

SUBPROCESS.doc:
Programs started as children that a runner of tests supervises
(docs/plans/unit-testing.md, M2): in a directory of their own, in a
process group (a job on Windows) that can be ended as one, under limits,
with the signals at their default actions, and waited for with what they
cost.

`Unix` and `Posix.Process` start and reap programs too. This adds what a
runner needs and they lack: the directory, the group, the limits and the
signals at the start, and the processor time and the memory at the end.

This signature is Rune's own. On Windows a job has limits of memory and of
processor time only, a signal's action is always the default, and ending
a group ends its job.

members.name: pid
members.doc:
A child's process: its number, as the system gives it.

A descriptor is given by its number too (`Posix.FileSys.fdToWord`):
`Posix`'s types are its own, and this structure is not part of it.

members.name: limits
members.spec: type limits = {addressSpace : int option, cpuTime : int option, fileSize : int option, core : int option}
members.doc:
Limits on a child, each `NONE` for none.

They are the bytes of address space it may hold, the seconds of
processor time it may take, the bytes of a file it may write (it gets
SIGXFSZ beyond them), and the bytes of a core dump (0 for none).

members.name: unlimited
members.doc:
No limits beyond this program's own.

**Example** `#addressSpace unlimited = NONE`

members.name: ended
members.spec:
type ended = {pid : pid, status : Posix.Process.exit_status, user : Time.time,
              system : Time.time, peakResident : int}
members.doc:
How a child ended, and what it cost: its user and system processor
time, and the most memory it held resident, in kilobytes (0 where the
system does not say).

members.name: spawn
members.spec:
val spawn : {program : string, args : string list, env : string list option, search : bool,
             dir : string option, stdin : int option, stdout : int option, stderr : int option,
             group : bool, limits : limits} -> pid
members.doc:
`spawn {program, args, env, search, dir, stdin, stdout, stderr, group, limits}`
starts `program` as a child, and is its process.

`args` are its arguments, its name first, as `Posix.Process.exec` takes
them; `env` its environment (`NONE`: this program's); `search` looks
for `program` on `PATH`; `dir` is the directory it starts in (`NONE`:
this program's); the three descriptors, by number, become its standard
input, output and error (`NONE`: this program's own); `group` puts it in a
process group of its own, which `kill` ends as one. Its signals start
at their default actions. A program that cannot be run is, on POSIX, a
child that exits with 126.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` when the child cannot be started.

members.name: wait
members.doc:
`wait pid` waits for the child `pid` to end (`NONE`: any child), and
is how it ended and what it cost.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` when there is no such child.

members.name: poll
members.spec: val poll : pid option -> ended option
members.doc:
`poll pid` is `wait pid` if the child has ended, and `NONE` at once if
it has not.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` when there is no such child.

members.name: kill
members.doc:
`kill (pid, s)` sends the signal `s` to the process group of the child
`pid`, which `spawn` made with `group`.

The group is the child and every process it started. On Windows it ends
the child's job.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` when there is no such group.

SUBSTRING.doc:
A stretch of a string, without a copy of it: a base string and a start and
a length inside it.

Taking a substring apart is free where taking a string apart is not, so a
program that scans text works on substrings and makes a string only of what
it keeps. The three numbers are what `base` gives back; `full s` is the
whole of `s`, `string ss` copies the stretch out. The functions that split
come in pairs, one for each end: `l` takes from the left and `r` from the
right.

The signature is that of `Substring`, over `String`, and of the optional
`WideSubstring`.

**See also** `STRING`, `CHAR`, `STRING_CVT`, `TEXT`, `MONO_VECTOR_SLICE`

> **Erratum** `SUBSTRING/span-exception`. The specification does not say in the
signature that `span` raises an exception, although its description does;
the exception is `General.Span`.

members.name: substring
members.doc:
The type of substrings: a base string, a start in it and a length.

> **Implementation** `Substring.substring/slice`. It is
`CharVectorSlice.slice`, the slice of a vector of characters, so the two
structures describe one type.

members.name: char
members.doc: The type of the characters: `Char.char` for `Substring`.

members.name: string
members.doc: The type of the strings these are substrings of.

members.name: sub
members.doc:
`sub (ss, i)` is the character of `ss` at position `i`, counting from the start of the substring.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i >= size ss`.

**Example** `sub (full "abc", 1) = #"b"`

members.name: size
members.doc:
`size ss` is the number of characters of `ss`.

**Example** `size (extract ("abcde", 1, SOME 3)) = 3`

members.name: base
members.spec: val base : substring -> string * int * int
members.doc:
`base ss` is the triple of the string that `ss` is a stretch of, where it starts in that string, and how long it is.

**Law** `base (substring (s, i, n)) = (s, i, n)` for `0 <= i andalso i <= size (full s) andalso 0 <= n andalso n <= size (full s) - i`

**Example** `base (substring ("hello", 1, 3)) = ("hello", 1, 3)`

**Counterexample** `base (substring ("", 0, ~1)) = ("", 0, ~1)`, for no
substring has a negative size.

members.name: extract
members.spec: val extract : string * int * int option -> substring
members.doc:
`extract (s, i, NONE)` is the stretch of `s` from position `i` to its end, and `extract (s, i, SOME n)` the `n` characters from `i`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0`, if `i > String.size s`, or if `n` is
given and `i + n > String.size s`.

> **Implementation** `Substring.extract/no-overflow`. The bounds are tested
so that they cannot overflow: an `i` and an `n` whose sum is no `int`
raise `Subscript`, not `Overflow`.

**Example** `string (extract ("abcde", 1, SOME 3)) = "bcd"`

members.name: substring
members.spec: val substring : string * int * int -> substring
members.doc:
`substring (s, i, n)` is the `n` characters of `s` from position `i`.

**Law** `substring (s, i, n) = extract (s, i, SOME n)`

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0`, `n < 0` or `i + n > String.size s`.

**Example** `string (substring ("hello", 1, 3)) = "ell"`

members.name: full
members.doc:
`full s` is the whole of `s` as a substring.

**Example** `string (full "abc") = "abc"`

members.name: string
members.doc:
`string ss` is the characters of `ss` as a string of their own.

This is where the copy happens.

**Law** `string (full s) = s`

**Example** `string (substring ("abcde", 1, 2)) = "bc"`

members.name: isEmpty
members.doc:
`isEmpty ss` is `true` when `ss` has no characters.

**Law** `isEmpty ss = (size ss = 0)`

**Example** `isEmpty (full "") = true`

members.name: getc
members.doc:
`getc ss` is `NONE` for the empty substring and `SOME (c, rest)` for the first character and what follows it.

It has the shape of a `StringCvt.reader`, so a substring is a stream
that a `scan` function can read from.

**Example** `Option.map (fn (c, rest) => (c, string rest)) (getc (full "ab")) = SOME (#"a", "b")`

members.name: first
members.doc:
`first ss` is `SOME` of the first character of `ss`, or `NONE` when it is empty.

**Example** `first (full "") = NONE`

members.name: triml
members.doc:
`triml k ss` is `ss` without its first `k` characters, or empty when it has at most `k`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `k < 0`.

> **Reading** `Substring.triml/Subscript-negative-k`. The specification says
that the exception is raised "when `triml k` is evaluated", before the
substring is given, so a partial application with a negative `k` raises
at once.

**Example** `string (triml 2 (full "hello")) = "llo"`

> **Reading** `Substring.triml/position-of-the-empty-result`. When `k` is more
than the size the result is empty, and the page does not say where in the
string it lies: here at the end of the substring for `triml` and at its
start for `trimr`. The suite checks that it is empty and lies inside the
same string.

members.name: trimr
members.doc:
`trimr k ss` is `ss` without its last `k` characters, or empty when it has at most `k`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `k < 0`, when `trimr k` is evaluated.

**Example** `string (trimr 2 (full "abcde")) = "abc"`

members.name: slice
members.spec: val slice : substring * int * int option -> substring
members.doc:
`slice (ss, i, NONE)` is the stretch of `ss` from position `i` on, and `slice (ss, i, SOME n)` the `n` characters from `i`.

The positions are those of `ss`, not of its base string, and the result
is a substring of the same base.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0`, if `i > size ss`, or if `n` is given and
`i + n > size ss`.

**Example** `string (slice (full "abcde", 1, SOME 2)) = "bc"`

members.name: concat
members.doc:
`concat l` is the string of the substrings of `l`, one after another.

**Raises** `Size` if the result would be longer than `String.maxSize`.

**Example** `concat [full "ab", full "c"] = "abc"`

members.name: concatWith
members.spec: val concatWith : string -> substring list -> string
members.doc:
`concatWith sep l` is the string of the substrings of `l` with `sep` between them.

**Raises** `Size` if the result would be longer than `String.maxSize`.

**Example** `concatWith "," [full "a", full "b"] = "a,b"`

members.name: explode
members.doc:
`explode ss` is the list of the characters of `ss`, in order.

**Example** `explode (full "ab") = [#"a", #"b"]`

members.name: isPrefix
members.doc:
`isPrefix s ss` is `true` when `ss` begins with the string `s`.

**Example** `isPrefix "ab" (full "abc") = true`

members.name: isSubstring
members.doc:
`isSubstring s ss` is `true` when `s` occurs anywhere in `ss`.

**Example** `isSubstring "bc" (full "abcd") = true`

members.name: isSuffix
members.doc:
`isSuffix s ss` is `true` when `ss` ends with the string `s`.

**Example** `isSuffix "cd" (full "abcd") = true`

members.name: compare
members.doc:
`compare (ss, tt)` orders two substrings by their characters, lexicographically.

What they are substrings of does not matter: only the characters they
hold.

**Law** `compare (ss, tt) = String.compare (string ss, string tt)`

**Example** `compare (full "ab", full "abc") = LESS`

members.name: collate
members.spec: val collate : (char * char -> order) -> substring * substring -> order
members.doc:
`collate cmp (ss, tt)` compares two substrings lexicographically with `cmp` for the characters.

**Example** `collate Char.compare (full "b", full "a") = GREATER`

members.name: splitl
members.spec: val splitl : (char -> bool) -> substring -> substring * substring
members.doc:
`splitl p ss` is the pair of the longest prefix of `ss` whose characters satisfy `p` and the rest.

**Law** `splitl p ss = (takel p ss, dropl p ss)` when `p` has no effects

**Example** `(fn (a, b) => (string a, string b)) (splitl Char.isAlpha (full "ab12")) = ("ab", "12")`

**Counterexample** `let val n = ref 0 fun p _ = (n := !n + 1; false) in ignore (splitl p (full "a")); !n end = let val n = ref 0 fun p _ = (n := !n + 1; false) in ignore (takel p (full "a"), dropl p (full "a")); !n end`, for the pair looks at the character twice.

members.name: splitr
members.spec: val splitr : (char -> bool) -> substring -> substring * substring
members.doc:
`splitr p ss` is the pair of what comes before the longest suffix whose characters satisfy `p`, and that suffix.

**Example** `(fn (a, b) => (string a, string b)) (splitr Char.isDigit (full "ab12")) = ("ab", "12")`

members.name: splitAt
members.spec: val splitAt : substring * int -> substring * substring
members.doc:
`splitAt (ss, i)` is the pair of the first `i` characters of `ss` and the rest.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i > size ss`.

**Example** `(fn (a, b) => (string a, string b)) (splitAt (full "abcd", 1)) = ("a", "bcd")`

members.name: dropl
members.doc:
`dropl p ss` is `ss` without the characters at its front that satisfy `p`.

**Example** `string (dropl Char.isSpace (full "  a b")) = "a b"`

members.name: dropr
members.doc:
`dropr p ss` is `ss` without the characters at its end that satisfy `p`.

**Example** `string (dropr Char.isSpace (full "ab  ")) = "ab"`

members.name: takel
members.doc:
`takel p ss` is the longest prefix of `ss` whose characters satisfy `p`.

**Example** `string (takel Char.isAlpha (full "ab1c")) = "ab"`

members.name: taker
members.doc:
`taker p ss` is the longest suffix of `ss` whose characters satisfy `p`.

**Example** `string (taker Char.isDigit (full "ab12")) = "12"`

members.name: position
members.spec: val position : string -> substring -> substring * substring
members.doc:
`position s ss` is the pair of what comes before the first occurrence of `s` in `ss`, and the rest from that occurrence on.

When `s` does not occur, the first component is all of `ss` and the
second is empty at its end, so the two always fit back together. The
empty string occurs at once, which makes the first component empty.

**Law** `let val (pref, suff) = position s ss in concat [pref, suff] = string ss end`

> **Erratum** `Substring.position/none-ends-after-the-substring`. The
specification describes the second component as "the longest suffix of
`ss` that has `s` as a prefix", and then writes the condition on the
index in a way that forgets that the occurrence has to lie inside `ss`:
an `s` that begins in `ss` and runs past its end is not an occurrence.

**Example** `(fn (a, b) => (string a, string b)) (position "lo" (full "hello")) = ("hel", "lo")`

members.name: span
members.doc:
`span (ss, tt)` is the stretch from the start of `ss` to the end of `tt`.

Both must be substrings of one string, and `tt` must not end before `ss`
begins; this is how the pieces that `splitl` and `position` gave are put
back together.

**Raises** `Span` if they are substrings of different strings, or if `tt`
ends before `ss` starts.

> **Reading** `Substring.span/equal-strings-built-separately`. "Unless `s <> s'`" is read as a comparison of the base strings by value: two equal
strings that were built separately count as one base.

**Example** `let val s = full "abcd" in string (span (slice (s, 0, SOME 1), slice (s, 2, SOME 1))) end = "abc"`

members.name: translate
members.doc:
`translate f ss` applies `f` to each character of `ss`, from left to right, and appends the strings it gives.

**Example** `translate (fn c => if c = #"a" then "A" else String.str c) (full "abc") = "Abc"`

members.name: tokens
members.spec: val tokens : (char -> bool) -> substring -> substring list
members.doc:
`tokens p ss` is the non-empty pieces of `ss` between the characters that satisfy `p`.

A run of delimiters counts as one, and the pieces are substrings of the
same base string, so nothing is copied.

**Law** `tokens p ss = List.filter (fn t => not (isEmpty t)) (fields p ss)`
when `p` has no effects: how often `p` is asked is the implementation's

**Example** `map string (tokens Char.isSpace (full " a  b ")) = ["a", "b"]`

> **Reading** `Substring.tokens/order`. The specification says the tokens
are derived "from left to right", and not how often `p` is asked: `p`
is applied once to each character, from left to right.

members.name: fields
members.spec: val fields : (char -> bool) -> substring -> substring list
members.doc:
`fields p ss` is the pieces of `ss` that the characters satisfying `p` separate.

Every delimiter ends a field, so `n` delimiters give `n + 1` fields,
empty ones included.

**Example** `List.map string (fields (fn c => c = #",") (full "a,,b")) = ["a", "", "b"]`

members.name: app
members.doc:
`app f ss` applies `f` to every character of `ss`, from left to right, for its effect.

**Example** `let val n = ref 0 in app (fn _ => n := !n + 1) (full "abc"); !n end = 3`

members.name: foldl
members.doc:
`foldl f init ss` combines the characters of `ss` from the left, as `List.foldl` does.

**Example** `foldl (op ::) [] (full "ab") = [#"b", #"a"]`

members.name: foldr
members.doc:
`foldr f init ss` combines the characters of `ss` from the right, as `List.foldr` does.

**Example** `foldr (op ::) [] (full "ab") = [#"a", #"b"]`

TERMINAL.doc:
The terminal of a program that edits what is typed at it, as a line
editor does: the window's size and its changes, keys read one by one
with a time limit, and a terminal put back as it was whatever way the
program ends (docs/plans/repl.md, D4 and D5).

The terminal is the process's own: keys are read from the standard
input and the program draws on the standard output. `Posix.TTY` sets a
terminal's modes too, but where this structure differs is in what the
runtime does beside: it puts the terminal back at exit, at a fatal
error and at a signal that ends the process, which a program cannot
do for itself; it counts the window's changes of size (`SIGWINCH`); and
on Windows it reads the console's records, with the console making the
same bytes of each key that a terminal of Unix sends, so that a program
decodes one language of keys everywhere. `lib/terminal` is built on it.

What `TextIO.stdIn` has read ahead into its buffer is not seen by
`read`: a program reads its terminal with one or the other while it is
raw.

> **Deviation** `TERMINAL/not-in-the-specification`. The specification
has `Posix.TTY` for a terminal's modes and nothing for a window's size,
a key read with a time limit or a console of Windows; this signature is
Rune's alone, and a program that uses it does not port.

**See also** `POSIX_TTY`, `RUNTIME`

members.name: size
members.spec: val size : unit -> {columns : int, rows : int} option
members.doc:
`size ()` is the columns and rows of the terminal's window, or `NONE`
when no standard stream is a terminal.

The terminal is the standard output's, or, when that is not one, the
standard input's or error's. A terminal that does not know its size
says 0 for both.

members.name: resizes
members.doc:
`resizes ()` is how many times the window has changed its size since
the first call of `resizes`, which starts the count.

A program asks it before it draws and draws the whole screen again
when it has grown. On Windows the changes are seen by `read`, while
the terminal is raw. `~1` where the system cannot count them.

members.name: enter
members.doc:
`enter {undo}` puts the terminal of the standard input in raw mode,
which the runtime undoes however the program ends.

Raw is each byte as it is typed, nothing echoed, no signal from a key
\-- Ctrl-C is the byte 3 -- and the output still translated, a newline
written as a carriage return and a newline. On Windows the console
makes each key the bytes a terminal of Unix sends, in UTF-8.

`undo` is what to write to the standard output to take back what the
program turned on itself with escapes (bracketed paste, a hidden
cursor): it is written when the terminal is put back, by `leave` or by
the runtime. The runtime puts the terminal back at exit, at a fatal
error, at `SIGTERM`, `SIGHUP` and `SIGQUIT`, and on a stop (`SIGTSTP`),
making it raw again when the process is continued and counting that
as a resize, since the screen may have changed meanwhile.

What the terminal was is kept from the first call, so a program can
enter and leave as often as it likes; to enter while raw changes
`undo`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` when the standard input is not a terminal, or a
console of Windows refuses VT input (before Windows 10 1511, or the
legacy console), or `undo` is longer than 256 bytes.

members.name: quiet
members.doc:
`quiet ()` puts the terminal of the standard input in quiet mode,
for while a program runs that the user may interrupt.

Quiet is nothing echoed and lines not edited, so that keys typed
ahead stay unseen until a program reads them, while a key still makes
its signal: Ctrl-C is the user's interrupt (`Runtime`). The runtime
puts the terminal back from quiet mode as it does from raw mode, and
`enter` and `quiet` go from one to the other; `quiet` has no `undo`.
The REPL holds the terminal quiet while what it compiled runs
(docs/repl.md).

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` as `enter` does.

members.name: leave
members.doc:
`leave ()` puts the terminal back as it was before `enter` or `quiet`,
writing `undo`; nothing when it is neither raw nor quiet.

members.name: read
members.spec: val read : Time.time option -> string option
members.doc:
`read wait` is the bytes typed at the terminal since the last `read`,
waiting for them at most `wait` (`NONE`: as long as it takes).

It is `SOME ""` when the time is up or a resize ended the wait, and
`NONE` at the end of the input. A key can arrive in two reads; the
bytes are those the terminal sent, so a key is decoded from what the
reads gave, not from one read.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` when the standard input is not a terminal, or the
read fails. The user's interrupt, where the program catches it
(`Runtime`), is raised where it ends the wait.

TEXT.doc:
The structures of one kind of text, gathered so that their types can be
named as one: characters, strings, substrings and the vectors and arrays
of characters, with the constraints that tie them together.

`Text` is the text of 8-bit characters, whose `Text.Char` is `Char` and
whose `Text.String` is `String`; the optional `WideText` is the same for
`WideChar`. A program that is to work at either kind takes the structure as
a functor argument and names the types through it.

**See also** `CHAR`, `STRING`, `SUBSTRING`, `MONO_VECTOR`, `MONO_ARRAY`

members.name: Char
members.doc: The characters: `Char` for `Text`, `WideChar` for `WideText`.

members.name: String
members.doc: The strings of those characters.

members.name: Substring
members.doc: Their substrings.

members.name: CharVector
members.doc: Their strings seen as immutable sequences.

members.name: CharArray
members.doc: Mutable sequences of those characters.

members.name: CharVectorSlice
members.doc: Slices of the vectors: the substrings, under their sequence interface.

members.name: CharArraySlice
members.doc: Slices of the arrays.

members.spec:
sharing type Char.char = String.char = Substring.char
  = CharVector.elem = CharArray.elem = CharVectorSlice.elem
  = CharArraySlice.elem
members.doc:
The element type of all of them is one type: the character.

> **Erratum** `TEXT/vector-constraint`. The specification writes the identity
of `CharVector.vector` with `String.string` as one more `sharing`
constraint. It cannot be written after the constraint on `String.string`
itself (Definition, rule 64: the type is no longer flexible), so it is
checked on values in the suite instead.

members.spec:
sharing type Char.string = String.string = Substring.string
  = CharVector.vector = CharArray.vector
  = CharVectorSlice.vector = CharArraySlice.vector
members.doc: And the sequence type of all of them is the string.
An array and the slices of arrays are of one type.
And a slice of a vector is what an array slice gives when it is copied out.

TEXT_IO.doc:
Text files and the standard streams: the imperative streams of characters,
with the ways of opening a file.

This is the signature a program reaches for first. It is `IMPERATIVE_IO`
over characters, so everything written there holds; what it adds is
`openIn`, `openOut`, `openAppend` and `openString`, the three standard
streams, `inputLine`, `print` and `scanStream`.

A text file holds characters; on the systems Rune runs on nothing is
translated, so what `output` writes is what `inputAll` reads back, newline
for newline. `BIN_IO` is the same for bytes.

`StreamIO` is the functional stream underneath, reached through
`getInstream` and `getOutstream`; `TEXT_STREAM_IO` describes it.

**See also** `IMPERATIVE_IO`, `TEXT_STREAM_IO`, `BIN_IO`, `STRING_CVT`,
`OS_FILE_SYS`

> **Erratum** `TEXT_IO/include-rewritten`. The page writes `include IMPERATIVE_IO` and then specifies `StreamIO` again as a
`TEXT_STREAM_IO`, which is not valid SML. What it means is that a
structure matching `TEXT_IO` also matches `IMPERATIVE_IO` and has a
`StreamIO` matching `TEXT_STREAM_IO`; that is what stands here, with the
substructure first, then the members of `IMPERATIVE_IO` in full, then the
ones of `TEXT_IO`.

> **Deviation** `TEXT_IO/WideTextIO-not-matched`. The optional `WideTextIO` is
not matched against this signature, because the types here are written
`string` and `char`; the suite checks that its readers and writers match
`PRIM_IO`, and that its vectors are the strings of `WideString` and its
elements the characters of `WideChar`, instead.

members.name: StreamIO
members.spec:
structure StreamIO : TEXT_STREAM_IO
  where type reader = TextPrimIO.reader
  where type writer = TextPrimIO.writer
  where type pos = TextPrimIO.pos
members.doc: The functional text streams underneath, with the readers and writers of `TextPrimIO`.

members.name: vector
members.doc: The type of what is read and written: `string`.

members.name: elem
members.doc: The type of the elements: `char`.

members.name: instream
members.doc: The type of the input streams.

members.name: outstream
members.doc: The type of the output streams.

members.name: input
members.doc:
`input f` is the characters that are there without waiting, and moves `f` past them.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the reader fails.

**Example** `input (openString "abc") = "abc"`

members.name: input1
members.doc:
`input1 f` is `SOME` of the next character, or `NONE` at an end of stream.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the reader fails.

**Example** `input1 (openString "ab") = SOME #"a"`

members.name: inputN
members.doc:
`inputN (f, n)` is `n` characters, or all there are before the next end of stream.

**Raises** `Size` if `n < 0`, or if the string to be returned would be
longer than `String.maxSize`.

**Example** `inputN (openString "abcd", 2) = "ab"`

members.name: inputAll
members.doc:
`inputAll f` is everything up to the next end of stream.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the reader fails; `Size` if the result would be longer
than `String.maxSize`.

**Example** `inputAll (openString "ab\ncd") = "ab\ncd"`

members.name: canInput
members.spec: val canInput : instream * int -> int option
members.doc:
`canInput (f, n)` is how many of `n` characters, at most, can be read without waiting, or `NONE`.

**Raises** `Size` if `n < 0`.

**Example** `canInput (openString "ab", 1) = SOME 1`

**Example** `canInput (openString (CharVector.tabulate (40, fn _ => #"a")), 40) = SOME 40`

members.name: lookahead
members.doc:
`lookahead f` is `SOME` of the next character without removing it, or `NONE` at an end of stream.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the reader fails.

**Example** `let val s = openString "ab" in (lookahead s, input1 s, input1 s, input1 s) end = (SOME #"a", SOME #"a", SOME #"b", NONE)`

members.name: closeIn
members.doc:
`closeIn f` closes the stream and the file underneath.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the file cannot be closed.

**Example** `let val f = openString "ab" in closeIn f; input f end = ""`

members.name: endOfStream
members.doc:
`endOfStream f` is `true` when nothing is left before the next end of stream.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the reader fails.

**Example** `endOfStream (openString "") = true`

members.name: output
members.doc:
`output (f, s)` writes the characters of `s`.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the stream is closed, with the cause `ClosedStream` and
nothing written, or if the file cannot be written to.

> **Implementation** `TextIO.output/no-translation`. On the POSIX systems the
suite runs on, a text file holds exactly the characters written to it:
no newline is translated and no character is dropped, for all 256
of them.

**Example** `let val p = OS.FileSys.tmpName () val out = openOut p in output (out, "hi"); closeOut out; inputAll (openIn p) before OS.FileSys.remove p end = "hi"`

members.name: output1
members.doc:
`output1 (f, c)` writes the single character `c`.

**Raises** `IO.Io` as `output` does.

members.name: flushOut
members.doc:
`flushOut f` hands what the stream holds to the file.

> **Reading** `TextIO.flushOut/closed-is-a-no-op`. Through `STREAM_IO` ("a
no-op on terminated streams", and a closed stream is terminated too),
flushing a closed outstream does nothing rather than raising.

members.name: closeOut
members.doc:
`closeOut f` flushes the stream and closes it and the file.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the flush or the close fails.

members.name: mkInstream
members.doc: `mkInstream s` is an imperative stream holding the functional stream `s`.

members.name: getInstream
members.doc:
`getInstream f` is the functional stream that `f` is at.

**Example** `Option.map #1 (StreamIO.input1 (getInstream (openString "ab"))) = SOME #"a"`

members.name: setInstream
members.doc: `setInstream (f, s)` makes `f` continue at `s`.

members.name: mkOutstream
members.doc: `mkOutstream s` is an imperative stream holding the functional stream `s`.

members.name: getOutstream
members.doc: `getOutstream f` flushes `f` and is the functional stream underneath.

members.name: setOutstream
members.doc: `setOutstream (f, s)` flushes what `f` holds and then makes it write to `s`.

members.name: getPosOut
members.doc:
`getPosOut f` flushes `f` and is the position it is now at.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the file has no positions, or the flush fails.

members.name: setPosOut
members.doc:
`setPosOut (f, opos)` flushes `f` and moves it to the position `opos`.

What is written afterwards replaces what stood there.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the file has no positions, or the flush fails.

members.name: inputLine
members.doc:
`inputLine f` is `SOME` of the next line, with its newline, or `NONE` at an end of stream.

A last line that runs into an end of stream gets a newline appended, so
every line ends in one.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the reader fails.

> **Reading** `TextIO.inputLine/does-not-pass-the-end-of-stream`. An
`inputLine` that gives `NONE` does not consume the end of stream it
found -- `TEXT_STREAM_IO.inputLine` returns no stream in that case, so
there is none to move on to -- and it keeps giving `NONE` even after the
file has grown. Poly/ML reads on there.

**Example** `let val s = openString "a\nb" in (inputLine s, inputLine s, inputLine s) end = (SOME "a\n", SOME "b\n", NONE)`

members.name: outputSubstr
members.doc:
`outputSubstr (f, ss)` writes the characters of the substring `ss`.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the stream is closed or the file cannot be written to.

> **Reading** `TextIO.outputSubstr/Io-function-is-output`. It is "equivalent
to `output`", so the `function` of an `IO.Io` it raises is `"output"`, as
MLton and Poly/ML report it. SML/NJ reports `"outputSubstr"`.

members.name: openIn
members.doc:
`openIn name` is a stream reading the file `name` from its start.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the file cannot be opened, with the system's error as
the cause and `"openIn"` as the `function`.

members.name: openOut
members.doc:
`openOut name` is a stream writing the file `name`, which it empties or creates.

> **Implementation** `TextIO.openOut/buffer-mode`. The mode is `LINE_BUF`
when the file is a terminal and `BLOCK_BUF` otherwise, as the
specification asks; but the stream itself holds nothing back. The VM
keeps the block and flushes every file at exit, so what a program writes
with `print` and what it writes through a stream reach the file in the
order it wrote them.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the file cannot be opened.

members.name: openAppend
members.doc:
`openAppend name` is a stream writing at the end of the file `name`, which it creates if it is not there.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the file cannot be opened.

members.name: openString
members.doc:
`openString s` is a stream reading the characters of `s`, and no file.

**Example** `inputAll (openString "xyz") = "xyz"`

members.name: stdIn
members.doc: The standard input of the program.

members.name: stdOut
members.doc: The standard output of the program.

members.name: stdErr
members.doc: The standard error of the program, which holds nothing back: its mode is `NO_BUF`.

members.name: print
members.doc:
`print s` writes `s` to `stdOut` and flushes it.

It is the `print` of the top-level environment.

members.name: scanStream
members.spec:
val scanStream : ((Char.char, StreamIO.instream) StringCvt.reader
                  -> ('a, StreamIO.instream) StringCvt.reader)
                 -> instream -> 'a option
members.doc:
`scanStream scan f` runs a scanner over `f` and moves `f` to where it stopped.

`scan` is a function of the shape that `StringCvt` describes: it takes a
reader and reads from a source, here the functional stream underneath.

> **Reading** `TextIO.scanStream/moves-only-on-success`. By the
implementation the page gives, the stream is moved to where the scanner
stopped when it returns `SOME`, and not at all when it returns `NONE`,
whatever the scanner read while trying.

**Example** `scanStream (Int.scan StringCvt.DEC) (openString " 42 rest") = SOME 42`

TEXT_STREAM_IO.doc:
The functional streams of `STREAM_IO` where the elements are characters,
with the two operations that only text has: reading a line and writing a
substring.

Everything of `STREAM_IO` holds here unchanged; the `include` fixes the
elements to `char` and the vectors to `string`.

**See also** `STREAM_IO`, `TEXT_IO`, `SUBSTRING`

members.name: STREAM_IO
members.spec:
include STREAM_IO
  where type vector = CharVector.vector
  where type elem = Char.char

members.name: inputLine
members.doc:
`inputLine f` is `SOME` of the next line, with its newline, and the stream after it, or `NONE` at an end of stream.

> **Reading** `TextIO.StreamIO.inputLine/last-line-without-a-newline`. A last
line that runs into an end of stream gets a newline appended, so that
every line returned ends in one, and the stream returned is past that
end of stream. At an end of stream itself it is `NONE`.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the reader fails.

**Example** `Option.map #1 (inputLine (TextIO.getInstream (TextIO.openString "a\nb"))) = SOME "a\n"`

members.name: outputSubstr
members.doc:
`outputSubstr (f, ss)` writes the characters of the substring `ss`.

It is `output (f, Substring.string ss)`, and so raises what that raises,
with `"output"` as the `function` of the `IO.Io`.

**Raises** `IO.Io` if the writer fails, or if the stream is closed or
terminated.

TIME.doc:
A length of time, and a point in time counted from a fixed reference.

A `time` is a duration. It is also how a moment is named: `now ()` is the
time since `zeroTime`, and a moment and a duration have one type, so
`now () + fromSeconds 10` is ten seconds hence and a difference of two
moments is a duration. Times may be negative.

The conversions take and give `LargeInt.int`, so that the range of a time
is not tied to `Int.int`; going the other way they truncate towards zero.
How fine a time is and how far it reaches is left to the implementation,
and a conversion or an addition whose result does not fit raises `Time`
rather than `Overflow`.

**See also** `DATE`, `TIMER`, `OS_PROCESS`

> **Implementation** `TIME.time/is-microseconds`. A time is a number of
microseconds held in an `int`, which reaches about 292,000 years either
way. Anything finer than a microsecond is lost, and `zeroTime` is the
epoch of the system's clock, 1 January 1970 UTC.

members.name: time
members.doc:
The type of a length of time.

Two times are equal when they are the same length.

members.name: Time
members.doc: Raised when a time cannot be made or converted: the value does not fit.

members.name: zeroTime
members.doc:
The zero of the arithmetic, and the reference point that `now` counts from.

> **Reading** `Time.zeroTime/lies-in-the-past`. It is "a common reference
point for all time values"; the suite takes it to lie in the past, so
`now ()` is greater.

**Example** `toSeconds zeroTime = 0`

members.name: fromReal
members.doc:
`fromReal r` is `r` seconds, its fraction truncated towards zero.

**Raises** `Time` if `r` is not a number, is infinite, or does not fit.

**Example** `toMilliseconds (fromReal 1.5) = 1500`

members.name: toReal
members.doc:
`toReal t` is `t` as a number of seconds, which may lose precision.

**Example** `Real.== (toReal (fromMilliseconds 1500), 1.5) = true`

members.name: toSeconds
members.doc:
`toSeconds t` is the whole seconds of `t`, truncated towards zero.

**Example** `toSeconds (fromMilliseconds 2010) = 2`

members.name: toMilliseconds
members.doc:
`toMilliseconds t` is the whole milliseconds of `t`, truncated towards zero.

**Example** `toMilliseconds (fromMicroseconds 2010999) = 2010`

members.name: toMicroseconds
members.doc:
`toMicroseconds t` is the whole microseconds of `t`, truncated towards zero.

**Example** `toMicroseconds (fromMilliseconds 2) = 2000`

members.name: toNanoseconds
members.doc:
`toNanoseconds t` is the whole nanoseconds of `t`, truncated towards zero.

> **Implementation** `Time.toNanoseconds/beyond-64-bits`. The result is a
`LargeInt.int` and is exact however large it is; a `LargeInt` of bounded
precision would raise `Overflow` instead.

**Example** `toNanoseconds (fromMicroseconds 3) = 3000`

members.name: fromSeconds
members.doc:
`fromSeconds n` is `n` seconds.

**Raises** `Time` if the time does not fit.

> **Implementation** `Time.fromSeconds/range-is-open`. Where the range ends
is not fixed; the suite asks only that a value either come out exact or
raise `Time`, never something else and never a wrong number.

**Example** `toMilliseconds (fromSeconds 3) = 3000`

members.name: fromMilliseconds
members.doc:
`fromMilliseconds n` is `n` milliseconds.

**Raises** `Time` if the time does not fit.

**Example** `toSeconds (fromMilliseconds 1500) = 1`

members.name: fromMicroseconds
members.doc:
`fromMicroseconds n` is `n` microseconds.

**Raises** `Time` if the time does not fit.

**Example** `toMicroseconds (fromMicroseconds 1234567) = 1234567`

members.name: fromNanoseconds
members.doc:
`fromNanoseconds n` is `n` nanoseconds, truncated to what a time can hold.

**Raises** `Time` if the time does not fit.

**Example** `toMicroseconds (fromNanoseconds 2999) = 2`

`t + u` is the sum of two times.

**Raises** `Time` if the sum does not fit.

> **Implementation** `Time.+/exact-until-it-raises`. Wherever the range ends,
doubling a time over and over stays exact until one step raises `Time`;
no step gives a wrong value or another exception.

**Example** `fromSeconds 1 + fromMilliseconds 500 = fromMilliseconds 1500`

`t - u` is `t` less `u`, which may be negative.

**Raises** `Time` if the difference does not fit.

> **Implementation** `Time.-/exact-until-it-raises`. As for `+`: exact until
a step raises `Time`.

**Example** `toSeconds (fromSeconds 5 - fromSeconds 2) = 3`

members.name: compare
members.doc:
`compare (t, u)` orders two times, the shorter first.

**Example** `compare (fromSeconds 1, fromSeconds 2) = LESS`

`t < u` is `true` when `t` is the shorter time.

**Example** `fromSeconds 1 < fromSeconds 2 = true`
`t <= u` is `true` when `t` is no longer than `u`.
`t > u` is `true` when `t` is the longer time.
`t >= u` is `true` when `t` is no shorter than `u`.

members.name: now
members.doc:
`now ()` is the time since `zeroTime`, by the clock of the system.

**Example** `now () > zeroTime = true`

members.name: fmt
members.doc:
`fmt n t` is `t` in seconds, with `n` digits after the decimal point and none when `n` is 0.

**Raises** `Size` if `n < 0`.

> **Reading** `Time.fmt/fixed-point`. The text has "fixed-point semantics":
the digit last kept is rounded to nearest, and since a time holds
microseconds every digit past the sixth is a zero.

**Example** `fmt 2 (fromMilliseconds 1500) = "1.50"`

**Example** `fmt 0 (fromMilliseconds 1500) = "2"`

**Example** `fmt 0 (fromMilliseconds 2500) = "3"`

members.name: toString
members.doc:
`toString t` is `fmt 3 t`: seconds with three digits of the fraction.

**Example** `toString (fromMilliseconds ~1500) = "~1.500"`

members.name: scan
members.doc:
`scan getc src` reads a number of seconds, after leading whitespace, and is the time and what is left.

What it reads is an optional sign, then digits, then optionally a point
and digits, or a point and digits alone.

**Raises** `Time` if the number does not fit.

> **Reading** `Time.scan/digits-past-the-sixth`. Any number of digits may be
written; those of the fraction after the sixth are dropped rather than
rounded, and a number too large for a time raises `Time`.

**Example** `Option.map (toMilliseconds o #1) (scan Substring.getc (Substring.full "1.5x")) = SOME 1500`

members.name: fromString
members.doc:
`fromString s` is `SOME` of the time that `s` begins with, after whitespace, or `NONE`.

**Law** `fromString s = StringCvt.scanString scan s`

**Raises** `Time` if the number does not fit.

**Example** `fromString " ~.25x" = SOME (fromMilliseconds ~250)`

> **Reading** `Time.fromString/nanoseconds-lost-or-kept`. As `scan` reads
it, the digits of the fraction after the sixth are dropped rather than
rounded: `"0.000000999"` is no microsecond.

TIMER.doc:
Stopwatches: how much processor time and how much wall-clock time have
passed since a timer was started.

A timer is started, not read and reset: `startCPUTimer ()` and
`startRealTimer ()` take a reading of the clocks, and `checkCPUTimer` and
`checkRealTimer` give the time since, as often as one likes. The two
`total` timers are the ones that were started when the program was, so
they measure the whole run.

Processor time is split into the time the program spent and the time the
system spent on its behalf, and `checkCPUTimes` separates out what the
garbage collector took.

**See also** `TIME`, `OS_PROCESS`

> **Reading** `TIMER/only-properties-are-checked`. What a timer reads is not a
value a test can predict; the suite checks that times are not negative,
that they do not go backwards, and that the equivalences the specification
states hold. A system that does not account for processor time may report
real time here.

members.name: cpu_timer
members.doc: The type of a processor-time timer.

members.name: real_timer
members.doc: The type of a wall-clock timer, a `Time.time` in the same way.

members.name: startCPUTimer
members.doc:
`startCPUTimer ()` is a timer that counts processor time from now.

**Example** `Time.>= (#usr (checkCPUTimer (startCPUTimer ())), Time.zeroTime) = true`

members.name: checkCPUTimes
members.doc:
`checkCPUTimes t` is the processor time since `t` was started, split into the collector's share and the rest.

`usr` is the time the program itself ran, `sys` the time the system
spent for it.

> **Implementation** `Timer.checkCPUTimes/gc-from-the-collector`. The VM adds
up the processor time of every collection, user and system apart, and
`gc` is how much of that has passed since the timer started; `nongc` is
the rest. A collection that grows the heap counts once.

members.name: checkCPUTimer
members.spec: val checkCPUTimer : cpu_timer -> {usr : Time.time, sys : Time.time}
members.doc:
`checkCPUTimer t` is the processor time since `t` was started, user and system time apart.

It counts the collector's share in, where `checkCPUTimes` reports it
separately.

members.name: checkGCTime
members.doc:
`checkGCTime t` is the processor time the collector took since `t` was started.

> **Implementation** `Timer.checkGCTime/user-time-of-the-collections`. It is
the `usr` field of what `checkCPUTimes` reports under `gc`; the system
time of a collection is in that record and not here.

members.name: totalCPUTimer
members.doc:
`totalCPUTimer ()` is the timer that was started when the program was.

> **Implementation** `Timer.totalCPUTimer/from-process-start`. The
"system-dependent initialization time" is the start of the process, so
the timer's base is zero processor time and what it reports is what the
whole run has used.

members.name: startRealTimer
members.doc: `startRealTimer ()` is a timer that counts wall-clock time from now.

members.name: checkRealTimer
members.doc:
`checkRealTimer t` is the wall-clock time since `t` was started.

**Example** `Time.>= (checkRealTimer (startRealTimer ()), Time.zeroTime) = true`

members.name: totalRealTimer
members.doc:
`totalRealTimer ()` is the wall-clock timer that was started when the program was.

> **Implementation** `Timer.totalRealTimer/from-initialisation`. It counts
from the moment the library was initialised, just before the program's
own code begins.

**Example** `Time.>= (checkRealTimer (totalRealTimer ()), Time.zeroTime) = true`

UNIX.doc:
Running another program and talking to it: a child process with a pipe
each way.

`execute` starts a program and gives a `proc`, from which the streams are
taken: what the child writes is read through `textInstreamOf`, and what it
is to read is written through `textOutstreamOf`. `reap` waits for it and
is its status. This is `Posix.Process`'s fork, exec and waitpid put
together, with the pipes made and the descriptors handed over; the
system starts the program itself, without a fork, which Windows does
not have.

The two type variables of `proc` say what its streams are, text or binary;
they are decided by which of the four functions is used on it, so a
top-level binding of a `proc` usually needs a type annotation, the value
restriction being what it is.

**See also** `POSIX_PROCESS`, `OS_PROCESS`, `TEXT_IO`, `BIN_IO`, `POSIX`

> **Erratum** `UNIX/opaque-in-the-page`. The page declares `structure Unix :> UNIX`, so `signal` is abstract there; the suite checks that it is
`Posix.Signal.signal` and that `exit_status` is
`Posix.Process.exit_status`, which the page requires where both structures
exist

members.name: proc
members.doc:
The type of a running child process, with the streams that talk to it.

The first type variable is the stream the child's output is read
through, the second the stream its input is written through.

members.name: signal
members.doc: The type of a signal, the one of `Posix.Signal`.

members.name: exit_status
members.spec:
datatype exit_status
  = W_EXITED
  | W_EXITSTATUS of Word8.word
  | W_SIGNALED of signal
  | W_STOPPED of signal
members.doc: How a process ended, or why it stopped; the `exit_status` of `Posix.Process`.

members.name: fromStatus
members.doc:
`fromStatus st` is what the status `st` says about how the process ended.

**Example** `fromStatus (OS.Process.system "exit 3") = W_EXITSTATUS 0w3`

members.name: executeInEnv
members.spec: val executeInEnv : string * string list * string list -> ('a, 'b) proc
members.doc:
`executeInEnv (path, args, env)` starts the program at `path` with the arguments `args` and the environment `env`.

The child gets a pipe each way; the parent's ends are closed when it
runs another program, so a later child does not hold them open.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the child cannot be made.

> **Implementation** `Unix.executeInEnv/exec-failure-is-126`. A child whose
`exec` fails ends with the status 126, as the page asks; that is what a
`reap` of it reports, rather than an exception in the parent. On
Windows, which starts a program without a child of this one's and
knows at once that it cannot be run, this raises `OS.SysErr`, which
the page allows as well.

members.name: execute
members.spec: val execute : string * string list -> ('a, 'b) proc
members.doc:
`execute (path, args)` is `executeInEnv` with the environment this process has.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the child cannot be made.

> **Reading** `Unix.execute/current-directory`. The page does not say which
directory the child runs in; it is this process's current one.

**Example** `let val p = execute ("/bin/echo", ["hi"]) in TextIO.inputAll (textInstreamOf p) before ignore (reap p) end = "hi\n"`

members.name: textInstreamOf
members.doc: `textInstreamOf pr` is the text stream that what `pr` writes is read from.

members.name: binInstreamOf
members.doc: `binInstreamOf pr` is the binary stream that what `pr` writes is read from.

members.name: textOutstreamOf
members.doc: `textOutstreamOf pr` is the text stream that `pr` reads what is written to it from.

members.name: binOutstreamOf
members.doc: `binOutstreamOf pr` is the binary stream that `pr` reads what is written to it from.

members.name: streamsOf
members.spec: val streamsOf : (TextIO.instream, TextIO.outstream) proc -> TextIO.instream * TextIO.outstream
members.doc: `streamsOf pr` is the pair of the text streams of `pr`.

members.name: reap
members.doc:
`reap pr` closes the streams of `pr`, waits for it to end, and is its status.

> **Reading** `Unix.reap/status-is-remembered`. The status is kept, so
reaping the same process again gives the same answer rather than
failing. A child that is merely stopped does not end the wait, since
`Posix.Process.W.untraced` is not asked for.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the wait fails.

**Example** `fromStatus (reap (execute ("/bin/sh", ["-c", "exit 4"]))) = W_EXITSTATUS 0w4`

members.name: kill
members.doc:
`kill (pr, s)` sends the signal `s` to the child `pr`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the signal may not be sent.

members.name: exit
members.doc:
`exit st` ends this program with the status `st`.

> **Reading** `Unix.exit/flushes`. It runs the `OS.Process.atExit` actions
and then leaves through the VM's exit, which flushes every file; that is
taken to satisfy "flushes and closes all I/O streams".

UNIX_SOCK.doc:
Sockets of the Unix family: an address is a path in the file system, and
the connection never leaves the machine.

This is `SOCKET` with the address family fixed. An address is made from a
path with `toAddr`; binding to it creates that entry in the file system,
and removing the entry is the program's own business.

`Strm` and `DGrm` also offer `socketPair`, which makes two sockets already
connected to each other -- the usual way to give a child process a channel
to its parent.

**See also** `SOCKET`, `INET_SOCK`, `GENERIC_SOCK`, `UNIX`

members.name: unix
members.doc: The type that marks the Unix family, and holds nothing.

members.name: sock
members.doc: The type of a socket of this family.

members.name: stream_sock
members.doc: The type of a stream socket of this family, listening or connected.

members.name: dgram_sock
members.doc: The type of a message socket of this family.

members.name: sock_addr
members.doc: The type of an address of this family: a path.

members.name: unixAF
members.doc:
The address family of the Unix sockets, for `Socket.familyOfAddr` to give back.

**Example** `Socket.AF.toString unixAF = "UNIX"`

members.name: toAddr
members.doc:
`toAddr p` is the address of the socket at the path `p`.

**Example** `Socket.familyOfAddr (toAddr "/tmp/s") = unixAF`

members.name: fromAddr
members.doc:
`fromAddr a` is the path that `a` names.

**Example** `fromAddr (toAddr "/tmp/s") = "/tmp/s"`

members.name: Strm
members.doc: Sockets of this family that carry a stream.

members.name: Strm.socket
members.doc:
`socket ()` is a new stream socket of this family.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if no socket can be made.

members.name: Strm.socketPair
members.doc:
`socketPair ()` is two stream sockets already connected to each other.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if no pair can be made.

members.name: DGrm
members.doc: Sockets of this family that send messages.

members.name: DGrm.socket
members.doc:
`socket ()` is a new message socket of this family.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if no socket can be made.

members.name: DGrm.socketPair
members.doc:
`socketPair ()` is two message sockets already connected to each other.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if no pair can be made.

VECTOR.doc:
Vectors: immutable sequences of a fixed length, of any element type.

A vector is indexed from 0 and is made once: there is no `update` that
changes one, only one that gives a new vector. `ARRAY` is the mutable
counterpart, `VECTOR_SLICE` describes a stretch of a vector without
copying it, and the `MONO_VECTOR` structures are the same thing for one
element type, which lets an implementation pack the elements.

The traversals come in pairs: `app`, `map`, `foldl`, `foldr`, `find` take
a function of an element, and `appi`, `mapi`, `foldli`, `foldri`, `findi`
one of the index and the element. `foldli` and `foldri` differ only in the
order they visit: both pass the index.

**See also** `ARRAY`, `VECTOR_SLICE`, `MONO_VECTOR`, `LIST`

> **Erratum** `VECTOR/vector-spec`. The specification writes `eqtype 'a vector = 'a vector`, which the Definition does not allow as a specification; it is
written here as an abbreviation of the top-level `vector`, which admits
equality when its element type does.

members.name: vector
members.doc: The type of vectors, the one of the top-level environment.

members.name: maxLen
members.doc:
The greatest length a vector may have.

> **Implementation** `Vector.maxLen/value`. 100000000; an array has the same
bound.

members.name: fromList
members.doc:
`fromList l` is the vector of the elements of `l`, in order.

**Raises** `Size` if `l` is longer than `maxLen`.

**Example** `fromList [1, 2] = fromList [1, 2]` for vectors with equal
elements are equal.

members.name: tabulate
members.doc:
`tabulate (n, f)` is the vector of `f 0`, `f 1`, ..., `f (n - 1)`.

`f` is applied in order of increasing index.

**Raises** `Size` if `n < 0` or `n > maxLen`, before `f` is applied at all.

**Example** `foldr (op ::) [] (tabulate (3, fn i => i * 2)) = [0, 2, 4]`

members.name: length
members.doc:
`length v` is the number of elements of `v`.

**Example** `length (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = 3`

members.name: sub
members.doc:
`sub (v, i)` is the element of `v` at position `i`, counting from 0.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i >= length v`.

**Example** `sub (fromList [1, 2, 3], 1) = 2`

members.name: update
members.doc:
`update (v, i, x)` is a new vector, like `v` but with `x` at position `i`.

`v` itself does not change: a vector is immutable, so this copies.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i >= length v`.

**Complexity** linear in `length v`.

**Example** `update (fromList [1, 2, 3], 1, 9) = fromList [1, 9, 3]`

members.name: concat
members.doc:
`concat l` is the vectors of `l` one after another.

**Raises** `Size` if the result would be longer than `maxLen`.

**Example** `concat [fromList [1], fromList [2, 3]] = fromList [1, 2, 3]`

members.name: appi
members.doc:
`appi f v` applies `f` to the index and the element of each position of `v`, from 0 up, for its effect.

**Example** `let val s = ref 0 in appi (fn (i, x) => s := !s + i * x) (fromList [1, 2, 3]); !s end = 8`

members.name: app
members.doc:
`app f v` applies `f` to every element of `v`, from 0 up, for its effect.

**Example** `let val s = ref 0 in app (fn x => s := !s + x) (fromList [1, 2, 3]); !s end = 6`

members.name: mapi
members.doc:
`mapi f v` is the vector of the results of `f` on the index and the element of each position.

**Example** `mapi (fn (i, x) => i + x) (fromList [10, 20]) = fromList [10, 21]`

members.name: map
members.doc:
