`map f v` is the vector of the results of `f` on each element, in order.

**Example** `map (fn x => x * 2) (fromList [1, 2]) = fromList [2, 4]`

members.name: foldli
members.doc:
`foldli f init v` combines the elements from the left, giving `f` the index as well.

**Example** `foldli (fn (i, x, acc) => i + x + acc) 0 (fromList [10, 20]) = 31`

members.name: foldri
members.doc:
`foldri f init v` combines the elements from the right, giving `f` the index as well.

**Example** `foldri (fn (i, x, acc) => (i, x) :: acc) [] (fromList [7, 8]) = [(0, 7), (1, 8)]`

members.name: foldl
members.doc:
`foldl f init v` combines the elements from the left, as `List.foldl` does.

**Example** `foldl (op ::) [] (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = [3, 2, 1]`

members.name: foldr
members.doc:
`foldr f init v` combines the elements from the right, as `List.foldr` does.

**Example** `foldr (op ::) [] (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = [1, 2, 3]`

members.name: findi
members.doc:
`findi p v` is `SOME (i, x)` for the first position whose index and element satisfy `p`, or `NONE`.

It stops at that position: `p` is not applied to what follows.

**Example** `findi (fn (_, x) => x > 1) (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = SOME (1, 2)`

members.name: find
members.doc:
`find p v` is `SOME x` for the first element that satisfies `p`, or `NONE`.

**Example** `find (fn x => x > 1) (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = SOME 2`

members.name: exists
members.doc:
`exists p v` is `true` when some element satisfies `p`; it stops at the first that does.

**Example** `exists (fn x => x > 2) (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = true`

members.name: all
members.doc:
`all p v` is `true` when every element satisfies `p`; it stops at the first that does not.

**Example** `all (fn x => x > 0) (fromList [1, 2, 3]) = true`

members.name: collate
members.spec: val collate : ('a * 'a -> order) -> 'a vector * 'a vector -> order
members.doc:
`collate cmp (v, w)` compares two vectors lexicographically with `cmp` for the elements.

The answer is that of `cmp` on the first pair of elements at the same
position that are not `EQUAL`; if there is none, the shorter vector is
`LESS`.

**Example** `collate Int.compare (fromList [1], fromList [1, 0]) = LESS`

VECTOR_SLICE.doc:
A stretch of a vector, without a copy of it: a base vector and a start and
a length inside it.

A slice is what a function takes when it is to work on part of a sequence:
passing `slice (v, i, SOME n)` costs nothing, where passing
`VectorSlice.vector` of it would copy. The three numbers are what `base`
gives back. Positions inside a slice are counted from its own start, so
`sub (sl, 0)` is its first element whatever `sl` begins at in its base.

**See also** `VECTOR`, `ARRAY_SLICE`, `MONO_VECTOR_SLICE`, `SUBSTRING`

members.name: slice
members.doc: The type of slices of a vector.

members.name: length
members.doc:
`length sl` is the number of elements of `sl`.

**Example** `length (slice (Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3, 4], 1, SOME 2)) = 2`

members.name: sub
members.doc:
`sub (sl, i)` is the element of `sl` at position `i`, counting from the start of the slice.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0` or `i >= length sl`.

**Example** `sub (slice (Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3], 1, NONE), 0) = 2`

members.name: full
members.doc:
`full v` is the whole of `v` as a slice.

**Example** `vector (full (Vector.fromList [1, 2])) = Vector.fromList [1, 2]`

members.name: slice
members.spec: val slice : 'a Vector.vector * int * int option -> 'a slice
members.doc:
`slice (v, i, NONE)` is the stretch of `v` from position `i` to its end, and `slice (v, i, SOME n)` the `n` elements from `i`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `i < 0`, if `i > Vector.length v`, or if `n` is
given and `i + n > Vector.length v`.

**Example** `vector (slice (Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3, 4], 1, SOME 2)) = Vector.fromList [2, 3]`

**Example** `length (slice (Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3], 1, NONE)) = 2`

> **Reading** `VectorSlice.slice/Subscript-not-Overflow`. When `i + n` is no
`int` the slice does not exist, and `Subscript` says so, never `Overflow`;
`subslice` is the same, and so are the slices of the monomorphic vectors.

members.name: subslice
members.spec: val subslice : 'a slice * int * int option -> 'a slice
members.doc:
`subslice (sl, i, NONE)` is the stretch of `sl` from position `i` on, and `subslice (sl, i, SOME n)` the `n` elements from `i`.

**Raises** `Subscript` if the positions are outside `sl`.

> **Reading** `VectorSlice.subslice/NONE-Subscript-beyond`. The bounds are
those of `sl`, not of the vector it is a slice of: a subslice cannot
reach back into the rest of the base vector.

**Example** `(fn (_, i, n) => (i, n)) (base (subslice (slice (Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 1, NONE), 1, SOME 2))) = (2, 2)`

members.name: base
members.spec: val base : 'a slice -> 'a Vector.vector * int * int
members.doc:
`base sl` is the triple of the vector that `sl` is a stretch of, where it starts in that vector, and how long it is.

**Example** `base (slice (Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3], 1, SOME 1)) = (Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3], 1, 1)`

members.name: vector
members.doc:
`vector sl` is a vector of the elements of `sl`, which is where the copy happens.

**Example** `vector (slice (Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3], 1, NONE)) = Vector.fromList [2, 3]`

members.name: concat
members.doc:
`concat l` is the vector of the elements of the slices of `l`, one after another.

**Raises** `Size` if the result would be longer than `Vector.maxLen`.

**Example** `concat [full (Vector.fromList [1]), full (Vector.fromList [2, 3])] = Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3]`

members.name: isEmpty
members.doc:
`isEmpty sl` is `true` when `sl` has no elements.

**Example** `isEmpty (slice (Vector.fromList [1], 1, NONE)) = true`

members.name: getItem
members.doc:
`getItem sl` is `NONE` for an empty slice and `SOME (x, rest)` for the first element and what follows it.

It has the shape of a `StringCvt.reader`, so a slice is a stream that a
`scan` function can read from.

**Example** `Option.map #1 (getItem (full (Vector.fromList [7, 8]))) = SOME 7`

members.name: appi
members.doc:
`appi f sl` applies `f` to the index and the element of each position, from 0 up, for its effect.

> **Reading** `VectorSlice.appi/index-in-the-slice`. The index is "that of
the corresponding element in the slice": it starts at 0 whatever the
slice begins at in its base vector. The same holds for `mapi`,
`foldli`, `foldri` and `findi`.

**Example** `let val s = ref [] in appi (fn (i, _) => s := i :: !s) (slice (Vector.fromList [0, 0, 0], 1, NONE)); !s end = [1, 0]`

members.name: app
members.doc:
`app f sl` applies `f` to every element, from 0 up, for its effect.

**Example** `let val s = ref 0 in app (fn x => s := !s + x) (full (Vector.fromList [1, 2])); !s end = 3`

members.name: mapi
members.doc:
`mapi f sl` is the vector of the results of `f` on the index and the element of each position.

**Example** `mapi (fn (i, x) => i + x) (slice (Vector.fromList [5, 6, 7], 1, NONE)) = Vector.fromList [6, 8]`

members.name: map
members.doc:
`map f sl` is the vector of the results of `f` on each element, in order.

**Example** `map (fn x => x + 1) (full (Vector.fromList [1, 2])) = Vector.fromList [2, 3]`

members.name: foldli
members.doc:
`foldli f init sl` combines the elements from the left, giving `f` the index as well.

**Example** `foldli (fn (i, _, acc) => i :: acc) [] (slice (Vector.fromList [9, 9, 9], 1, NONE)) = [1, 0]`

members.name: foldri
members.doc:
`foldri f init sl` combines the elements from the right, giving `f` the index as well.

**Example** `foldri (fn (i, _, acc) => i :: acc) [] (slice (Vector.fromList [9, 9, 9], 1, NONE)) = [0, 1]`

members.name: foldl
members.doc:
`foldl f init sl` combines the elements from the left, as `List.foldl` does.

**Example** `foldl (op ::) [] (full (Vector.fromList [1, 2])) = [2, 1]`

members.name: foldr
members.doc:
`foldr f init sl` combines the elements from the right, as `List.foldr` does.

**Example** `foldr (op ::) [] (full (Vector.fromList [1, 2])) = [1, 2]`

members.name: findi
members.doc:
`findi p sl` is `SOME (i, x)` for the first position whose index and element satisfy `p`, or `NONE`.

**Example** `findi (fn (_, x) => x > 1) (full (Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3])) = SOME (1, 2)`

members.name: find
members.doc:
`find p sl` is `SOME x` for the first element that satisfies `p`, or `NONE`.

**Example** `find (fn x => x > 1) (full (Vector.fromList [1, 2, 3])) = SOME 2`

members.name: exists
members.doc:
`exists p sl` is `true` when some element satisfies `p`.

**Example** `exists (fn x => x = 2) (full (Vector.fromList [1, 2])) = true`

members.name: all
members.doc:
`all p sl` is `true` when every element satisfies `p`.

**Example** `all (fn x => x > 1) (full (Vector.fromList [1, 2])) = false`

members.name: collate
members.spec: val collate : ('a * 'a -> order) -> 'a slice * 'a slice -> order
members.doc:
`collate cmp (sl, tl)` compares the elements of two slices lexicographically with `cmp`.

**Example** `collate Int.compare (full (Vector.fromList [1, 2]), full (Vector.fromList [1, 3])) = LESS`

WINDOWS.doc:
The operating system Windows: the registry, the configuration of the
machine, dynamic data exchange, programs started with a pipe each way, and
the codes a process ends with.

The structure is there on every system, so a program that names it
compiles anywhere. What asks Windows raises `OS.SysErr` on a system that
is not Windows, with the error `ENOSYS`: all of `Reg`, the values
`Config` reads from the machine, `DDE`, `execute` and the group around
it, `getVolumeInformation`, `findExecutable`, `launchApplication` and
`openDocument`. What asks nothing of Windows works everywhere: the flags
of `Key`, the platforms of `Config`, the codes of `Status`, `fromStatus`
and `exit` (below).

**See also** `OS_PROCESS`, `UNIX`, `BIT_FLAGS`, `TEXT_IO`, `BIN_IO`

> **Implementation** `WINDOWS/code-page`. Names, strings of the registry and
paths go to Windows through its code page (the `A` functions of Win32),
byte for byte; a path given as `/C:/...`, as `OS.FileSys` writes the paths
of a drive on Windows, is taken as `C:/...`.

members.name: Key
members.doc:
The rights to ask for when a key of the registry is opened or created,
as a set of flags.

members.name: Key.allAccess
members.doc:
All the rights below: `queryValue`, `enumerateSubKeys`, `notify`,
`createSubKey`, `createLink` and `setValue` together.

> **Implementation** `Windows.Key/the-unions-of-the-page`. `allAccess`,
`read` and `write` are the unions the page gives, without the
standard rights that `KEY_ALL_ACCESS`, `KEY_READ` and `KEY_WRITE` of
Windows add; the others are the `KEY_*` values of Windows.

**Example** `Key.allSet (Key.read, Key.allAccess) = true`

members.name: Key.createLink
members.doc: The right to make a symbolic link; the rest of the structure makes none.

members.name: Key.createSubKey
members.doc: The right to make subkeys.

members.name: Key.enumerateSubKeys
members.doc: The right to enumerate subkeys.

members.name: Key.execute
members.doc: The right to read, the same as `read`.

members.name: Key.notify
members.doc: The right to be told of changes.

members.name: Key.queryValue
members.doc: The right to read values.

members.name: Key.read
members.doc: The rights to read: `queryValue`, `enumerateSubKeys` and `notify` together.

members.name: Key.setValue
members.doc: The right to set values.

members.name: Key.write
members.doc: The rights to write: `setValue` and `createSubKey` together.

members.name: Reg
members.doc:
Keys of the registry: opening, making, deleting, enumerating, and the
values they hold.

members.name: Reg.hkey
members.doc: The type of an open key of the registry.

members.name: Reg.classesRoot
members.doc: The root `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT`: the kinds of files and the programs that open them.

members.name: Reg.currentUser
members.doc: The root `HKEY_CURRENT_USER`: the settings of the user of this process.

members.name: Reg.localMachine
members.doc: The root `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE`: the settings of the machine.

members.name: Reg.users
members.doc: The root `HKEY_USERS`: the settings of every user of the machine.

members.name: Reg.performanceData
members.doc: The root `HKEY_PERFORMANCE_DATA`: counters of performance, read and never kept.

members.name: Reg.currentConfig
members.doc: The root `HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG`: the profile of the hardware the machine runs with.

members.name: Reg.dynData
members.doc: The root `HKEY_DYN_DATA` of Windows 95 and 98, which no Windows of today opens.

members.name: Reg.create_result
members.spec:
datatype create_result
  = CREATED_NEW_KEY of hkey
  | OPENED_EXISTING_KEY of hkey
members.doc: What `createKeyEx` did.

members.name: Reg.createKeyEx
members.spec: val createKeyEx : hkey * string * Key.flags -> create_result
members.doc:
`createKeyEx (hkey, skey, regsam)` opens the subkey `skey` of `hkey` with the rights `regsam`, making it when it is not there.

The key is not volatile, and has no class and the default security,
as the page asks.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the key cannot be made or opened, as without
the right to.

members.name: Reg.openKeyEx
members.spec: val openKeyEx : hkey * string * Key.flags -> hkey
members.doc:
`openKeyEx (hkey, skey, regsam)` opens the subkey `skey` of `hkey` with the rights `regsam`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if there is no such key, or it may not be opened so.

members.name: Reg.closeKey
members.doc:
`closeKey hkey` closes the key `hkey`; a key at a root is left open.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `hkey` is not open.

members.name: Reg.deleteKey
members.doc:
`deleteKey (hkey, skey)` deletes the subkey `skey` of `hkey`, which may have no subkeys itself.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if there is no such key, it has subkeys, or it may not be deleted.

members.name: Reg.deleteValue
members.doc:
`deleteValue (hkey, valname)` deletes the value `valname` of `hkey`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if there is no such value, or it may not be deleted.

members.name: Reg.enumKeyEx
members.spec: val enumKeyEx : hkey * int -> string option
members.doc:
`enumKeyEx (hkey, ind)` is the name of the subkey number `ind` of `hkey`, counted from zero, or `NONE` past the last.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `ind` is negative.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the key cannot be read.

members.name: Reg.enumValueEx
members.spec: val enumValueEx : hkey * int -> string option
members.doc:
`enumValueEx (hkey, ind)` is the name of the value number `ind` of `hkey`, counted from zero, or `NONE` past the last.

**Raises** `Subscript` if `ind` is negative.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the key cannot be read.

members.name: Reg.value
members.spec:
datatype value
  = SZ of string
  | DWORD of SysWord.word
  | BINARY of Word8Vector.vector
  | MULTI_SZ of string list
  | EXPAND_SZ of string
members.doc: A value of the registry, by its kind.

members.name: Reg.queryValueEx
members.spec: val queryValueEx : hkey * string -> value option
members.doc:
`queryValueEx (hkey, name)` is the value `name` of `hkey`, or `NONE` when it has none of that name.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` for any other failure, as for want of the right to read.

members.name: Reg.setValueEx
members.spec: val setValueEx : hkey * string * value -> unit
members.doc:
`setValueEx (hkey, name, v)` sets the value `name` of `hkey` to `v`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if it may not.

members.name: Config
members.doc: What the system is, where it is kept, and who uses it.

members.name: Config.platformWin32s
members.doc: The platform Win32s, 32 bits on Windows 3.1, as `getVersionEx` names it.

members.name: Config.platformWin32Windows
members.doc: The platform of Windows 95, 98 and Me.

members.name: Config.platformWin32NT
members.doc: The platform of Windows NT and of every Windows since, which is what `getVersionEx` says today.

members.name: Config.platformWin32CE
members.doc: The platform of Windows CE.

members.name: Config.getVersionEx
members.spec:
val getVersionEx : unit -> {majorVersion : SysWord.word, minorVersion : SysWord.word,
                            buildNumber : SysWord.word, platformId : SysWord.word, csdVersion : string}
members.doc:
`getVersionEx ()` is the version of Windows: major, minor and build, the platform, and the service pack.

> **Implementation** `Windows.Config.getVersionEx/the-real-version`. The
version is the one Windows is, as `RtlGetVersion` gives it, and not
the one a program's manifest would make `GetVersionEx` answer: 10.0
and its build on Windows 11 too.

members.name: Config.getWindowsDirectory
members.doc: `getWindowsDirectory ()` is the directory of Windows, as Windows writes it: `C:\Windows`.

members.name: Config.getSystemDirectory
members.doc: `getSystemDirectory ()` is the system directory of Windows, as Windows writes it: `C:\Windows\system32`.

members.name: Config.getComputerName
members.doc: `getComputerName ()` is the name of the computer.

members.name: Config.getUserName
members.doc: `getUserName ()` is the name of the user of this process.

members.name: DDE
members.doc:
A client of DDE: a conversation with a service, on a topic, in which
commands are executed, each transaction waiting for its answer.

members.name: DDE.info
members.doc: The type of a conversation.

members.name: DDE.startDialog
members.doc:
`startDialog (service, topic)` starts a conversation with `service` on `topic`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if no service of that name answers on that topic.

members.name: DDE.executeString
members.spec: val executeString : info * string * int * Time.time -> unit
members.doc:
`executeString (info, cmd, retry, delay)` has the service of `info` execute `cmd`, trying again `retry` times, `delay` apart, while it is busy.

Each try waits for the service's answer for as long as `delay`, and
the tries are `delay` apart.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the command fails, or the service stays busy.

members.name: DDE.stopDialog
members.doc:
`stopDialog info` ends the conversation `info`.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if it has ended already.

members.name: getVolumeInformation
members.spec:
val getVolumeInformation : string -> {volumeName : string, systemName : string,
                                      serialNumber : SysWord.word, maximumComponentLength : int}
members.doc:
`getVolumeInformation root` is what Windows says of the volume whose root is `root`.

The name of the volume, the name of its file system (`NTFS`), its
serial number, and the longest name a file on it may have.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `root` is not the root of a volume.

members.name: findExecutable
members.doc: `findExecutable name` is the program Windows opens the file `name` with, or `NONE` when there is none.

members.name: launchApplication
members.doc:
`launchApplication (file, arg)` starts the program `file` with the argument `arg`, and does not wait for it.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if `file` is not a program, or cannot be started.

members.name: openDocument
members.doc:
`openDocument file` opens `file` with the program Windows opens it with.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if there is no such file or no such program.

members.name: simpleExecute
members.doc:
`simpleExecute (cmd, arg)` runs the program `cmd` with the arguments `arg`, and is its status when it ends.

It reads from the null device and writes to it; its standard error is
this process's.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the program cannot be started.

members.name: proc
members.doc:
The type of a program started by `execute`, with the streams that talk to it.

The first type variable is the stream its output is read through, the
second the stream its input is written through.

members.name: execute
members.doc:
`execute (cmd, arg)` starts the program `cmd` with the arguments `arg`, with a pipe each way.

Its standard error is this process's; this process's ends of the pipes
are not handed to programs started later.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the program cannot be started.

members.name: textInstreamOf
members.doc: `textInstreamOf pr` is a text stream from which what `pr` writes is read.

members.name: binInstreamOf
members.doc: `binInstreamOf pr` is a binary stream from which what `pr` writes is read.

members.name: textOutstreamOf
members.doc: `textOutstreamOf pr` is a text stream to which what `pr` reads is written.

members.name: binOutstreamOf
members.doc: `binOutstreamOf pr` is a binary stream to which what `pr` reads is written.

members.name: reap
members.doc:
`reap pr` closes the pipes of `pr`, waits for it to end, and is the code it ended with.

Reaping it again gives the same status at once, as the page asks.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` if the wait fails.

members.name: Status
members.doc:
The codes with which Windows ends a process that an exception ends:
the `STATUS_*` codes of Windows.

members.name: Status.status
members.doc: The type of the code a process ended with.

members.name: Status.accessViolation
members.doc: A read or write of memory the process may not touch, `STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION`.

members.name: Status.arrayBoundsExceeded
members.doc: An index beyond the bounds of an array, found by the processor, `STATUS_ARRAY_BOUNDS_EXCEEDED`.

members.name: Status.breakpoint
members.doc: A breakpoint reached with no debugger to take it, `STATUS_BREAKPOINT`.

members.name: Status.controlCExit
members.doc: The end of a program at ^C or at the close of its console, `STATUS_CONTROL_C_EXIT`.

members.name: Status.datatypeMisalignment
members.doc: Data read or written at an address it may not be at, `STATUS_DATATYPE_MISALIGNMENT`.

members.name: Status.floatDenormalOperand
members.doc: A denormal operand of floating point, `STATUS_FLOAT_DENORMAL_OPERAND`.

members.name: Status.floatDivideByZero
members.doc: A division of floating point by zero, `STATUS_FLOAT_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO`.

members.name: Status.floatInexactResult
members.doc: A result of floating point that is not exact, `STATUS_FLOAT_INEXACT_RESULT`.

members.name: Status.floatInvalidOperation
members.doc: An invalid operation of floating point, `STATUS_FLOAT_INVALID_OPERATION`.

members.name: Status.floatOverflow
members.doc: An overflow of floating point, `STATUS_FLOAT_OVERFLOW`.

members.name: Status.floatStackCheck
members.doc: The stack of the floating-point unit over- or underflowed, `STATUS_FLOAT_STACK_CHECK`.

members.name: Status.floatUnderflow
members.doc: An underflow of floating point, `STATUS_FLOAT_UNDERFLOW`.

members.name: Status.guardPageViolation
members.doc: A guard page of memory touched, `STATUS_GUARD_PAGE_VIOLATION`.

members.name: Status.integerDivideByZero
members.doc: A division of integers by zero, `STATUS_INTEGER_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO`.

members.name: Status.integerOverflow
members.doc: An overflow of integers, `STATUS_INTEGER_OVERFLOW`.

members.name: Status.illegalInstruction
members.doc: An instruction the processor does not have, `STATUS_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION`.

members.name: Status.invalidDisposition
members.doc: A handler of exceptions that answered what it may not, `STATUS_INVALID_DISPOSITION`.

members.name: Status.invalidHandle
members.doc: A handle that is not open, `STATUS_INVALID_HANDLE`.

members.name: Status.inPageError
members.doc: A page of memory that could not be read in, `STATUS_IN_PAGE_ERROR`.

members.name: Status.noncontinuableException
members.doc: An exception continued that may not be, `STATUS_NONCONTINUABLE_EXCEPTION`.

members.name: Status.pending
members.doc: An operation that has not ended yet, `STATUS_PENDING`.

members.name: Status.privilegedInstruction
members.doc: An instruction only the system may execute, `STATUS_PRIVILEGED_INSTRUCTION`.

members.name: Status.singleStep
members.doc: A step of a program traced with no debugger to take it, `STATUS_SINGLE_STEP`.

members.name: Status.stackOverflow
members.doc: The stack of a thread overflowed, `STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW`.

members.name: Status.timeout
members.doc: A wait that ran out of time, `STATUS_TIMEOUT`.

members.name: Status.userAPC
members.doc: A wait ended by a call queued for the thread, `STATUS_USER_APC`.

members.name: fromStatus
members.doc: `fromStatus s` is the code of Windows that the status `s` stands for.

members.name: exit
members.doc:
`exit st` runs the actions of `OS.Process.atExit`, flushes and closes the files, and ends this program with the code `st`.

> **Implementation** `Windows.exit/the-code-off-windows`. This is one of the
values that need no Windows, and the program ends with `st` wherever it
runs; but a system of POSIX gives a parent the low eight bits of a code
alone, where Windows gives the whole of it, which is what `reap` reads
back.

WORD.doc:
Words: integers of a fixed number of bits, without a sign, whose
arithmetic wraps round instead of overflowing, and which can be taken
apart bit by bit.

A word of `wordSize` bits holds the numbers from 0 to `2^wordSize - 1`;
every operation that would leave that range is taken modulo `2^wordSize`,
so nothing raises `Overflow` but the conversions to a type that cannot
hold the value. This is the type for bit sets, masks, hashes and whatever
is counted in bits rather than in numbers.

Where a word is read as a signed number (`toIntX`, `toLargeX`, `~>>`) the
top bit is the sign, as in two's complement. The functions with an `X` in
their name are those that sign-extend; the others fill with zeros.

The structures differ in their width: `Word` is the default one and
`Word8`, `Word16`, `Word32` and `Word64` are the sized ones; `LargeWord`
is the widest, and `SysWord` is what the operating system's flags and
numbers are counted in.

**See also** `INTEGER`, `INT_INF`, `BYTE`, `STRING_CVT`, `PACK_WORD`

members.name: word
members.doc:
The type of words of this structure.

> **Implementation** `Word.word/63-bits`. `Word.word` is the top-level `word`,
of 63 bits -- a word of the machine less the bit that tells a number from
a pointer. `Word64`, which is also `LargeWord`, has 64 bits on every
machine, and so has `SysWord`, a type of its own beside it: a word of
theirs is kept in a word of the machine where it fits 63 bits and in a
small object where it needs the 64th. `Word8`, `Word16` and `Word32` are
kept in a word of the machine whose upper bits are zero.

> **Implementation** `Word.word/constants-overloaded`. A word constant has the
word type that its context asks for, `Word8.word` as well as `word`, and
is checked against the range of that type when the program is compiled;
`~` is there for words too. Integer constants are overloaded at
`IntInf.int` and the `IntN`, real ones at `Real32.real`, and character and
string constants at `WideChar.char` and `WideString.string`.

members.name: wordSize
members.doc:
`wordSize` is the number of bits of a word of this structure.

**Example** `Word8.wordSize = 8` and `Word.wordSize = 63`

**Example** `Word64.wordSize = 64` and `LargeWord.wordSize = 64`

members.name: toLarge
members.doc:
`toLarge w` is `w` as a word of `LargeWord`, with zeros in the bits above `wordSize`.

**Law** `fromLarge (toLarge w) = w`

**Example** `Word8.toLarge 0wxFF = 0wxFF`

members.name: toLargeX
members.doc:
`toLargeX w` is `w` as a word of `LargeWord`, with the top bit of `w` copied into the bits above it.

**Law** `toLargeX w = toLarge w` when `w < << (0w1, Word.fromInt (Int.- (wordSize, 1)))`

**Example** `Word8.toLargeX 0wxFF = 0wxFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF` in Rune, where
`LargeWord.wordSize = 64`

members.name: toLargeWord
members.doc: `toLargeWord w` is another name for `toLarge`, which the specification deprecates.

members.name: toLargeWordX
members.doc: `toLargeWordX w` is another name for `toLargeX`, which the specification deprecates.

members.name: fromLarge
members.doc:
`fromLarge w` is the word of this structure with the low `wordSize` bits of `w`.

What does not fit is dropped: nothing is raised.

**Example** `Word8.fromLarge 0wx1FF = 0wxFF`

members.name: fromLargeWord
members.doc: `fromLargeWord w` is another name for `fromLarge`, which the specification deprecates.

members.name: toLargeInt
members.doc:
`toLargeInt w` is the number that `w` stands for, between 0 and `2^wordSize - 1`.

**Raises** `Overflow` if that number is no `LargeInt.int`, which cannot
happen where `LargeInt` is `IntInf`.

**Example** `Word8.toLargeInt 0wxFF = 255`

members.name: toLargeIntX
members.doc:
`toLargeIntX w` is the number that `w` stands for read as a signed one, between `~(2^(wordSize-1))` and `2^(wordSize-1) - 1`.

It never raises: `LargeInt` is at least as wide as every word.

**Example** `Word8.toLargeIntX 0wxFF = ~1`

members.name: fromLargeInt
members.doc:
`fromLargeInt i` is the word with the low `wordSize` bits of `i`.

A negative `i` is taken in two's complement, and what does not fit is
dropped.

**Law** `fromLargeInt (toLargeIntX w) = w`

**Example** `Word8.fromLargeInt ~1 = 0wxFF`

members.name: toInt
members.doc:
`toInt w` is the number that `w` stands for as an `Int.int`.

**Raises** `Overflow` if that number is outside the range of `Int.int`,
which a word as wide as an `int` can reach.

**Example** `Word8.toInt 0wxFF = 255`

**Example** `(Word64.toInt 0wxFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF handle Overflow => ~1) = ~1`

members.name: toIntX
members.doc:
`toIntX w` is the number that `w` stands for read as a signed one, as an `Int.int`.

**Raises** `Overflow` if that number is outside the range of `Int.int`.

**Example** `Word8.toIntX 0wxFF = ~1`, where `Word8.toInt 0wxFF = 255`.

members.name: fromInt
members.doc:
`fromInt i` is the word with the low `wordSize` bits of `i`.

A negative `i` is taken in two's complement.

**Example** `Word8.fromInt 256 = 0w0`

members.name: andb
members.doc:
`andb (a, b)` is the bitwise "and".

**Example** `andb (0wxF0, 0wx3C) = 0wx30`

members.name: orb
members.doc:
`orb (a, b)` is the bitwise "or".

**Example** `orb (0wxF0, 0wx0F) = 0wxFF`

members.name: xorb
members.doc:
`xorb (a, b)` is the bitwise exclusive "or".

**Example** `xorb (0wxFF, 0wx0F) = 0wxF0`

members.name: notb
members.doc:
`notb w` is `w` with every bit inverted.

**Law** `notb w = ~w - 0w1`

**Example** `Word64.notb 0w0 = 0wxFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF`

**Example** `Word.notb 0w0 = 0wx7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF`

`<< (w, n)` is `w` shifted left by `n` bits, with zeros coming in and what leaves the width dropped.

A shift of `wordSize` bits or more gives 0.

**Law** `<< (w, n) = w * (let fun pow e = if e = 0w0 then 0w1 else let val h = pow (Word.>> (e, 0w1)) in if Word.andb (e, 0w1) = 0w1 then 0w2 * h * h else h * h end in pow n end)`: `w` times 2 to the `n`, in the arithmetic
of this structure

**Example** `<< (0w1, 0w4) = 0w16`

**Example** `Word.<< (0w1, 0w64) = 0w0` for every bit is shifted out.

`>> (w, n)` is `w` shifted right by `n` bits, with zeros coming in.

A shift of `wordSize` bits or more gives 0.

**Law** `>> (w, n) = (if LargeInt.>= (Word.toLargeInt n, LargeInt.fromInt wordSize) then 0w0 else fromLargeInt (LargeInt.div (toLargeInt w, IntInf.pow (2, Word.toInt n))))`: `w` divided by 2 to the `n`

**Example** `Word8.>> (0wx80, 0w1) = 0wx40`

`~>> (w, n)` is `w` shifted right by `n` bits, with the top bit of `w` coming in.

A shift of `wordSize` bits or more gives 0 for a word whose top bit is
clear and a word of all ones for one whose top bit is set: it is the
division of a signed number by a power of two, rounded towards negative
infinity.

**Example** `Word8.~>> (0wx80, 0w1) = 0wxC0`

`a + b` is the sum, taken modulo `2^wordSize`.

**Example** `Word8.+ (0wxFF, 0w1) = 0w0`

`a - b` is the difference, taken modulo `2^wordSize`: it wraps round for `a < b`.

**Example** `Word64.- (0w0, 0w1) = 0wxFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF`

**Example** `Word.- (0w0, 0w1) = 0wx7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF`

`a * b` is the product, taken modulo `2^wordSize`.

**Example** `Word8.* (0wx10, 0wx10) = 0w0`

members.name: div
members.doc:
`a div b` is the quotient of two unsigned numbers, rounded down.

**Raises** `Div` if `b` is zero.

**Example** `0w7 div 0w2 = 0w3`

**Example** `(0w1 div 0w0 handle Div => 0w9) = 0w9`

members.name: mod
members.doc:
`a mod b` is what `div` leaves over.

**Raises** `Div` if `b` is zero.

**Law** `(a div b) * b + (a mod b) = a` for `b <> 0w0`

**Example** `0w7 mod 0w2 = 0w1`

**Counterexample** `(0w1 div 0w0) * 0w0 + (0w1 mod 0w0) = 0w1`, for there is
no dividing by zero.

members.name: compare
members.doc:
`compare (a, b)` orders two words as unsigned numbers.

**Example** `Word8.compare (0wxFF, 0w1) = GREATER`

`a < b`, `a <= b`, `a > b` and `a >= b` compare two words as unsigned numbers.

A word whose top bit is set is the larger, not the smaller: at `Word8`,
`0wxFF > 0w1`.

`a < b`, `a <= b`, `a > b` and `a >= b` compare two words as unsigned numbers.

A word whose top bit is set is the larger, not the smaller: at `Word8`,
`0wxFF > 0w1`.

`a < b`, `a <= b`, `a > b` and `a >= b` compare two words as unsigned numbers.

A word whose top bit is set is the larger, not the smaller: at `Word8`,
`0wxFF > 0w1`.

`a < b`, `a <= b`, `a > b` and `a >= b` compare two words as unsigned numbers.

A word whose top bit is set is the larger, not the smaller: at `Word8`,
`0wxFF > 0w1`.

`~w` is the negation modulo `2^wordSize`: the two's complement of `w`.

**Law** `~w = notb w + 0w1`, and `~ 0w0 = 0w0`

**Example** `Word8.~ 0w1 = 0wxFF`

members.name: min
members.doc:
`min (a, b)` is the smaller of the two, as unsigned numbers.

**Example** `Word8.min (0wx80, 0w1) = 0w1`

members.name: max
members.doc:
`max (a, b)` is the larger of the two, as unsigned numbers.

**Example** `Word8.max (0wx80, 0w1) = 0wx80`

members.name: fmt
members.doc:
`fmt radix w` is the text of `w` in the given base, without a prefix and without a sign.

The hexadecimal digits above 9 are the capitals `A` to `F`.

> **Erratum** `WORD/fmt-Ow`. The specification writes the hexadecimal prefix
of the samples as `Ow` with the letter O; it is `0w` with the digit
zero.

**Example** `fmt StringCvt.HEX 0w255 = "FF"`

members.name: toString
members.doc:
`toString w` is the text of `w` in base 16, with the digits `A` to `F` and no prefix.

**Law** `toString w = fmt StringCvt.HEX w`

**Example** `toString 0w255 = "FF"`

members.name: scan
members.doc:
`scan radix getc strm` reads a word in the given base from `strm`.

It skips initial white space and then takes an optional prefix and the
digits: `0w` in the bases other than `StringCvt.HEX`, and in that one
`0wx`, `0wX`, `0x` or `0X`, where `0w` alone is no prefix: of `"0w1F"`
the zero is read. There is no sign. The answer is `SOME (w, rest)`, or `NONE`
when no digit is there.

**Raises** `Overflow` if the digits name a number of more than `wordSize`
bits.

> **Reading** `Word.scan/DEC-bare-prefix-0w`. A prefix that no digit follows
is not a prefix, but its leading `0` is a digit: `"0wxg"` scans as 0 and
leaves `"wxg"`.

**Example** `Option.map #1 (scan StringCvt.BIN Substring.getc (Substring.full "0w101")) = SOME 0w5`

members.name: fromString
members.doc:
`fromString s` is the word that the text `s` begins with in base 16, or `NONE`.

**Raises** `Overflow` if the digits name a number of more than `wordSize` bits.

**Law** `fromString s = StringCvt.scanString (scan StringCvt.HEX) s`

**Example** `fromString "0wxff" = SOME 0w255`

**Example** `fromString "ff" = SOME 0w255`
